title: Jewish believers have not left the law
english: In the first book of our dictated reply to Celsus’s work entitled The True Doctrine, we ended at the speech addressed to Jesus that Celsus puts in the mouth of his Jew, since that book had reached a sufficient length. This book we choose to compose, making our defence against the charges he brings against those from the people of the Jews who have believed in Jesus. And this is the very first thing we note: why, having once decided to bring on a character, Celsus does not have his Jew speak to those who believe from among the Gentiles, but to those from among the Jews. Yet his argument would have seemed most persuasive had it been written against us. But perhaps the man who professes to know everything did not see what consistency required in the speech he gave his character.

Let us consider, then, what he says to those from among the Jews who believe. He says that they have left the law of their fathers, that, beguiled by Jesus, they have been quite ridiculously deceived, and that they have deserted to another name and another way of life. He did not even notice that those from among the Jews who believe in Jesus have not left the law of their fathers. For they live by it, and they have come to be named after the poverty of their interpretation of the law. For among the Jews the poor man is called Ebion, and those from among the Jews who have accepted Jesus as the Christ are called Ebionites.

Peter too appears to have kept for a long time the Jewish customs that follow the law of Moses, since he had not yet learned from Jesus to rise from the law according to the letter to the law according to the spirit. This we have learned from the Acts of the Apostles. For on the day after an angel of God had appeared to Cornelius, telling him to send “to Joppa” for Simon called Peter (Acts 10:3–5), “Peter went up to the upper room to pray, about the sixth hour. And he became hungry and wanted to eat. While they were preparing it, a trance came upon him, and he saw heaven opened and a vessel coming down, like a great sheet, let down by its four corners upon the earth; and in it were all the four-footed creatures and creeping things of the earth and the birds of the sky. And a voice came to him: ‘Rise, Peter, kill and eat.’ But Peter said, ‘By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common and unclean.’ And a voice came to him a second time: ‘What God has cleansed, you must not call common’ ” (Acts 10:9–15).

See in these words how Peter is presented as still keeping the Jewish customs about clean and unclean. And what follows makes clear that he needed a vision so that he would share the words of faith with Cornelius, who was not an Israelite according to the flesh, and with those who were with him; for he was still a Jew, living by the traditions of the Jews and looking down on those outside Judaism (Acts 10:28).

In the Epistle to the Galatians, too, Paul shows that Peter, still afraid of the Jews, stopped eating with the Gentiles, and when James came to him “he separated himself” from the Gentiles, “fearing those of the circumcision”; and the rest of the Jews and Barnabas did the same as he did (Galatians 2:12–13). And it was consistent that those who had been sent to the circumcision should not depart from the Jewish customs, when “those who were reputed to be pillars gave to Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship,” and went off themselves “to the circumcision,” so that those two might preach to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:9).

But why do I say that those who preached “to the circumcision” drew back and separated themselves from the Gentiles, when Paul himself also became “to the Jews a Jew, that he might win Jews” (1 Corinthians 9:20)? That is why, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles, he even brought an offering to the altar, to persuade the Jews that he was not an apostate from the law (Acts 21:21–26).

If Celsus had known all this, he would not have made his Jew say to those from Judaism who believe: “What possessed you, my fellow citizens, to leave the law of your fathers, and, beguiled by that man with whom we were just now arguing, to be so ridiculously deceived, and to desert us for another name and another way of life?”

title: The many things the disciples could not yet bear
english: Since we have now come to speak of Peter and of those who taught Christianity to the people of the circumcision, I think it not out of place to set down a saying of Jesus from the Gospel according to John, with its interpretation. It is written that he said: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when he comes, the Spirit of truth, he will guide you into all the truth; for he will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will speak” (John 16:12–13).

And we ask in this passage what the “many things” were that Jesus had “to say” to his disciples, but which they could not then “bear.” And I say: perhaps, since the apostles were Jews and had been brought up in the law of Moses according to the letter, he had “to say” to them what the true law is, and of what “heavenly things” the worship among the Jews was carried out “as a copy and shadow” (Hebrews 8:5), and of what “good things to come” the law about eating and drinking, festivals, new moons and sabbaths contained “a shadow” (Hebrews 10:1; Colossians 2:16–17). And these were the “many things” that he had “to say” to them.

But he saw that it is very hard to uproot from the soul doctrines that have been almost born with a man and brought up with him to the age of manhood, and that have persuaded those who received them that they are divine and that to unsettle them is impious; and very hard to prove them, by the surpassing worth of the “knowledge” that accords with Christ, that is, with the truth, to be “refuse” and “loss” (Philippians 3:7–8), so that the hearers would be persuaded. So he put it off to a more suitable time, the time after his passion and resurrection. For truly the help would have been offered out of season to those not yet able to receive it, since it would have overturned the conception of Jesus they had already received, that he was the Christ and the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16).

And consider whether understanding the words “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” in this way does not yield a meaning that is far from contemptible. For the “many things” are those that belong to the interpretation and clarification of the law in its spiritual sense; and at that time the disciples, born and brought up among the Jews, were somehow unable to “bear” them.

I think too that, because those things were a type, while what the Holy Spirit was going to teach them was the truth, it was for this reason said: “When he comes, the Spirit of truth, he will guide you into all the truth” (John 16:13), as if he were saying: into all the truth of the realities, while you, being occupied with their types, supposed that you were offering God the true worship.

And according to the promise of Jesus, “the Spirit of truth” came upon Peter, saying to him about the four-footed creatures and creeping things of the earth and the birds of the sky: “Rise, Peter, kill and eat” (Acts 10:13). And the Spirit came to him while he was still superstitious; for even to the divine voice he says: “By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common and unclean” (Acts 10:14). And he taught the doctrine of true and spiritual foods in the words “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts 10:15). And after that vision “the Spirit of truth,” guiding Peter “into all the truth,” told him the many things that he could not “bear” while Jesus was still with him in the flesh. But there will be another occasion for explaining these matters, which concern the interpretation of the law of Moses.

No LXX renumbering arises in this chapter.

title: Celsus’s ignorance of Jewish believers
english: But our present task is to expose the ignorance of Celsus, in whose book the Jew says to his fellow citizens and Israelites who have believed in Jesus: “What possessed you to leave the law of your fathers?” and what follows. Yet how have they left the law of their fathers who rebuke those who do not hear it, and say: “Tell me, you who read the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons,” as far as “which things are spoken as an allegory,” and what follows (Galatians 4:21–24)? And how have they left the law of their fathers who in their discourses always call to mind the heritage of their fathers, and say: “Or does not the law also say these things? For it is written in the law of Moses: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain’ (Deuteronomy 25:4). Is it for oxen that God cares? Or is he speaking altogether for our sake? For it was written for our sake,” and what follows (1 Corinthians 9:8–10)?

And how confusedly the Jew in Celsus says these things! He could have said more plausibly that some of you have left the customs on the pretext of interpretations and allegories; that others of you, while interpreting spiritually, as you profess, keep the customs of your fathers none the less; and that others of you, without interpreting, wish both to accept Jesus as the one foretold in prophecy and to keep the law of Moses as your fathers did, as though you had the whole meaning of the spirit in the wording.

But how could Celsus have made the facts of this matter plain? In what follows he made mention of godless sects wholly alien to Jesus, and of others that abandon the Creator, yet he did not know that there are also Israelites who believe in Jesus and have not left the law of their fathers. For it was not his aim to examine with a love of truth all that bears on the subject, so as to accept anything useful he might find. Rather, as an enemy, and one wholly bent on overthrowing such things the moment he heard them, he wrote them down.

title: The law as the beginning of the Gospel
english: Next, the Jew in his book says to those from the people who have believed: “Only yesterday or the day before, when we were punishing this man who was duping you, you turned away from the law of your fathers.” He said this without any accurate knowledge of what he was talking about, as we have shown.

After this, the following seems to me to show some cleverness: “Or how is it that you begin from our sacred writings, yet as you go on you dishonour them, though you can name no other starting point for your doctrine than our law?”

For it is true that for Christians the introduction comes from the sacred writings of Moses and the writings of the prophets; and after the introduction, the progress of those being introduced lies in the interpretation and clarification of these writings, as they seek the mystery “according to revelation,” “kept in silence through eternal ages,” but “now made manifest” in the words of the prophets and in the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 16:25–26). But those who advance do not, as you claim, dishonour what is written in the law. Rather they bestow greater honour on it, showing how great a depth of wise and secret sayings is held by those writings, which the Jews have not contemplated, since they read them rather superficially and as if they were myths.

And what is out of place in the law being the beginning of our doctrine, that is, of the gospel? For our Lord himself says to those who did not believe in him: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (John 5:46–47). Moreover, one of the evangelists, Mark, says: “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you’ ” (Mark 1:1–2; Malachi 3:1; Exodus 23:20), showing that the beginning of the gospel depends on the Jewish writings.

What, then, is said against us by Celsus’s Jew in the words: “For if anyone foretold to you that the Son of God would come to men, that prophet was ours, and our God’s”? And what charge against Christianity is it if John, who baptized Jesus, was a Jew (Matthew 3:13–17)? For it does not follow, because he was a Jew, that every believer, whether he comes to the word from the Gentiles or from the Jews, must keep the law of Moses according to the letter.

title: The kingdom given to the Gentiles
english: After this, although Celsus repeats himself about Jesus, saying now for the second time that he did wrong and paid the penalty at the hands of the Jews, we will not repeat our defence, but rest content with what we said before.

Next, his Jew belittles as stale the teaching about the resurrection of the dead, the judgment of God, and honour for the righteous but fire for the unrighteous; and by claiming that Christians are taught nothing new in these matters, he thinks he overturns Christianity. We must say to him that our Jesus, seeing that the Jews were doing nothing worthy of the lessons in the prophets, taught by a parable that “the kingdom of God” would be “taken away” from them “and given” to those from the Gentiles (Matthew 21:43). That is why one can truly see that all the teachings of the Jews of today are myths and idle talk, for they do not have the light of the knowledge of the Scriptures, while the teachings of Christians are truth. These are able to lift up and raise on high the soul and mind of a human being, and they persuade him to have a “citizenship” not like that of the Jews, somewhere here below, but “in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). This is evident among those who contemplate the greatness of the meanings in the law and the prophets, and who are able to present them to others.
translator_notes: The full stop printed after Ἰησοῦ in the staged text is treated as a comma; the sentence continues. Celsus’s charge in the first sentence is indirect speech in the Greek, so it is not put in quotation marks. Matthew 21:43 (end of the parable of the tenants, Matthew 21:33-43) reads ἀρθήσεται ἀφ’ ὑμῶν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ δοθήσεται ἔθνει; Origen paraphrases with ‘those from the Gentiles’. ‘The light of the knowledge’ may echo 2 Corinthians 4:6 (φωτισμὸν τῆς γνώσεως); not certain enough for an inline citation. The text repeats κάτω (‘below ... somewhere below’), possibly a scribal doubling; rendered once as ‘somewhere here below’. Origen’s polemic against the Jews of his day is translated as written, without softening.

title: Jewish customs and the hidden sense of the law
english: Let it be granted that Jesus kept all the customs of the Jews, even down to their sacrifices: what does this contribute to the claim that we should not believe in him as the Son of God? Jesus, then, is the Son of the God who gave the law and the prophets; and we who belong to the Church do not transgress that law. Rather, we have fled from the myth-making of the Jews, and we are disciplined and taught by the mystical contemplation of the law and the prophets.

For the prophets themselves do not let the meaning of what they say come to rest in the plain narrative, nor in the legislation that follows the words and the letter. In one place, when they are supposedly about to recount history, they say: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter riddles from the beginning” (Psalm 78:2). In another, praying about the law as obscure and as needing God for it to be understood, they say in prayer: “Unveil my eyes, and I will perceive your wonders out of your law” (Psalm 119:18).
translator_notes: LXX renumbering: Psalm 77:2 LXX = Psalm 78:2 English; Psalm 118:18 LXX = Psalm 119:18 English. Both quotations agree word for word with the LXX. τοῦτον οὐχ ὑπερβαίνομεν: the nearest masculine nouns are θεοῦ, Ἰησοῦς and νόμον; since ὑπερβαίνω is the usual verb for transgressing a law and Celsus’s charge is that Christians abandon the ancestral law, it is taken as ‘that law’. The sentence ‘Let it be granted ...’ answers Celsus’s claim (just before) that Jesus kept the Jewish customs; Celsus’s own words are not quoted in this chapter. The opening of the second paragraph is an anacoluthon in the Greek (καὶ γὰρ οἱ προφῆται ... ὅπου μέν φασιν ... ὅπου δέ ... λέγουσιν); rendered as two finished sentences.

title: Jesus was not boastful, false or unholy
english: Let them show where in Jesus there is found even a hint of a word spoken out of arrogance. For how is he arrogant who says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29)? Or how is he arrogant who, “during supper” (John 13:2), took off his garment in the presence of his disciples, tied a “towel” around himself, poured “water into the basin” (John 13:4–5), washed the “feet” of each one, rebuked the one who was unwilling to offer his, and said: “If I do not wash you, you have no part with me” (John 13:8)? Or how is he arrogant who says: “And I was among you, not as the one who reclines at table, but as the one who serves” (Luke 22:27)?

Let someone prove what lies he told, and set out which lies are great and which small, so as to show that Jesus told the great ones. There is also another way to refute the Jew: just as no lie is more of a lie than another, so neither is one lie greater than another; just as no truth is more true than another, or more greatly true.

And let Celsus’s Jew, above all, declare what Jesus’ unholy deeds were. Or is it unholy to draw people away from bodily circumcision, a bodily sabbath, bodily feasts, bodily new moons, and clean and unclean things, and to turn the mind toward a law that is worthy of God, true and spiritual (Romans 7:14), while the one who is an ambassador “for Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:20) knows how to become a Jew “to the Jews, that he may win Jews”, and “to those under the law as under the law, that he may win those under the law” (1 Corinthians 9:20)?
translator_notes: Origen answers Celsus’s Jew, who had charged (just before this chapter) that Jesus was boastful, told great lies and did unholy things; ‘the great ones’ echoes the Jew’s phrase τὰ μεγάλα ψευσάμενον, kept unquoted because Origen reports it indirectly. Matthew 11:29: ὅτι rendered ‘for’, as in the Gospel. John 13:2-8 is cited by phrases (δείπνου γινομένου, λέντιον, ὕδωρ εἰς τὸν νιπτῆρα, τοὺς πόδας, ἐὰν μὴ νίψω σε...); ἐκδυσάμενος is Origen’s paraphrase of τίθησιν τὰ ἱμάτια (13:4). Luke 22:27 is paraphrased (Gospel: ἐγὼ δὲ ἐν μέσῳ ὑμῶν εἰμι ὡς ὁ διακονῶν, after ‘who is greater, the one who reclines or the one who serves?’). ‘Spiritual law’ is a clear allusion to Romans 7:14 (ὁ νόμος πνευματικός ἐστιν). The list sabbath, feasts, new moons, clean and unclean may also echo Colossians 2:16; left uncited inline as uncertain. καθαρῶν καὶ ἀκαθάρτων has no noun; rendered ‘clean and unclean things’ (food laws are meant). ‘To refute him’ (αὐτὸν ἐλέγξαι): the person refuted is the Jew, made explicit in Pass B. Luke 22:27: κἀγὼ ἐγενόμην is ‘and I was’, not ‘I too’. The lie/truth sentence keeps Origen’s pair μᾶλλον (‘more’) and μειζόνως (‘greater, more greatly’).

title: Why the one foretold was rejected
english: He says that many others of the same kind as Jesus could also appear to those who wish to be deceived. Then let Celsus’s Jew show not many, nor even a few, but even one such as Jesus was: one who, with the power that was in him, brought into the human race a teaching and doctrines that benefit life, and turned people from the flood of sins.

He says that those who believe in Christ bring this charge against the Jews, that they have not believed in Jesus as God. On this point too we have already made our defence above, showing at the same time in what way we understand him to be God, and in what respect we call him man.

“And how,” he says, “could we, who declared to all people that one would come from God to punish the unrighteous, have dishonoured him when he came?” To make a defence against this, since it is so very silly, does not seem reasonable to me. It is as if someone else were to say: “How could we, who taught self-control, have done anything licentious? Or how could we, who champion justice, have done wrong?” For as such things are found among human beings, so it was a human thing that those who claimed to have believed the prophets when they spoke of the Christ who was to come should have disbelieved him when he came in accordance with what was prophesied. And if another reason must be added, we will say that the prophets foretold this very thing as well. Isaiah, at any rate, says plainly: “Hearing you will hear and will not understand, and seeing you will see and will not perceive; for the heart of this people has grown dull” (Isaiah 6:9–10), and what follows.

Let them tell us what it is that the Jews hear and what they see, when it is prophesied of them that they will not understand what is spoken and will not see in the way they ought what is seen. Yet it is plain that when they saw Jesus they did not see who he was, and when they heard him they did not grasp from his words the divinity in him, which was transferring God’s care from the Jews to those from the Gentiles who believe in him. So one can see that after the coming of Jesus the Jews have been wholly abandoned, and have nothing of what they once held sacred, nor even any sign that some divinity is among them. For there are no longer prophets or wonders among them, though traces of these are found to some extent among Christians, and some of them even “greater” (John 14:12); and if we are to be believed when we say so, we too have seen them.

Celsus’s Jew says: “Why would we have dishonoured the one whom we proclaimed beforehand? Was it so that we might be punished more than others?” To this too one can say that, because of their unbelief toward Jesus and all the other outrages they committed against him, the Jews will not only suffer more than others at the judgment in which we believe, but have already suffered. For what nation has been banished from its own mother city and from the place proper to its ancestral worship, except the Jews alone? And they have suffered this as the most ignoble of men; for though they sinned in many things, they suffered it for none of those so much as for what they dared against our Jesus.
translator_notes: The first two reports of Celsus’s Jew are indirect speech (φησί + infinitive) and are left unquoted; the two direct questions in the first person plural are in quotation marks. The hypothetical speaker (‘as if someone else were to say’) is Origen’s comparison, not Celsus. Isaiah 6:9-10 agrees with the LXX (ἀκοῇ ἀκούσετε ... ἐπαχύνθη γὰρ ἡ καρδία τοῦ λαοῦ τούτου); also quoted in Matthew 13:14-15 and Acts 28:26-27, but Origen names Isaiah. ‘Greater’ (μείζονα) alludes to John 14:12 (μείζονα τούτων ποιήσει). τί ἀκούουσι [τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις] καὶ τί βλέπουσι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις: Koetschau brackets the first τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις as a doubling; the clause is compressed and τί could also mean ‘why’; ‘what’ is chosen because the next sentence answers with what they saw and heard, namely Jesus. ἐπισκοπή rendered ‘care’ (God’s oversight or visitation). ὡς ἀγεννέστατοι is harsh and slightly awkward in the Greek; translated as printed. The full stop printed before ὡς διὰ τὰ κατὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ is treated as a comma. ‘Banished from its mother city’ refers to the expulsion of the Jews from Jerusalem after the revolts of 70 and 135; Origen’s polemic is translated as written, without softening. πολλοὺς ἂν ... φανῆναι τοιούτους: ἄν with the aorist infinitive in reported speech is taken as potential (‘could appear’), and τοιούτους ... ὁποῖος ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς as ‘of the same kind as Jesus’. ἠτιμάζομεν in the Jew’s two questions is rendered as a past unreal question (‘would we have dishonoured’). μεταβιβάζουσαν is present (‘was transferring’); πάλαι is ‘once, of old’.

title: Not the body but the Word is God
english: After this the Jew says: “How could we have regarded as God one who, among other things, as was commonly heard, displayed none of what he promised; and who, when we had convicted and condemned him and judged that he should be punished, was caught hiding and running away in the most disgraceful way, and was betrayed by the very men he called his disciples? And yet,” he says, “one who was God could neither flee nor be bound and led away; and least of all could one who was thought to be a saviour, and son and angel of the greatest God, be deserted and handed over by those who were with him, who had shared everything with him privately, and who had him for their teacher.”

To this we shall say that we too do not suppose that the body of Jesus, which was then seen and perceived by the senses, was God. And why do I speak of the body? Not even his soul, of which it is said: “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38; Mark 14:34). But just as, according to the Jews’ account, he who says “I am the Lord, the God of all flesh” (Jeremiah 32:27) and “Before me there was no other god, and after me there will be none” (Isaiah 43:10) is believed to be God, using the soul and body of the prophet as an instrument; and as, according to the Greeks, he who says “I know the number of the sand and the measures of the sea; I understand the mute, and I hear one who does not speak” (Herodotus, Histories 1.47) is held to be a god, speaking and being heard through the Pythia; so, according to us, the Word, who is God and Son of the God of the universe, said in Jesus: “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6), and “I am the door” (John 10:9), and “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51), and anything else like these.

We therefore charge the Jews with not regarding him as God, though the prophets in many places bear witness that he is a great power, and God in accordance with the God and Father of the universe. For we say that it was to him that the Father gave the command in the creation of the world recorded by Moses, saying “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3) and “Let there be a firmament” (Genesis 1:6), and all the rest that God commanded to come into being; and that it was to him he said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26); and that the Word, so commanded, made all that the Father enjoined on him. We say this not as our own conjecture, but because we believe the prophecies current among the Jews, in which these very words are said about God and the things he made: “For he spoke, and they came into being; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 33:9; Psalm 148:5). For if God commanded and the things made were created, who, in the mind of the prophetic Spirit, could be the one able to carry out so great a command of the Father, except he who is, if I may so name him, the living Word and “the Truth” (John 14:6)?

That the Gospels too do not know the one who said in Jesus “I am the way and the truth and the life” as someone circumscribed, as though he existed nowhere outside the soul and body of Jesus, is plain from many passages, and also from the few that we shall cite, which run as follows. John the Baptist, prophesying that the Son of God would very soon appear, not as one confined to that body and soul but as one who reaches everywhere, says of him: “Among you stands one whom you do not know, who comes after me” (John 1:26–27). If, then, he had thought that the Son of God was only where the visible body of Jesus was, how could he have said, “Among you stands one whom you do not know”? And Jesus himself, raising the thoughts of his disciples to think greater things about the Son of God, says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am among them” (Matthew 18:20). Of the same kind is his promise to the disciples when he says: “And behold, I am with you all the days until the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

We say this without separating the Son of God from Jesus; for after the saving dispensation the soul and body of Jesus have become, in the fullest sense, one with the Word of God. For if, according to the teaching of Paul, who says, “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17), everyone who has understood what it is to be joined to the Lord, and has been joined to him, is one spirit with the Lord, how much more, in a more divine and greater way, is that which was once composite one with the Word of God? He indeed showed among the Jews that he was “the power of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24) by the wonders he worked. Celsus suspected that these were done by sorcery; the Jews of that time, who had learned the tales about Beelzebul from I know not where, suspected that he cast out “demons by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons” (Matthew 12:24; Mark 3:22; Luke 11:15). Our Saviour refuted them there for speaking most absurdly, by pointing out that the kingdom of evil had not yet come to an end (Matthew 12:26; Mark 3:26). This will be clear to those who read the Gospel scripture with understanding; but this is not the time to explain it.
translator_notes: Celsus’s Jew speaks in direct speech (first person plural) and is quoted; the stray full stops in the staged text after ἄλλα and around φησίν are treated as commas. ὥσπερ ἐπηκούετο (‘as people heard’) is compressed: it may mean ‘as was reported of him’ or ‘as he was heeded’. ἄγγελον is rendered ‘angel’ (it can also mean ‘messenger’); σωτῆρα in the Jew’s mouth is lower case, ‘a saviour’. LXX renumbering: Jeremiah 39:27 LXX = Jeremiah 32:27 English (ἐγὼ κύριος ὁ θεὸς πάσης σαρκός); Psalm 32:9 LXX = Psalm 33:9 English. The words ‘he spoke and they came into being; he commanded and they were created’ stand identically in LXX Psalm 32:9 and LXX Psalm 148:5 (the Hebrew of 148:5 lacks ‘he spoke and they came into being’), so both are cited. Isaiah 43:10 agrees with the LXX. Genesis 1:26: Origen’s wording ‘according to our image and likeness’ compresses the LXX κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν. The Pythian verses are the Delphic oracle to Croesus in Herodotus 1.47 (certain); θεός there is lower case because it is Apollo. ὁ λόγος θεός: θεός is anarthrous, as Origen uses it of the Word; rendered ‘the Word, who is God’. κατὰ τὸν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν καὶ πατέρα rendered literally ‘in accordance with the God and Father of the universe’; it may mean ‘second to’ or ‘deriving from’; no interpretation is imposed. ἔμψυχος λόγος, literally ‘ensouled Word’, rendered ‘living Word’; Origen himself flags the term (ἵν’ οὕτως ὀνομάσω). οὐκ ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ σώματι ... τυγχάνοντα, literally ‘not being in that body and soul’, rendered ‘not as one confined to’, since the contrast is with φθάνοντα πανταχοῦ and περιγεγραμμένον; Origen does not deny that the Word was in Jesus (see the next paragraph). οἰκονομία rendered ‘the saving dispensation’: Origen may mean the Incarnation or its completion in the Passion and Resurrection, so the term is not narrowed. ἐπιβάλλοντες rendered ‘as our own conjecture’ (putting a thing forward on one’s own); contrasted with belief in the prophecies. John 1:26-27: Origen reads στήκει for ἕστηκεν. The Saviour’s reply (Matthew 12:25-26; Mark 3:23-26) is summarised by Origen: Mark 3:26 has τέλος ἔχει (‘has an end’), which his τέλος ἔχειν echoes. ‘The prophetic Spirit’ is capitalised as the Holy Spirit.

title: Jesus was not taken against his will
english: But what did Jesus promise and not do? Let Celsus set it out and prove it. He will not be able to, above all because what he says against Jesus, or against us, he supposes he draws either from things misheard, or from readings of the Gospels, or from Jewish stories.

Again, since the Jew says that “we convicted him, condemned him, and judged that he should be punished,” let them show how those who were seeking to contrive false testimony against him convicted him (Matthew 26:59–60); unless, perhaps, the great proof against Jesus was the one his accusers stated: “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God and to raise it up in three days’” (Matthew 26:61). For he himself “was speaking of the temple of his body” (John 2:21), while they, not knowing how to hear according to the speaker’s intention, thought that he meant the temple of stone, which the Jews honoured rather than honouring, as was right, the true temple of God the Word, of Wisdom and of Truth.

Let someone also tell us how Jesus “hid himself and slipped away most shamefully.” Let someone point out what in this deserved reproach. And since he says that he was also “caught,” I would reply that if being caught means being taken against one’s will, Jesus was not caught. For at the fitting time he did not prevent himself from coming into the hands of men, as “the Lamb of God,” so that he might take away “the sin of the world” (John 1:29). Indeed, “knowing all that was coming upon him, he went out and said to them, ‘Whom are you seeking?’ They answered, ‘Jesus of Nazareth.’ He said to them, ‘I am he.’ Judas also, who was betraying him, was standing with them. When he said to them, ‘I am he,’ they drew back and fell to the ground. So he asked again, ‘Whom are you seeking?’ And they said again, ‘Jesus of Nazareth.’ Jesus answered them, ‘I told you that I am he. So if you are seeking me, let these men go’” (John 18:4–8). Moreover, to the one who wanted to help him, who struck “the servant of the high priest” and cut off “his ear” (Matthew 26:51), he said: “Put your sword back into its place; for all who take the sword will perish by the sword. Or do you think that I cannot now call on my Father, and he will set beside me here more than twelve legions of angels? How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen this way?” (Matthew 26:52–54).

If anyone thinks that in these matters the accounts are fictions made up by those who wrote the Gospels, why are the words of those who speak out of enmity and hatred toward him and toward Christians not rather the fictions, and the accounts of those who proved the sincerity of their devotion to Jesus by enduring anything whatever for the sake of his words the truth? For that the disciples of Jesus should have taken on such endurance and steadfastness, even to death, while their minds were inventing about their teacher things that never were […]. And to fair-minded people it is abundantly clear that they were persuaded of what they recorded, from the fact that they endured such great and so many sufferings for the sake of the one they believed to be the Son of God.
translator_notes: Copy-text Koetschau marks a lacuna after τὰ μὴ ὄντα (printed as dots); the main clause that should follow (presumably something like ‘is not credible’) is lost, and it is left as [lacuna] rather than supplied. The Jew’s words in paragraph two repeat his charge from 2.9 (ἐλέγξαντες αὐτὸν καὶ καταγνόντες ἠξιοῦμεν κολάζεσθαι), so they are quoted; likewise “hid himself and slipped away most shamefully” (κρυπτόμενος ... διαδιδράσκων ἐπονειδιστότατα) and “caught” (ἑάλω). Matthew 26:61: Origen’s text has ἀναστῆσαι (‘raise up’) where Matthew reads οἰκοδομῆσαι (‘build’), perhaps under the influence of John 2:19–21 (ἐγερῶ); translated as Origen wrote it. Matthew 26:53: Origen puts ἄρτι (‘now’) before παρακαλέσαι and adds ὧδε (‘here’) after παραστήσει μοι; both kept. John 18:5, 18:7: Origen’s text lacks αὐτῷ / αὐτούς (‘him’, ‘them’), so they are not supplied. ‘The temple of God the Word, of Wisdom and of Truth’ (ναὸν θεοῦ τοῦ λόγου καὶ τῆς σοφίας καὶ τῆς ἀληθείας): the genitives could also be taken as ‘the temple of God, of the Word, of Wisdom and of Truth’; the sense (Jesus’ body as the true temple of the divine Word) is the same. The construction μᾶλλον ἢ ὡς ἐχρῆν τιμᾶσθαι is read as ‘rather than, as was right, the true temple being honoured’. ‘Coming into the hands of men’ (εἰς χεῖρας ἀνθρώπων) may echo Matthew 17:22 / Mark 9:31; possible allusion only, not cited inline. ‘Jesus of Nazareth’ renders Ἰησοῦν τὸν Ναζωραῖον.

title: Judas was not wholly against his teacher
english: Next, that he was “betrayed by those he called his disciples,” the Jew in Celsus learned from the Gospels, though he turned the one man Judas into many disciples, so as to seem to make the charge greater. But he did not go on to examine all that is recorded about Judas: that Judas fell into conflicting and opposed judgements about his teacher, and was neither against him with his whole soul, nor kept with his whole soul a pupil’s reverence for his teacher. For “he who betrayed him gave a sign” to the crowd that had come to seize Jesus, “saying, ‘The one I kiss is the man; seize him’” (Matthew 26:48). In this he kept something of his reverence for him; for had he not kept it, he would have betrayed him openly, without the pretence of a kiss.

Will this not, then, persuade everyone concerning Judas’s purpose, that together with his love of money and his wicked purpose to betray his teacher, he had something mixed into his soul, planted in him by the words of Jesus, which bore the look of a remnant, so to speak, of goodness? For it is written: “When Judas, who betrayed him, saw that he was condemned, he repented and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying, ‘I have sinned in betraying righteous blood.’ But they said, ‘What is that to us? See to it yourself.’ And throwing the pieces of silver into the temple, he withdrew, and went away and hanged himself” (Matthew 27:3–5).

If Judas, the lover of money, who also stole what was put into “the money box” for the poor (John 12:6), “repented and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,” it is clear that the teachings of Jesus were able to produce some repentance in him, and had not been utterly despised and spat out by the traitor. Moreover, the words “I have sinned in betraying righteous blood” were those of a man confessing his sin. See how burning and violent a grief arose in him from repentance for his sins, so that he could no longer bear even to live, but threw the money “into the temple,” withdrew, went away and hanged himself. For he passed sentence on himself, and so showed how much the teaching of Jesus could do even in Judas, the sinner, the thief and the traitor, who could not utterly despise what he had learned from Jesus.

Or will Celsus and those like him say that the passages which show that Judas’s defection was not complete, even after all he dared against his teacher, are fictions, and that only this is true, that one of the disciples betrayed him? And will they add to what is written that he betrayed him with his whole soul as well? That is implausible: to act in everything as an enemy would, both believing and disbelieving the same writings.

If we must also set out an argument about Judas that will put them to shame, we shall say that in the Book of Psalms the whole of the hundred and eighth Psalm (Psalm 109) contains the prophecy about Judas. It begins: “O God, do not pass over my praise in silence, for the mouth of a sinner and the mouth of a deceiver have been opened against me” (Psalm 109:1–2). It is also prophesied in it that Judas cut himself off from the number of the apostles because of his sin, and that another was chosen in his place (Acts 1:25–26); and this is shown in the words, “And let another take his office” (Psalm 109:8).

But come, suppose he was betrayed by one of his disciples who was worse disposed than Judas, and who had, as it were, poured away every word he had heard from Jesus: what does this contribute to an accusation against Jesus or against Christianity? And how does this prove the teaching false? We have also answered the points that come next in what we said before, showing that Jesus was not caught while running away, but willingly gave himself up for us all. It follows that, even if he was bound, he was bound willingly, teaching us to take such things upon ourselves for the sake of godliness, not unwillingly.
translator_notes: LXX renumbering: Origen’s ‘hundred and eighth Psalm’ (ὁ ἑκατοστὸς ὄγδοος ψαλμός) is Psalm 109 in English Bibles; his number is kept in the text and the English number given in the citation. Quoted verses LXX Psalm 108:1–2 and 108:8 = English Psalm 109:1–2 and 109:8; the last is also quoted of Judas in Acts 1:20, and ‘another was chosen in his place’ alludes to the choice of Matthias (Acts 1:25–26). ‘Betrayed by those he called his disciples’ quotes Celsus’s Jew from 2.9 (ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν ... ὧν ὠνόμαζε μαθητῶν προὐδόθη). The sentence τοῦτο μὲν οὖν οὐ πάντας πείσει ... χρηστότητος; is punctuated as a question in the copy-text and translated as one; it could also be read as a concession (‘This, then, will not persuade everyone ...’), but the following γέγραπται γάρ supports the question. Matthew 27:5 ‘withdrew’ (ἀνεχώρησε) is kept. John 12:6 (γλωσσόκομον, Judas a thief) is a clear allusion; ‘for the poor’ (εἰς λόγον τῶν πενήτων) draws on John 12:5–6. ‘Willingly gave himself up for us all’ (ἑκὼν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πάντων παρέδωκεν ἑαυτόν) is close to Romans 8:32 (ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πάντων παρέδωκεν αὐτόν, said of the Father) and Ephesians 5:2 / Galatians 2:20 (παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν); possible allusion only, not cited inline. ἐκχέαντος ... λόγους is taken as ‘poured away’ (kept nothing of) Jesus’ words. ‘Celsus and those like him’ renders οἱ περὶ τὸν Κέλσον. Matthew 27:4: Origen reads αἷμα δίκαιον (‘righteous blood’) where the common text has ἀθῷον (‘innocent’); rendered as Origen wrote it.

title: Pupils who turned against their teachers
english: Childish, too, seem to me such claims as this: that “a good general, who has led many tens of thousands, has never been betrayed; no, nor even a wicked robber chief, captain of utter villains, since he seemed useful to those with him. But he, betrayed by those under him, neither led them as a good general, nor, after deceiving his disciples, did he inspire in those he had deceived even the goodwill, if I may call it so, that men feel toward a robber chief.” For one could find many accounts of generals betrayed by their own people, and of robber chiefs captured because of men who did not keep their agreements with them. But let it be granted that no general or robber chief was ever betrayed: what does this contribute toward making it a point against Jesus that one of his pupils became his betrayer?

Since Celsus professes philosophy, we would ask him: was it a charge against Plato that Aristotle, after hearing him for twenty years, left him and attacked his teaching on the immortality of the soul, and called Plato’s Ideas “twitterings” (Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1.22, 83a33)? We might press the difficulty further and say: was Plato no longer strong in dialectic, or able to establish what he had thought out, once Aristotle had left him, and are Plato’s doctrines false for that reason? Or is it possible that, while Plato was right, as those who follow his philosophy would say, Aristotle proved wicked and ungrateful toward his teacher?

Chrysippus, too, is plainly attacking Cleanthes in many places in his writings, bringing in new views against what Cleanthes had taught, though Cleanthes had been his teacher when Chrysippus was still young and only beginning in philosophy. Yet Aristotle is said to have studied with Plato for twenty years, and Chrysippus to have spent no short time with Cleanthes; but Judas did not spend even three years with Jesus. From what is written in the lives of the philosophers one could find many things like those for which Celsus blames Jesus on account of Judas. The Pythagoreans used to build empty tombs for those who, after being turned to philosophy, ran back to ordinary life; and Pythagoras and his followers were not, for that reason, weak in argument and proof.
translator_notes: No Scripture in this chapter. The general/robber-chief argument is Celsus’s Jew’s, reported by Origen with ὅτι and set in quotation marks as his; the phrase ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω (‘if I may call it so’) could be Origen’s own aside (he uses it often) rather than Celsus’s, but it sits inside the reported argument and is kept there. ‘Twitterings’ (τερετίσματα): Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1.22, 83a33 (τὰ γὰρ εἴδη χαιρέτω· τερετίσματά τε γάρ ἐστι). Aristotle’s twenty years with Plato and Chrysippus’s studies under Cleanthes are standard biographical tradition (compare Diogenes Laertius 5.9; 7.179), not cited inline since Origen quotes no text; ‘the lives of the philosophers’ is kept lower-case as a general reference, not certainly Diogenes Laertius’s book. The Pythagorean cenotaphs for lapsed members are also reported by Iamblichus, Life of Pythagoras 73, and Origen returns to them in Against Celsus 3.51; not cited inline. ‘Ordinary life’ renders ἰδιωτικὸν βίον (the life of a layman, outside philosophy). ‘Not even three years’ reflects the Gospel chronology of Jesus’ ministry; no single verse cited.

title: Jesus foretold the persecution of his followers and the fall of Jerusalem
english: After this Celsus’s Jew says: “Though I have much to say about what happened in Jesus’ life, things that are true and unlike what Jesus’ disciples wrote, I deliberately pass them over.” What, then, are these true things, unlike what is written in the Gospels, that Celsus’s Jew passes over? Or is he using what passes for rhetorical skill, pretending that he has something to say, when in fact he had nothing from outside the Gospel to bring forward that could strike the hearer as true and as a clear accusation against Jesus and his teaching?

He charges the disciples with having invented the claim that Jesus foreknew and foretold everything that happened to him. That this too is true, whether Celsus likes it or not, we shall show from many other things the Saviour spoke prophetically, in which he foretold what would happen to Christians even in later generations. Who would not marvel at the prediction, “You will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations” (Matthew 10:18), and at whatever else he foretold about the persecution of his disciples? For on account of what doctrine, among all that have arisen among men, are others punished too, so that one of Jesus’ accusers could say that Jesus, seeing impious or false doctrines being prosecuted, thought he would lend dignity to this one too by an alleged prediction about it? If anyone had to be brought “before governors and kings” (Matthew 10:18) for their doctrines, who should it have been but the Epicureans, who do away with providence altogether, and the Peripatetics as well, who say that prayers and the sacrifices offered as to the divine achieve nothing?

But someone will say that the Samaritans too are persecuted for their religion. To him we shall reply: the Sicarii are put to death because of circumcision, as men who mutilate the body contrary to the established laws and to what is granted to the Jews alone. And you will not hear a judge asking whether a Sicarius who strives to live by this supposed religion will be released if he changes his mind, but led off to death if he holds firm. No, proof of circumcision is enough to have the man who underwent it put to death. Christians alone, in keeping with what their Saviour said, “You will be brought before governors and kings for my sake” (Matthew 10:18), are allowed by the judges, right up to their last breath, once they have forsworn Christianity, sacrificed according to the common customs and taken the oath, to go home and live without danger.

See whether it is not with great authority that these words are spoken: “Everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven; and everyone who denies me before men,” and the rest (Matthew 10:32–33). Go back with me in thought to Jesus as he says these things, and look at things prophesied that had not yet happened. See whether you would not say, if you disbelieved him, that he was talking nonsense and speaking in vain, since what he said would not come to pass; or, if you were in two minds about assenting to his words, whether you would not say: “If these things are fulfilled, and the teaching of Jesus’ words becomes established, so that governors and kings take pains to put to death those who acknowledge Jesus, then we shall believe that he says these things as one who has received great authority from God to sow this word in the human race, and who is convinced that it will prevail.”

Who will not marvel, going back in thought to him as he then taught and said, “This gospel will be preached in the whole world, as a testimony to them and to the nations” (Matthew 24:14), and seeing that, just as he said, the gospel of Jesus Christ has been preached throughout the world under heaven “to Greeks and barbarians, to wise and foolish” (Romans 1:14)? For the word spoken with power has prevailed over every kind of human nature, and no race of men can be found that has escaped receiving the teaching of Jesus.

Let Celsus’s Jew, who does not believe that Jesus foreknew all that happened to him, consider how, while Jerusalem still stood and the whole Jewish worship was carried on in it, Jesus foretold what would befall it at the hands of the Romans. For surely they will not say that Jesus’ own acquaintances and hearers handed down the teaching of the Gospels without writing and left their disciples without written records about Jesus. Now it is written in them: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near” (Luke 21:20). At that time there were no armies at all around Jerusalem, encircling it, enclosing it and besieging it. That began while Nero was still emperor and went on until the reign of Vespasian, whose son Titus destroyed Jerusalem: as Josephus writes, on account of James the Just, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ; but as the truth shows, on account of Jesus the Christ of God.
translator_notes: The Jew’s opening statement is in the first person (παραλείπω), so it is quoted directly. The disciples’ ‘invention’ charge is reported indirectly and is left unquoted. Matthew 10:18 is quoted three times; Origen’s first form keeps Matthew’s δέ (dropping the opening καί) and reads τοῖς ἔθνεσι; the later two forms drop δέ, one stopping before the verb and one at ἕνεκεν ἐμοῦ (‘nations’ kept for ἔθνη; ‘Gentiles’ is equally possible). Matthew 10:32-33: ‘acknowledge’ for ὁμολογέω ἐν (a Semitic construction, ‘confess in’); Origen cuts the quotation off with καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς, which the English keeps as ‘and the rest’. The ‘preached in the whole world’ saying merges Matthew 24:14 (κηρυχθήσεται τοῦτο τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ... ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ οἰκουμένῃ εἰς μαρτύριον πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσιν) with the wording of Matthew 26:13 / Mark 14:9 (ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ) and Matthew 10:18 (εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς καὶ τοῖς ἔθνεσιν); cited as Matthew 24:14, the closest whole saying. ‘Sow this word’ may echo the parable of the sower (Matthew 13:3-23), but that is uncertain and not cited inline. ‘Sicarii’: Origen uses the name for a group (apparently Samaritan) put to death for circumcision under the imperial ban, which exempted Jews; the English keeps his term. The passage in which Josephus says Jerusalem fell because of James is not in the surviving text of Josephus (Origen reports it again in Contra Celsum 1.47); ‘Jesus who was called Christ’ is Josephus’s phrase (compare Antiquities 20.200), not a Gospel citation. ‘The Christ of God’ is a title (compare Luke 9:20) and is not given an inline citation. The long sentence beginning ‘See whether you would not say’ is one Greek period with two branches (ἀπιστῶν μέν ... ἀμφιβάλλων δέ ... εἰ μὴ ὅτι); the English keeps both branches as one sentence and quotes the doubter’s imagined words.

title: Celsus would not even grant him foreknowledge
english: Celsus could, however, have accepted or conceded that Jesus foreknew what would happen to him, and then made it seem a trivial thing, as he did with the miracles when he said they were done by sorcery. He could indeed have said that many people, through divination by omens, by birds, by sacrifices or by horoscopes, have known what was going to befall them. But this he would not concede, as being the greater thing; whereas he has in a way accepted that Jesus worked the miracles, and seems to have discredited this under the pretext of sorcery.

Phlegon, however, in the thirteenth or fourteenth book, I think, of his Chronicles, even granted Christ foreknowledge of certain future events, although he confused what concerned Peter, taking it as said of Jesus; and he testified that the things foretold turned out as Jesus had said. Yet even he, through what he says about foreknowledge, declared, as if against his will, that the teaching found in the fathers of our doctrines was not without a more divine power.
translator_notes: ἐξευτελίζειν μὲν τοῦτο δοκεῖν is compressed: either ‘belittle this, so that it would seem trivial’ or ‘belittle this supposed [foreknowledge]’; rendered ‘made it seem a trivial thing’. οἰωνοί and ὄρνιθες both mean birds of omen; rendered ‘omens’ and ‘birds’ to keep both terms. δυνάμεις = ‘mighty works’, rendered ‘miracles’ as in the surrounding chapters. Phlegon of Tralles, Chronicles (Olympiads), books 13 or 14 by Origen’s own uncertain recollection (‘I think’). ‘The fathers of our doctrines’ (τοῖς πατράσι τῶν δογμάτων) means the founders of the Christian teaching, Jesus and the apostles; kept literal. No Scripture quoted.

title: The Gospel writers’ love of truth
english: Celsus says that Jesus’ disciples too, “having no excuse to offer for a notorious fact, invented this: the claim that he had foreknown everything.” He did not notice, or did not wish to notice, the love of truth in those who wrote. They admitted that Jesus had told his disciples beforehand, “You will all fall away this night” (Matthew 26:31), and that he spoke the truth, since they did fall away (Matthew 26:56); and that he had also prophesied to Peter, “Before the cock crows you will deny me three times” (Matthew 26:34), and that Peter denied him three times (Matthew 26:69–75).

If they had not been lovers of truth but, as Celsus supposes, writers of fiction, they would not have recorded Peter’s denial or the falling away of Jesus’ disciples. For even if these things did happen, who could have refuted their account by showing that this is how it turned out? And yet one would expect men who wished to teach the readers of the Gospels to despise death for the sake of confessing Christianity to have kept silent about these things. But as it is, seeing that the word would prevail over men by its power, they set down even things like these, which somehow would neither harm their readers nor give them a pretext for denial.
translator_notes: Celsus’s charge is given with ὅτι and a finite verb (ἐπενόησαν), which may report his own words; it is quoted as his, and ‘Celsus says’ follows the Greek. ἐπισκήψασθαι: ‘to plead (as an excuse)’; the sense is that the disciples had no way to explain away an obvious fact (the betrayal and death). Matthew 26:31: Origen omits ἐν ἐμοί (‘because of me’); the English follows his wording. Matthew 26:34 reads πρὶν ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι τρὶς ἀπαρνήσῃ με; Origen paraphrases with πρὸ ἀλεκτοροφωνίας (compare Mark 14:30, Luke 22:34, John 13:38). The fulfilment clauses (‘they did fall away’, ‘Peter denied him three times’) are allusions to Matthew 26:56 and 26:69-75 and are cited as such. τίς ... ἤλεγξε τὸν λόγον has no ἄν; it is taken as the potential sense ‘who would have exposed the account’, i.e. no outsider could have disproved it had the disciples left it out. οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως rendered ‘somehow’.

title: He truly died, so he truly rose
english: Very naively he says that the disciples wrote such things about Jesus to excuse what happened to him. “It is as if,” he says, “someone, while saying that a man is just, were to show him doing wrong; while saying he is holy, show him committing murder; while saying he is immortal, show him dead; and were to add to all this that he had foretold these things.” His example is plainly unlike the case. For there is nothing absurd in this, that one who had taken upon himself to be the pattern that would be set before mankind of how they ought to live should have shown how one ought to die for the sake of piety; and that is apart from the fact that his dying for men has been of some benefit to the whole universe, as we showed in the previous book.

Then he thinks that the whole admission of his suffering confirms the case against him rather than refuting it. For he has not seen how much has been worked out philosophically on this point in Paul, and said by the prophets. It also escaped him that one of those in the heretical sects has said that Jesus suffered these things in appearance, without really suffering. Not knowing this, he said: “For you did not even say that he seemed to impious men to suffer these things but did not suffer; no, you openly admit that he suffered.” But we do not apply “seeming” to his suffering, so that his resurrection too may not be false but true. For if one who truly died rose again, he truly rose; but one who only seemed to have died did not truly rise.

Since unbelievers mock the teaching about the resurrection of Jesus Christ, we shall cite Plato too, who says that Er the son of Armenius rose from the pyre after twelve days and gave an account of those in Hades (Plato, Republic 10.614b). And since we are addressing unbelievers, the story in Heraclides about the woman who did not breathe will not be wholly useless at this point. Many, too, are recorded to have come back from their tombs, not only on the same day but even on the next. What wonder, then, if one who had wondrously done many things beyond human power, things so plain that those who cannot look the fact of their happening in the face slander them by putting them in the same class as sorceries, also had something more in his own death, so that his soul left the body of its own will and, after setting certain things in order outside it, came back again when it wished?

John records Jesus as having said something of this kind in the words: “No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again” (John 10:18). And perhaps this is why he went out of the body beforehand: to preserve it, and so that his legs would not be broken like those of the robbers crucified with him. “For the soldiers broke the legs of the first, and of the other who was crucified with him; but when they came to Jesus and saw that he had breathed his last, they did not break his legs” (John 19:32–33).

So we have answered this question too: “How then is it credible that he foretold it?” As for “How is the dead man immortal?”, let whoever wishes learn that it is not the dead man who is immortal, but the one who rose from the dead. So not only is the dead man not immortal, but not even Jesus before his death, the composite being, was immortal, since he was going to die. For no one who is going to die is immortal; one is immortal when he will die no more. “Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him” (Romans 6:9), even if those who have not been able to grasp how these words are meant would rather it were not so.
translator_notes: ‘He’ at the start is not named; in context it is Celsus (through his Jew). εὐήθως rendered ‘naively’. σκοπός: ‘mark, goal, pattern’; rendered ‘pattern’. ‘In the previous book’ (ἐν τῷ πρὸ τούτου λόγῳ): Book 1, probably 1.31, on Jesus’ death benefiting the world. Paul and the prophets on the suffering are a general reference, not a quotation, so no inline citation. τινὰ τῶν ἐν ταῖς αἱρέσεσι is singular (‘one of those in the heresies’), kept singular as ‘one of those in the heretical sects’; a docetist is meant. δοκήσει / τὸ δοκεῖν: ‘in appearance’ / ‘seeming’. Plato, Republic 10.614b (Er son of Armenius, on the pyre on the twelfth day). Heraclides: Heraclides of Pontus, whose work on the woman without breath (Περὶ τῆς ἄπνου) is reported by Diogenes Laertius 8.60-61; not cited inline because Origen names only ‘Heraclides’. ψυχή in John 10:18 is rendered ‘soul’ (English Bibles have ‘life’) because Origen’s argument is about the soul leaving the body. οἰκονομησαμένη ... τινα ἔξω αὐτοῦ (‘having arranged certain things outside it’) probably alludes to the descent to Hades (compare 2.43), but Origen does not say so here; rendered ‘after setting certain things in order outside it’. The source text has stray full stops before ὅτε βούλεται and in ‘τού. του’; read as running text. John 19:33 reads εἶδον ἤδη αὐτὸν τεθνηκότα; Origen has ἰδόντες ὅτι ἐξέπνευσεν (‘saw that he had breathed his last’); the English follows Origen. ὁ σύνθετος: Jesus as composite (soul and body) before death. Romans 6:9 quoted with δέ added; the final clause κἂν μὴ βούλωνται has no expressed object and is rendered ‘would rather it were not so’.

title: Meeting a foreknown death is no folly
english: Very foolish too is this: “What god or spirit or sensible man, foreseeing that such things would happen to him, would not avoid them if he could, but would run into what he foreknew?” Socrates, at any rate, knew that he would drink the hemlock and die; and he could, had he listened to Crito, have slipped out of prison and suffered none of this (Plato, Crito 44b). But he chose, as seemed reasonable to him, what was better for him: to die as a philosopher rather than to live unworthy of philosophy. Leonidas too, the Spartan general, knowing he was on the point of dying with the men at Thermopylae, did not scheme to live on in shame, but said to those with him, “Let us take our breakfast as men who will dine in Hades.” Those who care to collect such stories will find many.

What wonder, then, if Jesus, knowing what would happen, did not avoid it but met the very things he foreknew? Even Paul, his disciple, having heard what would happen to him once he went up to Jerusalem, went straight to meet the dangers, rebuking those who wept around him and tried to stop him from going up to Jerusalem (Acts 21:10–14). And many in our own time, knowing that if they confessed Christianity they would die, but if they denied it they would be released and recover their property, have despised life and of their own free will chosen death for the sake of piety.
translator_notes: The quoted question is Celsus’s (introduced only by τό, continuing his Jew’s objections). δαίμων in Celsus’s mouth means a lesser divine being, not an evil spirit; rendered ‘spirit’. The source has a stray full stop after οὐκ ἂν; read as one question. Socrates: Plato, Crito 44b, where Crito urges him to escape. Leonidas’s saying (‘breakfast ... dine in Hades’) is found in Plutarch’s Sayings of the Spartans and Diodorus Siculus 11.9.4; not cited inline because Origen gives no source and the exact wording differs between the accounts. Paul: Acts 21:10-14 (Agabus’s prophecy; ‘What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?’). ὁμόσε τοῖς κινδύνοις ἐχώρησεν: ‘went to close quarters with the dangers’, rendered ‘went straight to meet the dangers’.

title: Foreknowledge did not undo their weakness
english: Next after this, the Jew in Celsus says another silly thing: “How, if he foretold both the one who would betray him and the one who would deny him, would they not have feared him as a god, so that the one would no longer betray him and the other would not deny him?” (compare Matthew 26:21–25, 34). But the most wise Celsus did not see the contradiction in this passage. If Jesus foreknew as God, and his foreknowledge could not prove false, then it was not possible either for the man known as the future betrayer not to betray, or for the man shown to be the future denier not to deny. But if it was possible for the one not to betray and the other not to deny, so that not betraying and not denying would have come about in those who had learned of these things beforehand, then the one who said, “This man will betray and that man will deny,” was no longer speaking the truth.

For if he foreknew the man who would betray him, he saw the wickedness from which the betrayal would come, and this wickedness was in no way overturned by the foreknowledge. And again, if he had grasped who would deny him, he foretold that this man would deny him because he saw the weakness from which the denial would come; and that weakness was not going to be overturned so suddenly by the foreknowledge.

And where does he get this: “But they themselves betrayed and denied him without caring for him at all”? For it has been shown concerning the betrayer that it is false that he betrayed his teacher without having had any regard for him at all. And this is shown no less concerning the one who denied him, who after the denial “went out and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75; Luke 22:62).
translator_notes: In Celsus’s mouth θεός of Jesus is rendered ‘a god’ (house convention for the Jew’s sceptical voice); in Origen’s own argument (‘if he foreknew as God’) it is capitalised. τὸν ἐλεγχθέντα ἀρνησόμενον: ‘the man shown (exposed) to be the future denier’. ‘It has been shown concerning the betrayer’ refers back to Origen’s earlier argument in Book 2 (around 2.11) that Judas kept some regard for his teacher. ‘Went out and wept bitterly’ matches Matthew 26:75 and Luke 22:62 verbatim; both cited. The Celsus question alludes to the Gospel predictions of the betrayal and denial (Matthew 26:21–25, 34; parallels Mark 14:18–21, 30; John 13:21–26, 38); cited with ‘compare’.

title: The outcome proves the prophecy true
english: Superficial too is this remark: “For surely even when a man who is being plotted against learns of it in advance and tells the plotters beforehand, they give it up and are on their guard.” For many have plotted even against people who had learned of the plot in advance.

Next, as though drawing the conclusion of his argument, he says: “So it was not because these things had been foretold that they happened, for that is impossible; but since they happened, the foretelling is proved false. For it is altogether impossible that those who had heard beforehand should still betray and deny.” But once his premises have been overturned, the conclusion is overturned with them: “It was not because these things had been foretold that they happened.” We say that these things both happened, as things that could happen, and that, since they happened, the foretelling is shown to be true; for truth about things to come is judged by the outcome. False, then, is what he said in these terms, that the foretelling is proved false; and Celsus has said to no purpose: “For it is altogether impossible that those who had heard beforehand should still betray and deny.”
translator_notes: The staged text has (οὐκ) in angle-bracket sense, an editorial supplement in Celsus’s repeated conclusion; read with it, since it repeats the ‘not because’ of the conclusion just quoted. Staged punctuation puts full stops at ‘ἐπεὶ γέγονεν.’ and ‘εἰρημένον.’; read as one sentence each (‘since they happened the foretelling is shown true’; ‘false is what he said, that the foretelling is proved false’). Typo οτι for ὅτι read. ἀποτρέπονται καὶ φυλάσσονται taken as middle with the plotters as subject (‘they turn back and are on their guard’). No Scripture quoted.

title: Foreknowledge does not cause what it foresees
english: After this let us see how he puts it. “He foretold these things,” he says, “being a god, and what was foretold certainly had to happen. So a god brought his own disciples and prophets, with whom he dined and drank, to the point of becoming impious and unholy, when he above all ought to have done good to all men, and especially to those who shared his table. Or would one who had shared a man’s table not afterwards plot against him, while one who had feasted with a god became his plotter? And, what is still more absurd, the god himself plotted against those at table with him, by making them traitors and impious men.”

Since you wish me to answer even those arguments of Celsus that seem to me trivial, we shall say this in reply. Celsus thinks that what is prophesied by some kind of foreknowledge comes to pass because it was prophesied. We do not grant this. We say that the one who prophesied is not the cause of what will be on the ground that he foretold it would happen; rather, what will be, which would have been even if it had not been prophesied, gave the one who foreknew it the cause for foretelling it. And all of this lies within the foreknowledge of the one who prophesies it: when it is possible for a given thing to happen and possible also for it not to happen, one particular one of the two will come about. And we do not say that the one who foreknows takes away the possibility of its happening or not happening and says, as it were, something like this: “This will certainly be, and it cannot turn out otherwise.” This principle extends to all foreknowledge of anything that lies in our power, whether in the divine Scriptures or in the histories of the Greeks. And what the logicians call the “lazy argument”, which is a sophism, will not be a sophism as far as Celsus is concerned; but by sound reasoning it is a sophism.

To make this understood, I shall use from Scripture the prophecies about Judas, or our Saviour’s foreknowledge of him as the one who would betray him; and from the Greek histories, the oracle given to Laius, granting for the present that it is true, since that does not harm the argument. Concerning Judas, then, the hundred and eighth Psalm (Psalm 109 in English Bibles) speaks in the person of the Saviour; it begins: “O God, do not pass over my praise in silence; for the mouth of a sinner and the mouth of a deceitful man have been opened against me” (Psalm 109:1–2). If you observe what is written in the psalm, you will find that, just as he was foreknown as the one who would betray the Saviour, so he was also the cause of the betrayal, and because of his wickedness deserved the curses spoken in the prophecy. For let him suffer these things, it says, “because he did not remember to show mercy, and persecuted a poor and needy man” (Psalm 109:16). So he could have remembered “to show mercy” and not persecuted the one whom he persecuted; but though he could, he did not do so, and betrayed him instead, so that he deserves the curses pronounced against him in the prophecy.

Against the Greeks we shall use what was said in this way to Laius, whether the tragic poet set it down in its very words or in words of equal force. It is said to him, then, by the one who indeed foreknew what would be: “Do not sow the furrow of children against the will of the gods; for if you beget a child, the one born of you will kill you, and all your house will walk through blood” (Euripides, Phoenician Women 18–20). In this too, then, it is clearly shown that it was possible for Laius not to sow “the furrow of children”, for the oracle would not have commanded him what was not possible; and it was also possible for him to sow, and neither of the two was forced upon him. But because he did not take care not to sow “the furrow of children”, it followed from his having sown that he suffered the tragedy of Oedipus and Jocasta and their sons.

The so-called lazy argument too, which is a sophism, is of this sort: it is put hypothetically to a sick man and, as a sophism, dissuades him from using a physician to regain his health. The argument runs like this: “If it is fated for you to recover from the illness, you will recover whether you call in the physician or not. But if it is fated for you not to recover from the illness, you will not recover whether you call in the physician or not. Now either it is fated for you to recover from the illness or it is fated for you not to recover. Therefore you call in the physician in vain.” But against this argument something like the following is wittily set: “If it is fated for you to beget children, you will beget children whether you lie with a woman or not. But if it is fated for you not to beget children, you will not beget children whether you lie with a woman or not. Now either it is fated for you to beget children or not to beget them. Therefore you lie with a woman in vain.” For just as in this case, since it is out of the question, indeed impossible, that a man who has not lain with a woman should beget children, lying with a woman is not resorted to in vain, so, if recovery from illness comes by way of medicine, the physician is necessarily called in, and it is false that “you call in the physician in vain.”

We have brought in all this because of what the most wise Celsus set down when he said: “Being a god, he foretold, and what was foretold certainly had to happen.” If by “certainly” he means “under compulsion”, we shall not grant it to him, for it was possible for it not to happen as well. But if he says “certainly” in the sense of “it will be”, which nothing prevents from being true even though it is possible for it not to happen, this does no harm to the argument. For it did not follow from Jesus’ having truly foretold what concerned the traitor, or what concerned the one who denied him, that he himself became the cause of their impiety and unholy deed. He who, as we hold, knew “what was in man” (John 2:25) saw the traitor’s wicked character, and saw what he would dare because he loved money and did not hold firmly to what he ought to think about his teacher; and so, among many other things, he said this too: “He who has dipped his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me” (Matthew 26:23).
translator_notes: LXX renumbering: Origen’s ‘hundred and eighth Psalm’ (LXX 108) is Psalm 109 in English Bibles; the opening quoted is LXX 108:1b–2a = Psalm 109:1–2 (the title verse is not counted in English numbering), and ‘because he did not remember to show mercy...’ is LXX 108:16 = Psalm 109:16. The wording ‘in the hundred and eighth Psalm’ is kept as Origen wrote it; the parenthetical gives the English number. The Laius oracle is Euripides, Phoenissae 18–20 (Origen: ‘the tragic poet’); Euripides reads τέκνων ἄλοκα and δι᾿ αἵματος where Origen’s text has παίδων ἄλοκα and δι᾿ αἱμάτων, which fits Origen’s own caveat ‘whether in the very words or their equivalent’. δαιμόνων βίᾳ: ‘against the will of the gods’ (pagan gods, lower case). The ‘lazy argument’ (ἀργὸς λόγος) is the Stoic school name for this fatalist sophism; the ‘witty’ counter-argument (the begetting case) is the one Chrysippus is reported to have used, but Origen names no source, so none is given inline. Staged punctuation breaks several sentences (‘προφήτας. μεθ᾿ ὧν’, ‘ἔσται. ὅπερ’, ‘ἀληθὲς. κἂν’, ‘γενέσθαι. οὐδὲν’, ‘τρυβλίον. ἐκεῖνός’); read continuously. Editorial supplements in round brackets in the staged text, (δὲ), (τοῦ), (σαφῶς), (γὰρ), (ἀληθῶς), are read as part of the text. ‘Since you wish’ (βούλει) addresses Ambrose, the dedicatee. θεός in Celsus’s quoted words rendered ‘a god’, ‘the god himself’ (house convention); ‘his disciples and prophets’ is as the Greek has it. Matthew 26:23 cited for ‘he who has dipped his hand with me in the dish’ (the wording is Matthew’s, with ἐκεῖνος for οὗτος); compare Mark 14:20. ‘Knew what was in man’: John 2:25 (Origen keeps the article τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ). φιλάργυρος may allude to John 12:6 (Judas the thief); not explicit enough to cite inline. Matthew 26:23 has ἐν τῷ τρυβλίῳ; Origen’s εἰς τὸ τρυβλίον is a minor variant of no consequence.

title: Table companions have often turned traitor
english: See too how superficial, and how plainly false, this statement of Celsus is. He declared that one who had shared a man’s table would not plot against him; and if he would not plot against a man, much less would one who had feasted with a god become his plotter. For who does not know that many who have shared salt and table have plotted against those who shared their hearth? The history of Greeks and barbarians is full of such examples. The iambic poet of Paros, reproaching Lycambes for breaking his agreements after “salt and table”, says to him: “You broke a great oath, and salt and table” (Archilochus).

Those who care for learning from histories, and have given themselves wholly to it, leaving aside the more necessary studies about how one ought to live, will cite more examples showing that men who shared a table with others plotted against them.
translator_notes: Origen here restates Celsus’s point in indirect form (ἀποφηναμένου ὅτι...), so no quotation marks are used for it; the rendering ‘much less would one... become his plotter’ gives the sense of πολλῷ πλέον ... οὐκ ἄν (literally ‘much more would not’). The ‘iambic poet of Paros’ is Archilochus; the line ὅρκον δ᾿ ἐνοσφίσθης μέγαν ἅλας τε καὶ τράπεζαν is his fragment against Lycambes (usually numbered fr. 173 West; the number is not given inline). Staged text σλοις is a typo for ὅλοις (‘wholly’), read so. Staged full stops after ἐπιβουλεύσειε, συνθήκας ἀθετήσαντα and μαθήματα read as commas. No Scripture quoted.

title: A charge he cannot prove
english: Then, as though he had drawn his argument together with tightly fitted proofs and logical steps, he said: “And, what is still more absurd, the god himself plotted against those at table with him, by making them traitors and impious men.” For he could not show how Jesus either plotted against his disciples or made them traitors and impious men, except from the chain of reasoning he imagined, which even an ordinary person could very easily refute.
translator_notes: Staged ης read as ἧς (relative). ὡς συναγαγὼν ἀραρυίαις ἀποδείξεσι is ironic (‘as though he had drawn his argument together with tightly fitted proofs’). θεός in Celsus’s quoted words rendered ‘the god’ (house convention). ‘Against his disciples’ makes explicit the object of ἐπεβούλευσεν, which is the same disciples named in the next clause; no new content added. No Scripture quoted.

title: He took a body that could feel pain
english: After this he says: “If he had resolved on these things and was punished in obedience to the Father, it is clear that, since he was a god and willed it, what was done to him in accordance with his own will was neither painful nor grievous.” He did not see that he was contradicting himself in the same breath. For if he granted that Jesus was punished, since he had resolved on these things and in obedience to the Father gave himself up, it is clear that he was punished, and it was not possible that what the punishers inflicted should not be painful; for pain does not depend on the will. But if, because he willed it, what was inflicted was neither painful nor grievous, how did he grant that “he was punished”?

He did not see that, once Jesus had taken up the body that comes through birth, he took it up as a body capable of pains and of the grievous things that befall those who are in bodies, provided we do not take “grievous” to mean something that depends on the will. So, just as he willingly took up a body not altogether different in nature from human flesh, so together with the body he also took up what is painful and grievous in it. It was not in his power not to suffer these things, since it lay with those who were dealing with him to inflict grievous and painful things upon him.

We have already answered above that if he had willed not to come into the hands of men, he would not have come. But he came, because he willed it, for the reason already given, that his dying for men would benefit the whole universe.
