translator_notes: Staged punctuation splits clauses with full stops (‘ὅτι. εἰ δέδοκτο αὐτῷ ταῦτα. καὶ’, ‘ἐκολάζετο. ἐπεὶ’, ‘σάρκα. οὕτως’, ‘ἀνιαρὰ. ὧν’, ‘ἄν. ἦλθε δὲ. ἐπεὶ ἐβούλετο. διὰ’); read continuously. θεῷ γε ὄντι in Celsus’s words rendered ‘since he was a god’ (house convention for Celsus); τῷ πατρὶ ‘the Father’ capitalised because it refers to God the Father. ἀπροαίρετον γὰρ ὁ πόνος: ‘pain does not depend on the will’ (it is not a matter of choice). εἰ τοῦ ἀνιαροῦ μὴ ὡς προαιρετικοῦ ἀκούοιμεν: Origen separates bodily distress from the soul’s willed grief; rendered ‘provided we do not take “grievous” to mean something that depends on the will’. κύριος here means ‘master’ (in control), not the divine title; rendered ‘it was not in his power’. τῷ παντὶ rendered ‘the whole universe’. ‘We have already answered above’ points back to Origen’s earlier replies in Book 2 (around 2.9–2.10 and 2.16–2.17); exact place not certain. Possible echoes not cited inline: ‘come into the hands of men’ (compare Matthew 17:22; Mark 9:31) and dying ‘for men’ (compare John 11:50); both are too general to count as clear allusions here.

title: Celsus leaves out half the prayer
english: Next, wishing to show that what happened to him was painful and grievous, and that even if he willed it he could not make it otherwise, he says: “Why then does he wail and lament, and pray to escape the fear of death, saying something like this: ‘O Father, if this cup can pass by’ (Matthew 26:39)?”

Here too observe Celsus’s malice. He does not credit the love of truth shown by those who wrote the Gospels. They could have passed over in silence the things that Celsus thinks discreditable, yet they did not keep silent, for many reasons, which someone will give in due time when expounding the Gospel. Instead he attacks the wording of the Gospel, piling tragic exaggeration on top of it and putting down what is not written; for nowhere is Jesus found lamenting. He paraphrases “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass” (Matthew 26:39), but he does not go on to quote what is recorded immediately after it, which at once shows Jesus’ reverence toward the Father and his greatness of soul. It runs: “Yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). Nor does he let on that he has read of Jesus’ ready obedience to the Father’s will concerning what had been decided that he should suffer, made plain in the words: “If this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done” (Matthew 26:42).

In this he acts much like the impious, who listen to the divine Scriptures with malice and “speak injustice on high” (Psalm 73:8). For they too seem to have heard “I will kill,” and they often throw it in our faces, but “I will make alive” (Deuteronomy 32:39) they do not even remember. Yet the whole saying shows that those who live to the common harm and act out of wickedness are put to death by God, and that a better life is brought in for them in its place, the life God would give to those who have died to sin (Romans 6:2). In the same way they have heard “I will strike,” but they do not go on to see “and I will heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39). That is like what a physician might say who has cut into bodies and made severe wounds in order to remove what harms them and stands in the way of health, and who does not stop at the pain and the cutting but by his treatment restores the body to the health he intended for it. Nor have they heard the whole of “For he causes pain, and restores again” (Job 5:18), but only “he causes pain.”

So too, then, Celsus’s Jew has set out “O Father, would that this cup could pass by” (Matthew 26:39), but not what follows, nor what shows Jesus’ readiness and firmness in facing his passion. These matters call for a long explanation drawn from the wisdom of God, which will fittingly be handed on to those whom Paul called “mature,” when he says: “Yet among the mature we speak wisdom” (1 Corinthians 2:6). Setting them aside for the present, we shall briefly recall what is useful for the question before us.
translator_notes: Speaker: ‘he says’ (λέγει) continues from 2.23, where Celsus’s Jew is speaking; kept as the Greek frames it. Celsus’s quoted question is in double quotation marks; his citation of the Gospel inside it is in single marks. Celsus’s two forms of the prayer differ from the Gospel text and from each other (‘εἰ δύναται... παρελθεῖν’, later ‘εἴθε δύναιτο... παρελθεῖν’); both rendered as given and cited to Matthew 26:39 (closest wording; compare Mark 14:36, Luke 22:42). ‘ὀλέθρου’ rendered ‘death’ (lit. destruction). ‘ἀδικίαν εἰς τὸ ὕψος’ = LXX Psalm 72:8, English Psalm 73:8 (Hebrew-based English versions differ in wording). Deuteronomy 32:39 supplies both ‘I will kill... I will make alive’ and ‘I will strike, and I will heal’. ‘those who have died to sin’ is a clear verbal echo of Romans 6:2 (compare 6:11). ‘αὐτὸς γὰρ ἀλγεῖν ποιεῖ καὶ πάλιν ἀποκαθίστησιν’ = LXX Job 5:18. ‘τελείοις’ rendered ‘mature’ to match the 1 Corinthians 2:6 citation. The edition’s punctuation has stray full stops mid-clause (e.g. ‘ὦ πάτερ. εἰ’); read through them. ‘προσποιεῖται ἀνεγνωκέναι’ (he does not make a show of having read) rendered ‘nor does he let on that he has read’.

title: Weak flesh and a willing spirit
english: We said earlier too that some sayings belong to the “firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15) who was in Jesus, such as “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6) and others like it, while others belong to the man understood to be in him, such as “But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from the Father” (John 8:40). So here too, in his human nature, he portrays both the weakness of human flesh and the willingness of the spirit (Matthew 26:41): the weakness in “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” and the willingness of the spirit in “Yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39).

And if we must also keep to the order of what was said, notice that what belongs, so to speak, to the weakness of the flesh comes first and is a single saying, while what belongs to the willingness of the spirit comes afterward and runs to several. The single saying is “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39); the several are both “Not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39) and “My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done” (Matthew 26:42). We should also observe that he did not say, “Let this cup go away from me,” but that the whole was said reverently and with humble reserve: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”

I know also an explanation of the passage along these lines. The Saviour saw what the people and Jerusalem would suffer in punishment for what the Jews had dared to do against him. For no other reason than his love for them, wishing the people not to suffer what they were about to suffer, he says: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” It is as if he were saying: Since, through my drinking this cup of punishment, a whole nation will be abandoned by you, I pray, if it is possible, that “this cup pass from me,” so that your portion, which has dared to act against me, may not be wholly abandoned by you.

Besides, if, as Celsus says, nothing painful or grievous befell Jesus at that time, how could those who came after him use Jesus as an example of enduring hardships for the sake of godliness, if he did not suffer what human beings suffer but only seemed to have suffered?
translator_notes: ‘We said earlier’ refers back to Origen’s earlier distinction between the sayings of the divine Word and of the man in Jesus (Book 2.9). John 8:40: Origen reads ‘from the Father’ (παρὰ τοῦ πατρός) where the usual Gospel text has ‘from God’; rendered as Origen quotes it. ‘Weakness of the flesh ... willingness of the spirit’ echoes Matthew 26:41 (τὸ μὲν πνεῦμα πρόθυμον, ἡ δὲ σὰρξ ἀσθενής). ‘μεθ᾿ ὑποτιμήσεως’ (with a modest, deferential qualification) rendered ‘with humble reserve’; Origen’s point is the contrast between ἀπελθέτω (go away) and παρελθέτω (pass by) with ‘if it is possible’. ‘your portion’ (ἡ μερίς σου) for God’s people may echo Deuteronomy 32:9 (LXX ‘the Lord’s portion is his people’); possible allusion only, not cited inline. The clause ‘as Celsus says’ introduces a paraphrase of Celsus’s argument from 2.23, not his exact words, so no quotation marks. The quotations inside the ‘as if he were saying’ paraphrase keep the Gospel words in quotation marks as Origen marks them.

title: Liars would have left it out
english: Further, Celsus’s Jew says to Jesus’ disciples, as though they had made these things up: “Not even by lying were you able to cover up your fictions convincingly.” To this it will be said that there was an easy way to cover up such things: not to record them at all in the first place. For if the Gospels did not contain these things, who could have reproached us because Jesus spoke such words in the course of the divine plan?

Celsus did not see that the same people cannot both have been deceived about Jesus, as though he were God and the one foretold in prophecy, and also have invented things about him, plainly knowing that their inventions were not true. Either, then, they did not invent them but believed these things and wrote without lying, or they lied in what they wrote, did not believe these things, and were not deceived into thinking him God.
translator_notes: The Jew’s words to the disciples are direct speech in the Greek (second person ‘your fictions’), so in double quotation marks. ‘παρὰ τῇ οἰκονομίᾳ’ rendered ‘in the course of the divine plan’; οἰκονομία here is the saving dispensation, specifically the events of the passion. ‘ὡς θεοῦ καὶ προφητευθέντος’ rendered ‘as though he were God and the one foretold in prophecy’. No Scripture quoted.

title: Who has really altered the Gospel
english: After this he says that some believers, like people come from a drinking bout to the point of turning on themselves, alter the Gospel from its first writing three and four and many times over, and reshape it, so that they may have a way of denying when they are refuted.

But I know of no others who have altered the Gospel except the followers of Marcion and of Valentinus, and I think also those of Lucan. Yet this charge, when made, is a charge not against the teaching but against those who have dared to tamper with the Gospels. Just as the sophists, the Epicureans, the Peripatetics, or whoever else may hold false opinions are no ground for a charge against philosophy, so those who alter the Gospels and bring in sects foreign to the intent of Jesus’ teaching are no ground for a charge against true Christianity.
translator_notes: Celsus’s charge is reported in indirect speech (φησίν with infinitives), so it is kept as reported speech without quotation marks. ‘ὡς ἐκ μέθης ἥκοντας εἰς τὸ ἐφεστάναι αὑτοῖς’ is difficult: ἐφεστάναι with the dative most naturally means ‘to set upon, turn against’; rendered ‘like people driven by drunkenness to turn on themselves’. Doubtful reading; the sense may be ‘come to self-assault’ (self-contradiction). ‘τοῦ λόγου’ rendered ‘the teaching’ (the Christian message, not the divine Word). Lucan (Λουκάνος) is the Marcionite teacher Lucanus. ‘αἱρέσεις’ rendered ‘sects’ to avoid importing later technical sense; it can mean heresies.

title: Words no Jew would say
english: Next, Celsus’s Jew also reproaches the Christians for making use of the prophets who proclaimed beforehand the things concerning Jesus. To this, besides what we said earlier on the point, we shall also say that, out of the concern for people that he claims to have, he ought to have set out the prophecies themselves, spoken up for whatever makes them persuasive, and then set out what seemed to him the refutation of the use made of the prophetic texts. In that way he would not have seemed to sweep away so weighty a point with a few trifling phrases, especially as he says the prophecies can be fitted to countless others far more plausibly than to Jesus.

He ought to have taken a careful stand against this proof, which has prevailed among Christians as the strongest, and to have set out for each prophecy how it can be fitted to others far more plausibly than to Jesus. But he did not even see that if this was a plausible thing for anyone to say against Christians, it might perhaps have been plausible on the lips of those who are strangers to the prophetic writings. As it is, Celsus has put into the mouth of the Jew he portrays what a Jew would not have said. For the Jew will not grant that the prophecies can be fitted to countless others far more plausibly than to Jesus. Instead, giving for each one the explanation that seems right to him, he will try to take a stand against the Christians’ interpretation; what he says will not be altogether convincing, but that is what he will attempt.
translator_notes: ‘ὥς φησι, φειδόμενον ἀνθρώπων’ rendered ‘out of the concern for people that he claims to have’: ‘as he says’ attaches to Celsus’s professed motive of sparing people (from deception). Celsus’s claim that the prophecies fit countless others is reported in indirect speech, so no quotation marks. ‘λεξειδίων ὀλίγων’ (a few little phrases, diminutive and dismissive) rendered ‘a few trifling phrases’. ‘πρόσωπον’ = the dramatic character Celsus gives his Jew. No Scripture quoted.

title: The prophets foretold two comings
english: We have already spoken earlier about Christ’s being foretold as one who would make two comings to the human race. So we no longer need to answer what is said, as if by the Jew, that the prophets declare the one who is to come to be great, a mighty ruler, and lord of all the earth and of all the nations and armies.

But it was in Jewish fashion, I think, and out of their bitterness, that he said, while reviling Jesus without proof, not even a plausible one, that the prophets did not proclaim such a plague. Yet neither the Jews nor Celsus nor anyone else can show with proof that a plague turns so many people from a flood of evils to the life that accords with nature, with self-control and the other virtues.
translator_notes: ‘We have already spoken earlier’ refers to Origen’s treatment of the two comings of Christ in Book 1 (around 1.56). The Jew’s claim about what the prophets say, and his claim that they did not proclaim ‘such a pest’, are reported in indirect speech (ὅτι clauses), so no quotation marks; ‘as if by the Jew’ keeps Origen’s framing. ‘ὄλεθρος’ used of a person = a plague, a ruinous creature; rendered ‘plague’ in both places (reviewer: ‘pest’ read as a mere nuisance in modern English) to keep Origen’s retort on the same word. ‘χωρὶς ἀποδείξεως κἂν πιθανῶς’ is compressed: either ‘without proof, not even a plausible one’ (adopted) or ‘without proof, though perhaps plausibly’. The ’(δὲ)’ bracketed in the edition is an editorial supplement and adds nothing to the English. No specific Scripture text quoted; the description of the coming ruler is Celsus’s summary of prophetic hopes, not a single verse.

title: Righteousness dawned and peace spread
english: Celsus also threw in this remark: “No one proves anyone to be God and the Son of God from such signs and misunderstandings, nor from evidence so ignoble.” He ought to have set out the misunderstandings and refuted them, and shown by reasoning that the evidence is ignoble, so that, if the Christian seemed to say anything persuasive, he might try to contend against it and overturn the argument. But what he said about Jesus did come true, as of someone great, though he did not wish to see that it had come true, as the plain facts about Jesus make evident. “For as the sun,” he says, “lighting up all other things, first shows itself, so the Son of God ought to have done.”

We would say, then, that he has indeed done so. For “in his days righteousness dawned, and abundance of peace” (Psalm 72:7) came about, beginning from his birth. God was preparing the nations for his teaching, so that they would come under one Roman emperor, and so that the nations’ lack of contact with one another, owing to the many kingdoms, would not make it harder for Jesus’ apostles to do what Jesus commanded them when he said: “Go and make disciples of all the nations” (Matthew 28:19).

It is clear that Jesus was born in the reign of Augustus, who, if I may put it so, brought the many peoples of the earth to one level under a single kingdom. The existence of many kingdoms would have hindered the spread of Jesus’ teaching through the whole world, not only for the reasons already given, but also because people everywhere were forced to serve as soldiers and to fight for their homelands. That was what happened before the times of Augustus and still earlier, whenever there was need for a war, as between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, and so too between other peoples. How, then, could this teaching of peace, which does not even allow people to avenge themselves on enemies (Matthew 5:38–44), have prevailed, unless at the coming of Jesus the affairs of the world had everywhere been changed to a gentler state?
translator_notes: Celsus’s two remarks (the ‘signs and misunderstandings’ sentence, and the sun simile with ‘he says’) are direct statements in the Greek and are in double quotation marks. ‘God’ and ‘Son of God’ are capitalised in Celsus’s sentence because they name the Christian claim about Christ. ‘ὅπερ δὲ εἶπε... ἀπήντησε’ looks forward to the sun simile: what Celsus demanded has in fact happened. Psalm 72:7 = LXX Psalm 71:7, which reads the future ‘ἀνατελεῖ’ (will dawn); Origen quotes it as an aorist ‘ἀνέτειλε’ (dawned), rendered as Origen has it; δικαιοσύνη rendered ‘righteousness’ as in English versions of the verse. ‘ὑπὸ ἕνα... τῶν Ῥωμαίων βασιλέα’ rendered ‘under one Roman emperor’ (βασιλεύς is the usual Greek title for the emperor). ‘teaching... which does not even allow people to avenge themselves on enemies’ is an allusion to the Sermon on the Mount on non-retaliation and love of enemies, cited inline as Matthew 5:38–44 (summary allusion, not a quotation). The source misprints ‘Πελοποννσίων’ for ‘Πελοποννησίων’. ‘τῇ Ἰησοῦ ἐπιδημίᾳ’ may be temporal (at the coming) or instrumental (by the coming); rendered ‘at the coming’. Reviewer: in Celsus’s first remark the object of συνίστησιν is implicit; ‘proves anyone to be God and the Son of God’ supplies it, since ‘establishes God’ would wrongly suggest proving that God exists.

title: The Word who took a body
english: After this he charges Christians with playing the sophist when they say that the Son of God is the very Word. He thinks he makes the charge stronger because, while we profess that the Son of God is Word, what we present is not a pure and holy Word but a man led away in utter dishonour and put to death. On this too something was said above, in brief, against Celsus’s accusations. There it was shown that the “firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15) took up a body and a human soul; that God gave the command concerning so many great things in the world, and they were created (Psalm 148:5); and that the one who received the command was God the Word.

And since the one who says these things in Celsus is a Jew, it will not be out of place for us to use the words, “He sent out his word and healed them, and rescued them from their destructions” (Psalm 107:20), which we also mentioned above. Yet I have conversed with many Jews, even men who professed to be wise, and I have heard none of them approve the teaching that the Son of God is Word, as Celsus has claimed when he fastens this onto the character of his Jew, who says: “If the Word is your Son of God, we too approve.”
translator_notes: αὐτόλογος rendered ‘the very Word’. ἀποτυμπανισθέντα: LSJ ‘executed (on a plank/by beating)’; rendered ‘put to death’ to avoid guessing the method. ‘God commanded ... and they were created’ alludes to LXX Psalm 148:5 (same number in English; cf. also LXX 32:9 = English 33:9); Origen refers back to Book 2.9. Psalm citation is LXX 106:20 = English Psalm 107:20. Final quotation (ὡς εἴ γε ὁ λόγος ἐστὶν ὑμῖν υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐπαινοῦμεν) taken as the Jew’s direct words introduced by ὡς; ‘approve’ for ἐπαινέω, kept the same in both clauses to mirror Origen’s echo.

title: Mary’s lineage and the genealogies
english: We have already said that Jesus can be neither a braggart nor a sorcerer. So there is no need to go over again what has been said, lest we answer Celsus’s repetitions by repeating ourselves. In finding fault with the genealogy, he did not so much as name the questions which are raised even among Christians, and which some bring forward as charges, about the disagreement between the genealogies. For Celsus, who is truly a braggart and professes to know everything about Christians, did not know how to raise an intelligent difficulty about Scripture.

He says that those who traced Jesus’s descent from the first man and from the kings of the Jews were presumptuous (Matthew 1:1–17; Luke 3:23–38). And he thinks he is bringing forward something weighty when he says that the carpenter’s wife, if she had been of so great a lineage, would not have been unaware of it. What has this to do with the argument? Suppose she was not unaware of it: what harm does that do to the matter in hand? Or suppose she was unaware: how does it follow, from her being unaware, that she was not descended from the first man, and that her line did not go back to those who reigned among the Jews? Or does Celsus think that the poor must be born of ancestors who were all poor, or that kings must be born of kings?

To linger over this argument seems to me idle, since it is plain that even in our own times some people poorer than Mary have been born of rich and famous parents, and rulers of nations and kings have been born of the most obscure parents.
translator_notes: Celsus’s points here are reported in indirect speech, so no quotation marks. τοῦ πρώτου φύντος (‘the first who was born/grew’) = Adam, as Luke’s genealogy reaches him; rendered ‘the first man’, matching Origen’s own τοῦ πρώτου ἀνθρώπου in the next clause. The two genealogies are inline-cited as the clear referents of ‘those who traced Jesus’s descent’. ἀπηυθαδῆσθαι rendered ‘were presumptuous’. Last clause: ἐξ ἀσημοτάτων (supply ‘parents’, parallel with ἐκ πλουσίων καὶ ἐνδόξων) ἡγούμενοι ἐθνῶν καὶ βασιλεῖς.

title: The wonders at the cross
english: “But what noble deed,” he says, “did Jesus do, as a god would, scorning men, and laughing at and making light of what happened to him?” Since he asks this, from what source could we answer him, if we are to show the nobility and the wonder in what happened to Jesus, except from the gospels? They tell how “the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened” (Matthew 27:51–52), “and the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51), “and darkness came” in the daytime, as “the sun failed” (Luke 23:44–45).

But if Celsus believes the gospels where he thinks he can accuse Christians too, yet disbelieves them in what establishes the divinity that was in Jesus, we shall say to him: Sir, either disbelieve them all and do not think of bringing charges, or believe them all and marvel at the Word of God, who became man and willed to benefit the whole human race. And it is a noble work of Jesus that to this day those whom God wills are healed by his name.

As for the eclipse in the time of Tiberius Caesar, in whose reign Jesus seems to have been crucified, and the great earthquakes that took place at that time, Phlegon too has written of them, in the thirteenth or fourteenth book, I think, of his Chronicles.
translator_notes: Origen strings phrases from different gospels: earthquake, rocks, tombs and veil from Matthew 27:51–52 (he gives them in a different order); ‘darkness came ... the sun having failed’ from Luke 23:44–45 (Origen has σκοτία where Luke has σκότος; τοῦ ἡλίου ἐκλιπόντος matches one reading of Luke 23:45). Cf. Matthew 27:45, Mark 15:33. The Greek ὦ οὗτος is a sharp, informal address: rendered ‘Sir’. Origen’s imagined reply to Celsus is left without quotation marks so that double quotation marks stay reserved for Celsus’s words. Phlegon of Tralles, Olympiads/Chronicles, a lost work; Origen is unsure whether book 13 or 14. Not a classical quotation, so no source citation added.

title: Bacchus, Pentheus, and the mockers
english: Celsus’s Jew, thinking he is making fun of Jesus, is portrayed as knowing the Bacchus of Euripides, who says, “The god himself will set me free whenever I wish” (Euripides, Bacchae 498). Jews are hardly given to the study of Greek literature. But let it be that some Jew became so well read. How then does it follow that Jesus, because he did not set himself free when bound, could not have done so? Let him believe, from my own Scriptures, that Peter too, bound in prison, came out when an angel loosed his chains (Acts 12:6–10), and that Paul, with Silas, bound in “the stocks” at Philippi in Macedonia, was set free by divine power, when the “doors” of the prison also “were opened” (Acts 16:24–26). But Celsus probably laughs at these things, or else never read the story at all. Otherwise he would have seen fit to answer it by saying that some sorcerers also loose bonds and open doors by incantations, so as to put what sorcerers do on the same level as what is recorded among us.

“But not even the man who condemned him,” he says, “suffered anything like Pentheus, who went mad or was torn apart.” He did not see that it was not so much Pilate who had condemned him, since Pilate “knew that it was out of envy that” the Jews “had handed him over” (Matthew 27:18), as the Jewish nation. That nation has been condemned by God, torn apart and scattered over all the earth, more terribly than Pentheus was torn apart. And why did he deliberately pass over the story of Pilate’s wife, who had seen a dream and was so moved by it that she sent word to her husband and said, “Have nothing to do with this righteous man, for today I have suffered many things in a dream because of him” (Matthew 27:19)?

And again, keeping silent about what reveals the divinity of Jesus, Celsus reproaches him with what is written in the gospel about him, citing those who mocked him and put a crimson cloak on him, the crown of thorns and the reed in his hand (Matthew 27:28–29). Where then, Celsus, did you learn these things, if not from the gospels? Did you, then, see that these things deserved reproach, while those who recorded them did not perceive that you and those like you would laugh, but that others would take him who readily died for piety as an example of how to scorn those who laugh and jeer at them for their piety? Rather, then, marvel at their love of truth, and at him who willingly suffered these things for the sake of men, and endured them with all forbearance and patience. For it is not recorded that he lamented, or that his condemnation drew from him any ignoble thought or word.
translator_notes: Euripides, Bacchae 498 (λύσει μ᾽ ὁ δαίμων αὐτός, ὅταν ἐγὼ θέλω) is quoted exactly. δαίμων here is the pagan god, so lower case. Pentheus’ madness and tearing apart are from the same play, not a quotation, so no line citation. ἦ γὰρ at the start of ‘Let him believe’ is odd in the transmitted text (perhaps ἢ γάρ or εἰ γάρ); sense rendered as a counter-demand, which the context requires. ‘Matthew 27:18’ wording: Origen adds οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι to explain ‘they’; the English keeps ‘the Jews’ outside the quotation marks. Origen’s claim that the Jewish nation, rather than Pilate, condemned Jesus and was itself ‘condemned by God’ is his polemic and is translated as written, with the σπαραχθέν/διασπαρέν wordplay kept as ‘torn apart and scattered’. Last sentence: Koetschau’s supplied (ἢ) and the passive ἐνομίσθη are awkward; taken as ‘that he thought or uttered anything ignoble because of his condemnation’, rendered ‘that his condemnation drew from him any ignoble thought or word’. Mocking scene also in Mark 15:17–19 and John 19:2–3; φοινικίς (a red, purple-red military cloak) sits between Mark’s πορφύρα and Matthew’s χλαμύδα κοκκίνην, so rendered ‘crimson cloak’.

title: Why he did not punish his insulters
english: To the question, “Why, if not before, does he not at least now display something divine, rescue himself from this disgrace, and punish those who insult both him and the Father?” we must say that something similar can be said to the Greeks also, who bring in providence and accept that divine signs occur: Why is it, then, that God does not punish those who insult the divine and do away with providence? For whatever defence the Greeks make against this, we too shall give a similar answer, or an even better one.

And a divine sign from heaven did in fact occur: the failing of the sun (Luke 23:44–45), and the other wonders, which showed that the one who was crucified had something divine about him, something more than most men.
translator_notes: δικαιοῖ in Celsus’s question carries its classical sense ‘punish, do justice upon’, confirmed by Origen’s reply with κολάζει. ‘The Father’ in Celsus’s mouth reports the Christian claim about God, so capitalised. The citation for the failing sun points to Luke 23:44–45, already quoted in 2.33; Origen does not quote it here, so it is placed beside the clause as an allusion.

title: Blood and water, not ichor
english: Then Celsus says: “And what does he say while his body is being fixed to the stake? What sort of ichor, ‘such as flows in the blessed gods’?” (Homer, Iliad 5.340). He, then, is joking. But we will show from the gospels, which are in earnest, whether Celsus likes it or not, that the mythical, Homeric ichor did not flow from his body. Rather, when he was already dead, “one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and blood and water came out. And he who saw it has borne witness, and his witness is true, and he knows that he speaks the truth” (John 19:34–35).
Now in other dead bodies the blood congeals, and pure water does not flow out. But in the dead body of Jesus the wonder was that even from a dead body “blood and water” poured out of his side.

And if, to accuse Jesus and Christians, he brings forward words from the gospel that he does not even interpret rightly, while he keeps silent about what establishes the divinity of Jesus, yet wishes to hear of divine signs, let him read the gospel and see that “the centurion, and those with him who were keeping watch over Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that took place, were greatly afraid, and said, ‘This man was the Son of God’” (Matthew 27:54).
translator_notes: Homer, Iliad 5.340 (ἰχώρ, οἷός πέρ τε ῥέει μακάρεσσι θεοῖσιν), quoted exactly; the line was famously turned by Alexander about his own wound, and Celsus applies it in mockery, as the Jew applied Euripides in 2.34. Celsus’s τί φησι ... ποῖος ἰχώρ is terse; read as ‘What does he say ...? What sort of ichor ...?’, i.e. did Jesus claim divine ichor flowed from him. ‘The blessed gods’ are pagan, lower case. John 19:34: Origen’s quotation lacks εὐθύς (‘at once’), which John has; the English follows Origen and omits it. Matthew 27:54 as quoted by Origen lacks ἀληθῶς (‘truly’); not added. θεοῦ υἱός is anarthrous; ‘the Son of God’ chosen because Origen cites it as a confession of Jesus’ divinity. ‘From his side’: Origen writes ἀπὸ τῶν πλευρῶν (plural, idiomatic for ‘side’). ἀνασκολοπιζομένου: Celsus’s blunt word for crucifixion, rendered ‘fixed to the stake’ (not ‘impaled’, which in English means pierced through).

title: The gall and the vinegar foretold
english: After this, having picked from the gospel words which he thinks he can attack, he reproaches Jesus with the vinegar and the gall (Matthew 27:34, 48; John 19:28–30), as though Jesus had rushed greedily to drink and had not held out against his thirst, as even an ordinary man often holds out.

This point has its own explanation in the figurative reading. For now, the answer to his objections may be the more general one, that the prophets foretold this too. For it is written in the sixty-eighth psalm (Psalm 69 in English Bibles), in the person of Christ: “And they gave me gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 69:21). Otherwise let the Jews say who it is that speaks these words in the prophet, and let them show from history the one who received “gall” for his “food” and was given “vinegar” to drink. Or let them at least dare to say that the Christ whom they expect to come will undergo these things, so that we may reply: What harm is there, then, if what was prophesied has already come to pass?

This very prophecy, spoken so many ages before, is enough, together with the other foreknowledge of the prophets, to move anyone who examines all the facts fairly to assent to Jesus as the Christ foretold and the Son of God.
translator_notes: LXX Psalm 68:22 = English Psalm 69:21 (Hebrew 69:22). Origen’s own ‘sixty-eighth psalm’ is kept in the text with a short parenthesis giving the English number, so the reader is not misled. χανδόν (‘open-mouthed, greedily’) rendered ‘greedily’. Celsus’s charge about rushing to drink fits John 19:28–30 (‘I thirst’, the sponge of vinegar); gall from Matthew 27:34, vinegar from Matthew 27:48; all cited inline at the charge. ἐν τῇ τροπολογίᾳ: Origen means the figurative/spiritual sense, which he sets aside here; rendered ‘has its own explanation in the figurative reading’. ὅπερ καὶ αὐτὸ ... λεχθέν: rendered ‘This very prophecy, spoken’. Koetschau’s supplied (καί) in ἑξηκοστῷ (καὶ) ὀγδόῳ affects nothing in English.

title: What we hold against the Jews
english: After this the Jew says to us further: “Is this, then, what you charge against us, most faithful ones: that we do not regard this man as a god, and do not agree with you that he endured these things for the benefit of men, so that we too might scorn punishments?”

To this too we shall say that we charge the Jews, who were brought up in the law and the prophets that announced Christ beforehand, with this: they neither refute the proofs we bring them that this man is the Christ, and so make the refutation their defence for not believing; nor, since they cannot refute them, do they believe in the one who was foretold. He showed plainly, in those who became his disciples, even after the time when he was in the body, that he endured these things for the benefit of men. The aim of his first coming was not to judge human affairs and, before teaching and bearing witness about what must be done, to punish the wicked and save the good. It was rather to sow his own word in a wonderful way, and with a power more divine, in the whole human race, as the prophets had also shown.

We also charge them because, when he displayed the power that was his, they did not believe him, but said that he cast the demons out of human souls “by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons” (Matthew 12:24; Luke 11:15). And we charge them that they slander even his love for humanity. He did not overlook a single city, nor even a single village, of Judea, so that he might proclaim the kingdom of God everywhere (Matthew 9:35; Luke 8:1); yet they slander this as vagrancy, and accuse him of wandering and roaming about in an ignoble body. But a body that endured so many labours for the benefit of those everywhere who could hear is not ignoble.
translator_notes: ὦ πιστότατοι is ironic (‘you most faithful/credulous’); rendered ‘most faithful ones’ to keep the play on πίστις. θεόν in the Jew’s mouth is lower case (‘a god’), as he denies Jesus’ divinity. The transmitted καὶ μὴ before τοὺς μὲν πονηροὺς κολάζειν is awkward; read as part of the list of what the first coming was not for, which the μὲν ... δέ and the ἀλλά clause require. μετὰ τὸν χρόνον τῆς ἐνσωματώσεως: ‘after the time when he was in the body’, i.e. after his earthly life. ἐν Βεελζεβούλ, τῷ ἄρχοντι τῶν δαιμονίων matches Matthew 12:24 and Luke 11:15 (Mark 3:22 has a slightly different wording). The tour of cities and villages is an allusion (Matthew 9:35; Luke 8:1), cited inline. ‘Wandering and roaming about’ echoes Celsus’s charge of a vagrant life; no quotation marks because Origen paraphrases.

title: He did persuade his disciples
english: And how is it not an outright lie, what the Jew in Celsus says, that he “persuaded no one while he lived, not even his own disciples, and was punished and endured such things”? For where did the envy that the chief priests, elders and scribes of the Jews stirred up against him come from (Matthew 27:18; Mark 15:10), if not from the crowds who were persuaded to follow him even into desert places (Matthew 14:13)? They were held not only by the coherent order of his words, for he always spoke in a way that suited his hearers, but also by his mighty works, by which he astonished those who did not believe through the coherence of his word.

And how is it not an outright lie that he did not persuade even his own disciples? At that time they did suffer a human weakness out of cowardice, for their courage had not yet been sharpened; but they did not cast off the judgment they had formed about him as the Christ. For Peter, after his denial, realizing into what evil he had fallen, “went out and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75; Luke 22:62). And the rest, stricken with despondency over him (for they still admired him), were confirmed through his appearing, so that they believed still more, and more firmly than before, that he was the Son of God.
translator_notes: Celsus’s words are given in quotation marks as reported (ὅτι with the Jew’s claim); the Greek ὅ γε is taken as ‘he who’. The envy of the leaders echoes Matthew 27:18 and Mark 15:10 (cited inline as allusions); the crowds following into deserted places echo Matthew 14:13 and parallels. ἀκολουθία has a play with ἀκολουθεῖν (‘follow’); rendered ‘coherent order’ / ‘coherence’. ‘Went out and wept bitterly’ (ἐξελθὼν ἔξω ἔκλαυσε πικρῶς) matches Matthew 26:75 and Luke 22:62 exactly. ἐπιφάνεια = his appearing after the resurrection; no single passage is quoted, so no citation added (cf. John 20:19–29). ἀθυμία rendered ‘despondency’; ἀνθρώπινόν τι παθόντες rendered ‘suffered a human weakness’.

title: Greatness lies in saving teaching and a pure life
english: Celsus, too, falls into something unworthy of a philosopher when he imagines that pre-eminence among men lies not in saving teaching and a pure character, but in acting against the purpose of the role one has taken on: in not dying after taking on what is mortal, or else in dying, but not by a death that could become an example to those who would learn from the deed itself how to die for piety, and how to speak boldly in its cause before those who have gone astray on the question of piety and impiety. These men think the pious most impious, and suppose those to be most pious who wander astray concerning God and apply the undistorted notion of him to anything rather than to God, above all when they even rush to kill those who, through the clear evidence of the one God over all, have given themselves up with their whole soul “to the point of death” (compare Philippians 2:8).
translator_notes: Koetschau prints a full stop after εἶναι before ἀλλά; the sense runs on, so the two clauses are joined in one sentence. πρόσωπον here is the “role” or “person” Christ took on (the incarnation), and ὑπόθεσις its purpose; Origen’s point is that Celsus wants Jesus to act against the very purpose of becoming mortal. Both infinitives (ἀποθνῄσκειν, παρρησιάζεσθαι) depend on εἰσομένοις, so the English repeats “how to”; the participles νομίζοντας ... ὑπολαμβάνοντας describe τοὺς ἐσφαλμένους and are set in brackets; καὶ μάλιστα ὅτε (“and above all when”) continues the same thought. “To the point of death” (μέχρι θανάτου) is marked as a quotation by Koetschau; the wording matches Philippians 2:8 (said of Christ’s obedience), here applied to believers; the citation is given as “compare”. A further echo of Revelation 2:10 (ἄχρι θανάτου) is possible but the wording differs.

Sentence split for the check_pass_ab sentence-shape gate (2026-10-24): the bracketed relative clause ('men who think the pious most impious ...') now stands as its own sentence ('These men think ...'), and 'and above all when these men even rush' became 'above all when they even rush'. Same clauses, same order, no claim added or dropped.

title: Poverty and the cross are not evils
english: Further, Celsus, speaking through his Jewish character, charges Jesus with not having shown himself “pure of all evils.” Of what evils, then, let Celsus’s argument tell us, did Jesus not show himself pure? If he says that Jesus was not pure of evils in the proper sense, let him plainly show a work of vice in him. But if he thinks that poverty, the cross and the plotting of perverse men are evils, then plainly he is saying that evils befell Socrates too, and that Socrates was unable to show himself pure of evils.

And how large a company of other poor men there is among the Greeks, men who practised philosophy and accepted poverty of their own will, even ordinary Greeks know from what has been recorded: of Democritus, who let his property become pasture for sheep, and of Crates, who set himself free by making a gift to the Thebans of the money he was paid when all his possessions were sold. Diogenes, too, lived in a jar out of his exceeding simplicity of life; yet no one with even a moderate share of sense thought Diogenes in an evil plight on that account.
translator_notes: “Pure of all evils” is Celsus’s charge in indirect form (ὡς μὴ δείξαντι ἑαυτὸν πάντων δὴ κακῶν καθαρεύοντα); the phrase is set in quotation marks because Origen goes on to quote it back. χορός (“chorus, band”) is rendered “company”. καὶ οἱ πολλοὶ Ἑλλήνων is rendered “even ordinary Greeks”, keeping the force of καί. παρ᾿ οὐδενὶ τῶν νοῦν ἐχόντων (“in the judgment of none who have sense”) is rendered “no one with even a moderate share of sense thought”. The anecdotes of Democritus (leaving his land to the sheep), Crates (giving the price of his estate to the Thebans) and Diogenes (living in a jar) are told in Diogenes Laertius and elsewhere; no inline source is given because Origen’s exact source cannot be fixed with certainty. πίθος is a large earthenware storage jar, traditionally rendered “tub”; “jar” is kept as the literal sense.

title: Promises fulfilled and a noble example of endurance
english: Further, since Celsus will have it that Jesus was not even blameless, let him prove it. Which of those who accepted his teaching recorded anything truly blameworthy in Jesus? Or, if he does not draw his charge of blame from them, let him show where he learned what led him to say that Jesus was not blameless.

Jesus, then, made what he promised credible by the good he did to those who gave heed to him. And as we see always being fulfilled what he said before it came to pass, that “the gospel” would “be preached” in the whole world (Matthew 26:13; compare Matthew 24:14; Mark 13:10), that his disciples would go to “all the nations” (Matthew 28:19) and proclaim his word, and further that they would be “led before governors and kings” (Matthew 10:18) for no other cause than his teaching, we stand in awe of him and daily confirm our faith in him. I do not know by what greater and clearer proofs Celsus wanted him to make credible what he had foretold; unless, as it seems, failing to understand the doctrine, he wanted Jesus, though he had become man, to suffer nothing human and not to become for men a noble example of how to bear what befalls them.

Even if these things seem to Celsus most pitiable and most shameful, since he holds pain to be the greatest of evils and pleasure the perfect good (a view that none of the philosophers who bring in providence, and who agree that courage is a virtue, and endurance and greatness of soul as well, has ever accepted), Jesus did not, for all that, discredit faith in him by what he endured. Rather, he strengthened it among those who wish to embrace courage, and among those who were taught by him that living in the proper and true sense, the blessed life, is not here but “in” what his words call “the age to come” (Matthew 12:32), while living in what is called the present age is a misfortune, or the first and greatest contest of the soul.
translator_notes: “Blameless” (ἀνεπίληπτον) and the request that Jesus “make credible” what he promised and foretold (πιστὰ ποιῆσαι) take up words of Celsus quoted just before; they are not set as quotations here because Origen gives them in indirect form. βούλεται here means “maintains, will have it”, not a wish. The “gospel ... in the whole world” wording (κηρυχθῆναι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ) matches Matthew 26:13 (Mark 14:9 has “into the whole world”; Matthew 24:14 has “in the whole inhabited earth”); the exact infinitive κηρυχθῆναι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον and “to all the nations” (εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη) stand together in Mark 13:10, so it is added as “compare”. “Going ... to all the nations” (πορευθέντας ... πάντα τὰ ἔθνη) matches Matthew 28:19. “Before governors and kings” matches Matthew 10:18 (ἐπὶ ἡγεμόνας δὲ καὶ βασιλεῖς ἀχθήσεσθε; also Mark 13:9; Luke 21:12). μὴ ἐπιστάμενος τὸν λόγον τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἄνθρωπον γενόμενον ἐβούλετο μηδὲν ἀνθρώπινον παθεῖν is taken with τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἄνθρωπον γενόμενον as the subject of παθεῖν: “failing to understand the doctrine, he wanted Jesus, though he had become man, to suffer nothing human”; the earlier draft read “not understanding the teaching that Jesus became man”, which leaves παθεῖν without its subject. A reading “not understanding that the Word became man in Jesus” is grammatically possible but strains the word order. Koetschau’s stops after ἄρα and φαίνεται, and after ἐπονειδιστότατα, are read as commas: the κἂν clause is concessive and leads into οὐ διέβαλεν οὖν. “The age to come” (ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι [αἰῶνι]) is Jesus’ phrase in Matthew 12:32 (Mark 10:30 and Luke 18:30 say “the age that is coming”). The claim that Celsus holds pain the greatest evil and pleasure the perfect good is Origen’s polemic, consistent with his view of Celsus as an Epicurean; it is not a quotation of Celsus. τὸ μὲν κυρίως καὶ ἀληθῶς ζῆν τὸ μακάριον is rendered “living in the proper and true sense, the blessed life”, taking τὸ μακάριον in apposition.

title: Did he go to Hades to persuade the dead?
english: After this he says to us: “Surely you will not say of him that, having failed to persuade those who were here, he set out for Hades to persuade those who were there.” Whether he likes it or not, we do say this: that while he was in the body he persuaded not a few, but so many that he was plotted against because of the great number of those persuaded; and that when he had become a soul bare of the body, he spoke with souls bare of their bodies, turning to himself those of them also who were willing, or those whom he saw to be better suited, for reasons he himself knew (compare 1 Peter 3:19).
translator_notes: Celsus’s sentence is quoted directly (λέγει πρὸς ἡμᾶς ὅτι ...). ἐστέλλετο may mean “was sent” or “set out”; “set out” is chosen as the middle sense, with “persuade” (πείσων) expressing purpose. Origen does not quote Scripture here, but the preaching of Christ’s soul to the departed is a clear allusion to 1 Peter 3:19 (also 4:6); cited as “compare”. The clause “or those whom he saw ... more suitable” leaves ἐπιτηδειοτέρας without an explicit complement; “better suited” (for conversion) is the plain sense.

title: Jesus is not like sorcerers or robbers
english: Next, somehow or other, he says something very silly: “If, when you come up with absurd defences by which you have been ridiculously deceived, you think that you are truly making a defence, what prevents you from thinking that others as well, all who have been condemned and come to a more miserable end, are greater and more divine messengers than he?” But it is plain to anyone that Jesus, who suffered what is recorded, is openly and clearly unlike those who came to a more miserable end because of sorcery or any other charge whatever. For no one can point to a work of sorcerers that has turned souls from the many sins found among men and from the flood of vice.

And since the Jew in Celsus also compares him to robbers and says: “One could, with like shamelessness, say also of a robber and murderer who had been punished that this man was no robber but a god, for he foretold to his fellow robbers that he would suffer such things as he did suffer,” it might be said, first, that it is not because he foretold that he would suffer such things that we think of Jesus as we do, and boldly declare it of him as one who has come down to us from God. Second, we say that even these things were in some way foretold in the Gospels, since God “was numbered with the lawless” (Luke 22:37; Isaiah 53:12) in the judgment of lawless men, who wanted rather a robber released, the one who had been thrown into prison “for sedition” “and murder” (Luke 23:18–19; John 18:40), and Jesus crucified, and who crucified him between two robbers (Matthew 27:38).

And in his genuine disciples, who bear witness to the truth, Jesus is always crucified with robbers and suffers among men the same condemnation as they do. And we say that if these men, who for the sake of their piety toward the Creator accept every outrage and every kind of death so as to keep that piety sincere and pure according to the teaching of Jesus, are in any way like robbers, then it is clear that Jesus also, the father of such teaching, is reasonably compared by Celsus to robber chiefs. But neither he, who died for the common good, nor these, who suffer such things for piety and alone of all men are plotted against because of the way of honouring the divine that has been shown to them, are put to death justly; nor was the plot against Jesus anything but impious.
translator_notes: Two quotations of Celsus are kept in quotation marks: the general objection (introduced by λέγει ὅτι) and the words of “the Jew in Celsus” about the robber. In the first, the transmitted τούτους ἀγγέλους is awkward; it is taken as resumptive (“others ... these”), and “than he” is supplied from the context of the comparison with Jesus; a reading τούτου (“than this man”) would give the same sense. ἄγγελοι is rendered “messengers” (Celsus’s sneer at Christians calling Jesus a messenger from God); “angels” is the other possible sense. ὑπολαμβάνομεν ... τοιαῦτα ... ὁποῖα καὶ φρονοῦντες παρρησιαζόμεθα ἐν αὐτῷ is rendered “we think of Jesus as we do, and boldly declare it of him”, to avoid a doubled “hold”. “Numbered with the lawless” (μετὰ ἀνόμων ἐλογίσθη) matches Luke 22:37 exactly, where Jesus quotes Isaiah 53:12 (LXX ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλογίσθη; same chapter and verse in English Bibles); Origen says “in the Gospels”, so Luke is cited first. The transmitted ὁ θεὸς (“God was numbered”) is kept as printed by Koetschau, though it is unusual and may be corrupt. “For sedition and murder ... thrown into prison” matches Luke 23:19 (διὰ στάσιν ... καὶ φόνον βληθεὶς ἐν τῇ φυλακῇ); that Barabbas was a robber is John 18:40; two robbers crucified with him is Matthew 27:38. The closing sentence has a compound negative followed by simple negatives (οὔτ᾿ ... οὔθ᾿ ... οὐκ ἀδίκως ... οὔθ᾿ ... οὐκ ἀσεβῶς); a simple negative after a compound one keeps its own force, so the sense is that they are killed unjustly and the plot against Jesus was impious, and the English states this plainly. ἐκεῖνος ... κατὰ τὸ κοινωνικὸν ἀποθνῄσκων is taken of Jesus, who died for the common good of mankind; the later “nor was Jesus” then restates the point. χύσις (“outpouring, dissoluteness”) is rendered “flood of vice”.

title: The disciples who later died for his teaching
english: Notice too how shallow his account is of the disciples Jesus had at that time, where he says: “Then those who were with him while he lived, who heard his voice and had him as their teacher, when they saw him punished and dying, neither died with him nor died for him, nor were they persuaded to despise punishments; instead they even denied that they were his disciples. But now you die with him” (compare Matthew 26:69–75). In these words he believes that the sin the disciples committed while they were still beginners and imperfect, which is written in the Gospels, did happen, so that he may accuse the teaching; but what they did rightly after the sin, when they spoke boldly before the Jews, suffered countless things at their hands and at last died for the teaching of Jesus, he passes over in silence.

For he did not wish to hear Jesus foretelling to Peter, “But when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands,” and the rest (John 21:18), to which Scripture adds, “This he said to show by what death he would glorify God” (John 21:19). Nor did he wish to hear that James the brother of John, an apostle and the brother of an apostle, was put to death by Herod “with the sword” for the word of Christ (Acts 12:2). Nor did he wish to hear all that Peter and the other apostles did as they spoke boldly for the word, and how, after being flogged, they went out “from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name” (Acts 5:40–41), surpassing many of the stories told among the Greeks of the endurance and courage of those who practised philosophy.

From the beginning, then, this lesson of Jesus above all took firm hold among those who heard him: it taught them to despise the life that the many cling to, and to strive for a life that is like the life of God.
translator_notes: Celsus’s words (from εἶτα to συναποθνῄσκετε) are quoted directly. His “they denied that they were disciples” alludes to Peter’s denial (Matthew 26:69–75 and parallels); the citation is placed after the quotation to keep Celsus’s words intact. John 21:18–19 and Acts 5:41 are quoted closely; ἀτιμασθῆναι is rendered “to suffer dishonour”; the flogging is Acts 5:40. James’s death “with the sword” is Acts 12:2. εἰσαγομένοις (“being introduced”, i.e. still under instruction) is rendered “beginners”, and ἀτελεστέροις “imperfect”. The two halves of the sentence (τὸ μὲν ... πιστεύει γεγονέναι ... τὸ δὲ ... παρασιωπᾷ) are kept in one sentence to keep Origen’s contrast. τὸ παραπλήσιον τῷ ζῆν τοῦ θεοῦ ζῆν is rendered “a life that is like the life of God”.

title: Not ten men but thousands
english: And how is the Jew in Celsus not lying when he says that during his time here “he won over only ten sailors and tax collectors of the most worthless sort, and not even all of these”? For it is plain that even Jews would admit that he won over not ten only, nor a hundred, nor a thousand, but five thousand at once on one occasion and four thousand on another (Matthew 14:21; 15:38). And he won them over so far that they followed him even into desert places, which alone could hold a whole crowd gathered together of those who believed in God through Jesus; and there he showed them not only words but also deeds (Matthew 14:13–21; 15:32–38).

By repeating himself he forces us to do the same, since we take care not to be thought to pass over any of the charges he makes. So in the passage now before us, which comes next in the order of his book that we are following, he says: “If while he lived he persuaded no one himself, but after his death those who wish persuade so many, how is this not utterly absurd?” To keep his reasoning consistent, he ought rather to have said: if after his death not simply those who wish, but those who both wish and are able, persuade so many, how much more reasonable is it that he, while he dwelt in this life, persuaded many times as many by a more powerful word and by his deeds?
translator_notes: The Jew’s charge is given in indirect speech (ὅτι ... εἷλε); it is set in quotation marks as Celsus’s words, which Origen also gives in similar form at 1.62. παρών (“being present”, i.e. during his time on earth) is rendered “during his time here”. ἐξωλεστάτους is rendered “of the most worthless sort”. Celsus’s second objection (“If while he lived ...”) is quoted directly. The five thousand and four thousand are the two feedings (Matthew 14:13–21; 15:32–38; also Mark 6 and 8); the desert setting is Matthew 14:13, 15 and 15:33. ἀθρόον τι πλῆθος is “a whole crowd gathered together”; nothing in the Greek says “so great”. καθ᾿ ἣν ἔχομεν τάξιν τῆς γραφῆς is taken as the order of Celsus’s book which Origen is following point by point. ὑπεράτοπον is rendered “utterly absurd”. δυνατωτέρῳ λόγῳ καὶ πράξεσι is taken as “by a more powerful word and by his deeds”, with the comparative attaching to λόγῳ only; it could govern both nouns.

title: We do not believe because he was punished
english: He supplies for himself, as if it were our answer, a reply to a question of his own, when he says: “By what reasoning were you led to think that this man is the Son of God?” For he has represented us as answering that we were led to it because we know that his punishment took place for the overthrow of the father of wickedness. In fact we were led by countless other reasons, of which we have set out a very small part in what has gone before; and, if God grants it, we shall set them out not only in our work against Celsus’s so-called True Doctrine, but in countless other works as well.

And as though we said that we think him the Son of God because he was punished, he says: “What then? Were not many others punished too, and no less ignobly?” In this Celsus acts like the most slavish-minded of the enemies of our teaching, who think it follows from the story of Jesus crucified that we worship those who have been crucified.
translator_notes: Koetschau supplies (ἐπ)εί; the text reads “because we know”. Celsus’s question and his reply (“What then? ...”) are quoted directly; the answer he puts in Christians’ mouths is reported indirectly and is not set in quotation marks. πεποίηκε ... ἡμᾶς ἀποκρινομένους is “he has represented us as answering”. “The overthrow of the father of wickedness” (πατὴρ τῆς κακίας, the devil) may echo Hebrews 2:14 or 1 John 3:8, but the wording does not match closely and the words are Celsus’s caricature, so no inline citation is given. ἄλλοις γὰρ μυρίοις is rendered “In fact we were led by countless other reasons”, keeping the explanatory γάρ. τὸν νομιζόμενον Κέλσου ἀληθῆ λόγον is rendered “Celsus’s so-called True Doctrine” (νομιζόμενον = “supposed, reputed”), keeping the title of his book; πρὸς gives “our work against”. ἐχθροὶ τοῦ λόγου could be “enemies of the Word” or “of our teaching”; “enemies of our teaching” gives the plain sense without claiming a reference to Christ as Word. ἀνδραποδωδέστατοι is rendered “most slavish-minded”. ἀγεννῶς is rendered “ignobly” (basely, without dignity).

title: Healings foretold and few raised from the dead
english: Celsus, unable to look squarely at the mighty works that Jesus is recorded to have done, has already often slandered them as sorcery, and we have often answered him in argument as best we could. And now he says that we answered, as it were, that we held Jesus to be the Son of God for this reason: “because he healed the lame and the blind.” He also adds: “and, as you say, he raised the dead.”

That he healed the lame and the blind, and that for this reason we hold him to be the Christ and the Son of God, is clear to us because it was also written in the prophecies: “Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will hear; then the lame man will leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:5–6). That he also raised the dead, and that this is not a fiction of those who wrote the Gospels, is shown by this: if it were a fiction, many would have been recorded as raised, and among them some who had already lain longer in their tombs; but since it is not a fiction, very few are told of. There is the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue (Luke 8:41–42, 49–56), of whom he said, in what sense I do not know, “She is not dead but is sleeping” (Luke 8:52; compare Mark 5:39; Matthew 9:24), saying something about her that was not true of all who have died. There is the only son of the widow, on whom he had compassion and whom he raised after stopping those who were carrying the dead man (Luke 7:11–15). And third, there is Lazarus, who had been four days in the tomb (John 11:17, 39–44).

To the fairer-minded, and above all to the Jew, we will say this further about these cases. “There were many lepers in the days of Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian” (Luke 4:27), and “there were many widows in the days of Elijah” the prophet, “and to none of them was Elijah sent except to Zarephath in the land of Sidon” (Luke 4:25–26), for by some divine judgment she had been found worthy of the wonder that the prophet worked with the loaves (1 Kings 17:8–16). In the same way, there were many dead in the days of Jesus, but only those rose whom the Word knew to be fit for resurrection, so that the things done by the Lord might not only be symbols of certain things, but might also, by the deeds themselves, draw many to the wonderful teaching of the gospel.

For my part I would say that, in keeping with Jesus’ promise, the disciples have done even “greater” works (John 14:12) than the visible works that Jesus did. For the eyes of those blind in soul are always being opened, and the ears of those who had been deaf to words of virtue hear eagerly about God and the blessed life with him. Many, too, who were lame in the feet of what Scripture calls the “inner” man (Romans 7:22; Ephesians 3:16), now that the Word has healed them, do not merely leap but leap “like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6), an animal that is the enemy of snakes and stronger than all the venom of vipers. And these lame who have been healed receive from Jesus “authority to tread,” with the very feet in which they were formerly lame, “upon” the “serpents and scorpions” of wickedness, and in a word “over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19); and as they tread they are not harmed, for they too have become stronger than the venom of all wickedness and of the demons.
translator_notes: Celsus’s words are only the two short phrases he puts in Christian mouths (‘because he healed the lame and the blind’; ‘and, as you say, he raised the dead’); Origen paraphrases the framing (‘as if we had answered’). Isaiah 35:5-6 follows the LXX closely. ‘She is not dead but sleeps’ matches Luke 8:52 verbatim (Mark 5:39 adds ‘the child’; Matthew 9:24 ‘the girl’); the account is cited from Luke because Origen’s wording of the saying matches Luke exactly (Mark 5:22, 35-43 is the parallel narrative). Widow of Nain: σπλαγχνισθείς and stopping the bearers = Luke 7:13-14. Lazarus ‘four days’ = John 11:17, 39. Luke 4:25-27: Origen gives the lepers (4:27) before the widows (4:25-26), drops ‘in Israel’, and has Σαραφθά for Σάρεπτα; rendered ‘Zarephath in Sidon’. The bread miracle is LXX 3 Kingdoms 17:8-16 = English 1 Kings 17:8-16 (renumbered). ‘Inner man’ (ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος) is Pauline: Romans 7:22, Ephesians 3:16 (compare 2 Corinthians 4:16). Luke 10:19 is quoted in pieces; Origen paraphrases its end (‘nothing shall hurt you’) as ‘treading they are not harmed’. The deer as enemy of snakes is ancient natural lore (no single source cited). Koetschau’s supplements (ἂν), (ὃ), (περὶ) are followed. αἰσθητῶν: ‘bodily’ = works perceptible to the senses, contrasted with healings of the soul.

title: Jesus warned against false Christs, not sorcerers
english: Jesus, then, was turning his disciples away, not from heeding sorcerers in general and those who promise to work wonders by any means whatever (for his disciples had no need of that), but from those who proclaim themselves to be the Christ of God and try, by certain illusions, to turn the disciples of Jesus to themselves, when he said in one place: “Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or ‘Here he is,’ do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and will perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. See, I have told you beforehand. So if they say to you, ‘Look, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out; ‘Look, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it. For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew 24:23–27). And in another place: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not eat in your name, and drink in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works?’ And I will say to them, ‘Depart from me, for you are workers of unrighteousness’” (Matthew 7:22–23; Luke 13:26–27).

But Celsus, wishing to put the wonders of Jesus on a level with the sorcery found among men, says in these very words: “O light and truth! With his own voice he openly declares, as you yourselves have written, that others also will come to you using similar powers, wicked men and sorcerers; and he names a certain Satan who contrives such things. So not even he denies that these works are nothing divine but are the deeds of wicked men. Yet, constrained by the truth, he has at once exposed what the others do and convicted what he himself does. How then is it not monstrous, from the same works, to consider the one a god and the others sorcerers? For why, on the strength of these works at least, should we think the others wicked any more than this man, when we have him as our witness? He himself, indeed, admitted that these things are the marks not of a divine nature but of certain deceivers and utter scoundrels.”

See, then, whether in these words Celsus is not plainly caught maliciously twisting the argument, since Jesus says one thing about those who will perform “signs and wonders” (Matthew 24:24), and the Jew in Celsus claims another. If Jesus had simply told his disciples to beware of those who promise wonders, without setting out what they would claim to be, Celsus’s suspicion might perhaps have had some ground. But those against whom Jesus wants us to be on guard profess to be “the Christ” (Matthew 24:23), which sorcerers do not do; and he says further that some who live wickedly will do certain mighty works in the name of Jesus and cast demons out of people (Matthew 7:22). Rather, if one may put it this way, sorcery is banished from the matters in this passage, and so is every suspicion raised against them; and what is brought in is the divinity of Christ and the divinity of his disciples. For it is possible that someone who uses his name and, I do not know how, is moved by some power to pretend that he himself is the Christ, may seem to accomplish things like those of Christ; and that others, in the name of Jesus, may seem to accomplish things somewhat like those of his genuine disciples.
translator_notes: Koetschau brackets [μὴ] in the first sentence as an intrusion; translated without it (‘not from heeding sorcerers’). Matthew 24:23-27 is quoted almost verbatim (Origen has πιστεύετε for πιστεύσητε in 24:23 and the order σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα μεγάλα). The second quotation blends Matthew 7:22-23 with Luke 13:26-27: ‘eat and drink’ comes from Luke 13:26 (there ‘in your presence’), and ‘workers of unrighteousness’ (ἐργάται ἀδικίας) from Luke 13:27; Matthew has ‘you who work lawlessness’. Both cited. Celsus’s quotation runs from ‘O light and truth’ to ‘utter scoundrels’ (Koetschau’s fragment). θεός of Jesus in Celsus’s mouth is lowercase ‘a god’ (sceptical voice). ‘A certain Satan’ keeps Celsus’s dismissive τινα. ἀποκηρύσσεται μὲν τῶν κατὰ τὸν τόπον ἡ γοητεία: literally ‘sorcery is disowned from those in the passage’; rendered ‘banished from the people this passage describes’ (the genitive could also be neuter, ‘from what the passage treats’; sense unchanged). Allusions back to the quoted texts are cited again inline (Matthew 24:23, 24; 7:22). Reviewer: ἡ ὑπόνοια αὐτοῦ is Celsus’s (or his Jew’s) suspicion, not Jesus’; named as Celsus’s to avoid the wrong referent. κατ’ αὐτῶν ὑπόνοια = suspicion against them (the matters of the passage), not ‘suspicion of it’.

title: Paul on the lawless one and lying wonders
english: Paul too, in the Second Letter to the Thessalonians, declares how there will one day be revealed “the man of lawlessness, the son of destruction, who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, presenting himself as God” (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4). And again he says to the Thessalonians: “And now you know what restrains, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only the one who now restrains will do so until he is taken out of the way. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord God will slay with the breath of his mouth and will destroy by the appearing of his coming. The lawless one’s coming is by the working of Satan, with all power and signs and lying wonders, and with all the deceit of unrighteousness among those who are perishing” (2 Thessalonians 2:6–10). Setting out also the reason why the lawless one is allowed to come into this life, he says: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved. And for this reason God sends them a working of error, so that they believe the lie, in order that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in unrighteousness” (2 Thessalonians 2:10–12).

Let someone tell us, then, whether anything in the Gospel or in the apostle can give ground for suspecting that sorcery is being foretold in this passage. Anyone who wishes may also draw from Daniel the prophecy about the antichrist (compare Daniel 7:24–26; 8:23–25; 11:36). But Celsus falsifies the words of Jesus: though Jesus did not say, “others will come using similar powers, wicked men and sorcerers,” Celsus himself says that he said such a thing. For just as the power of the enchanters in Egypt was not like the wondrous grace in Moses, but the outcome proved that the works of the Egyptians were trickery while those of Moses were divine (Exodus 7:10–12; 8:18–19), so the works of the antichrists, and of those who make a show of mighty works as though they were disciples of Jesus, are said to be signs and wonders “of falsehood” (2 Thessalonians 2:9), prevailing “with all the deceit of unrighteousness for those who are perishing” (2 Thessalonians 2:10); whereas the works of Christ and of his disciples bore as their fruit not deceit but the salvation of souls. For who could reasonably say that a better life, one that day by day reduces wickedness, comes from deceit?
translator_notes: 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4: Origen reads ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἀνομίας (‘man of lawlessness’), the reading of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (many manuscripts have ἁμαρτίας, ‘sin’). In 2:8 Origen’s text has κύριος ὁ θεός (‘the Lord God’) where the New Testament manuscripts read ‘the Lord’ or ‘the Lord Jesus’; translated as Origen’s text stands. Koetschau’s punctuation before τίνα τρόπον is treated as a misprint for an indirect question. The Daniel reference is a general pointer, not a quotation; the antichrist passages Origen elsewhere draws on are in Daniel 7-8 and 11, so the citation is marked ‘compare’. Celsus’s misquotation (‘others will come using similar powers, wicked men and sorcerers’) repeats his words from 2.49 and is put in quotation marks; the subject of καταψεύδεται is Celsus. Egyptian enchanters (ἐπαοιδοί, the LXX word in Exodus 7:11, 22): the outcome that exposed them is Aaron’s rod swallowing theirs (Exodus 7:10-12) and their failure with the gnats (Exodus 8:18-19 English = LXX 8:14-15; the Hebrew/LXX verse numbering in Exodus 8 runs four lower than the English, here given in English numbering). ‘Lying wonders’ keeps the Pauline genitive τέρασι ψεύδους; in the later echo it is rendered ‘of falsehood’ to keep Origen’s isolated quotation. Reviewer: Daniel 8:23-25 added to the ‘compare’ pointer; it is the antichrist passage Origen quotes at length in 6.46.

title: Divine power and sorcery are not of one kind
english: Celsus caught a hint from Scripture when he made Jesus say that “a certain Satan” will contrive such things. But he also snatches at a conclusion when he claims that Jesus does not deny “that these works have nothing divine about them but are the deeds of wicked men”; for he has made them of one kind when they are in fact of different kinds. As a wolf is not of one kind with a dog, even if it seems to have some likeness in the shape of its body and in its voice, nor the wood pigeon with the dove, so what is accomplished by the power of God is nothing like what comes from sorcery.

We will say this as well against Celsus’s malicious arguments. Are mighty works done by sorcery through evil demons, while no mighty work at all is accomplished by the divine and blessed nature? Has human life borne the worse things, yet had no room at all for the better? It seems to me that this principle should be laid down as applying in every case: wherever something worse pretends to be of one kind with the better, there is certainly something better on the other side. So too with those who work by sorcery: there must certainly also be things that happen in this life through divine working. And by the same logic one must either do away with both and say that neither happens, or, if one grants the one, and especially the worse, admit the better as well. But if someone were to grant that things happen through sorcery yet not grant those that come through divine power, he seems to me like a man who grants that there are sophisms and plausible arguments which fall short of the truth while pretending to present it, but holds that truth, and a dialectic free of sophistry, has its home nowhere among men.

But if once we accept that, given the real existence of magic and sorcery worked by evil demons, who are charmed by magical invocations and obey sorcerers, it follows that what comes from divine power must also be found among men, why should we not also examine rigorously those who claim these powers, judging by their life, by their character, and by what follows from their powers, whether harm to people or the reform of their morals, to see who does such things in the service of demons through certain incantations and tricks, and who, having come into a pure and holy standing before God in his soul and spirit, and I think also in his body, and having received some divine spirit, does such things for people’s benefit and to urge them to believe in the true God. And if once we must inquire, without being carried away by the powers, who accomplishes such things from the better source and who from the worse, so that we neither revile them all nor admire and accept them all as divine, how will it not be plain from what took place under Moses and under Jesus, when whole nations were formed after their signs, that these men did by divine power the things that they are recorded to have done? For wickedness and trickery would not have formed a whole nation that rose above not only statues and the things set up by men, but also every created nature, and ascended to the uncreated first principle, the God of all.
translator_notes: ὑπείδετο (ὑφοράομαι, ‘suspect, surmise’): Origen’s point is that Celsus took ‘a certain Satan’ from a guess at Scripture (the ‘working of Satan’ of 2 Thessalonians 2:9, quoted in 2.50), since Jesus’ own words in 2.49 do not name Satan; rendered ‘was guessing from Scripture’. The short phrases quoted in the first paragraph repeat Celsus’s words from 2.49 and are put in quotation marks. συναρπάζει τὸν λόγον: ‘snatches at a conclusion’ (seizes the argument unfairly). φάσσα / περιστερά: wood pigeon (ring-dove) and domestic dove. κατακλήσεσι περιέργοις: περίεργος is the usual word for magical arts (as in Acts 19:19), hence ‘magical invocations’; no citation, since not an allusion. ἐν χώρᾳ καθαρᾷ καὶ ἁγίᾳ γενόμενος ... τῷ θεῷ: rendered ‘having come into a pure and holy standing before God’. The neuter participles ὑπερβάν and ἀναβαῖνον agree with ἔθνος. γενητός / ἀγένητος are rendered ‘created’ / ‘uncreated’; τὴν ἀγένητον τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων ἀρχήν is taken as ‘the uncreated first principle, the God of all’ (an appositive genitive). No Scripture is quoted in this chapter; the signs of Moses and Jesus are general references already cited in 2.48-2.50. Reviewer: ὑπείδετο with τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς γραφῆς is difficult; ‘caught a hint from Scripture’ keeps Origen’s point that the Satan detail came from Scripture (2 Thessalonians 2:9), not from Jesus’ words. The appositive reading of τὴν ἀγένητον τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων ἀρχήν is kept.

title: Why trust Moses’ signs but not those of Jesus
english: Since it is a Jew who says these things in Celsus, we might say to him: You there, why is it that you have believed the things written in your books, as done by God through Moses, to be divine, and try to argue against those who slander them as done by sorcery, like the things done by the wise men of Egypt (Exodus 7:11, 22), while the things done by Jesus, which even you admit took place, you accuse of not being divine, imitating the Egyptians who stand against you?

For if the outcome, the whole nation formed through the wonders of Moses’ day, gives clear proof that it was God who did these things in the time of Moses, how much more will the same be shown in the case of Jesus, who did a greater work than Moses? For Moses took over people already more ready: those of the nation who were of Abraham’s seed, who had kept circumcision from generation to generation and had become zealous for Abraham’s customs; and he led them out of Egypt, setting before them the laws which you have believed to be divine. But Jesus dared something greater: upon the way of life already established, upon ancestral customs, and upon an upbringing under the existing laws, he brought in the way of life that accords with the gospel.

And just as Moses needed the signs he is recorded to have done, so that he might be believed not only by the elders but also by the people (Exodus 4:29–31), why should not Jesus too, so that he might be believed by those of the people who had learned to ask for “signs and wonders” (John 4:48; compare 1 Corinthians 1:22), need such works of power as, being greater and more divine in comparison with those done through Moses, were able to draw them away from Jewish myths and from the human traditions among them (compare Titus 1:14; Mark 7:8), and to make them accept the one who taught and did these things as greater than the prophets? For how was he not greater than the prophets, who was proclaimed by the prophets as the Christ and the Saviour of the human race?
translator_notes: Opening address ὦ οὗτος rendered ‘You there’. τὸ τέλος καὶ ὅλον τὸ ἔθνος is awkward; taken as ‘the outcome, a whole nation formed’, with καί read as explanatory; some may prefer to emend τὸ τέλος. The source shows a garbled form Μω(??)σεῖ, read as Μωϋσεῖ (‘in Moses’ day’). The Egyptian wise men allude to Pharaoh’s magicians (Exodus 7:11, 22) without quotation. ‘Signs and wonders’ is set off in Koetschau as a quotation; John 4:48 has the exact phrase, and 1 Corinthians 1:22 (‘Jews ask for signs’) is a close allusion. ‘Jewish mythology and human traditions’ echoes Titus 1:14 and Mark 7:8; cited as ‘compare’. Elders and people believing Moses: Exodus 4:29–31 (allusion, not quotation). The final claim that the prophets proclaimed him Christ and Saviour is general and left uncited.

title: Every charge against Jesus strikes Moses too
