english: Indeed, everything that the Jew in Celsus says to those who believe in Jesus can be turned equally into a charge against Moses, so that one may say that the sorcery of Jesus either does not differ at all from that of Moses or is very like it, since both, as far as the words of Celsus’s Jew go, can be brought under the same charges. For example, about Christ the Jew in Celsus says: “But O light and truth! With his own voice Jesus openly declares these things, as you yourselves have recorded: that others too will come to you using like powers, wicked men and sorcerers” (compare Matthew 24:24).

But about Moses, one who disbelieves the writings of Moses, whether an Egyptian or anyone at all, might say to the Jew: ‘But O light and truth! With his own voice Moses openly declares, as you yourselves have recorded, that others will come to you using like powers, wicked men and sorcerers. For it is written in your law: “If a prophet arises among you, or one who dreams a dream, and gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass of which he spoke to you, saying, Let us go and follow other gods, whom you do not know, and let us serve them, you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or of the one who dreams that dream” (Deuteronomy 13:1–3), and so on.’

And the one who slanders the words of Jesus says that he even names a certain Satan as contriving such things; but the one who turns this against Moses will say that Moses too names a prophet who dreams dreams as contriving such things. And just as the Jew in Celsus says of Jesus: “So that not even he himself denies that these things, at least, are nothing divine, but are the works of wicked men,” so the one who disbelieves the writings of Moses will set out the passage already quoted and say the same to him: ‘So that not even Moses himself denies that these things, at least, are nothing divine, but are the works of wicked men.’ He will do the same with this too: ‘Compelled by the truth, Moses at one stroke both laid bare the deeds of others and convicted his own.’

And when the Jew also says: “How then is it not monstrous, from the same works, to think the one a god and the others sorcerers?” someone might say to him, on account of the words of Moses set out above: ‘How then is it not monstrous, from the same works, to think the one a prophet of God and his servant (Numbers 12:7), and the others sorcerers?’

And since Celsus, dwelling on this point, added this too to the words I have set out and turned against Moses: “For why, on the strength of these things at least, should we think the others wicked rather than this man, when we have him as our witness?” we too shall add something like this to what has been said: ‘For why, on the strength of these things at least, should we think those wicked whom Moses says must not be obeyed when they display signs and wonders, rather than Moses, on account of the very words by which he slandered others over signs and wonders?’

Saying more to the same effect, so as to seem to strengthen his argument, he says: “These things, at any rate, he himself admitted to be the marks not of a divine nature but of certain deceivers and utter scoundrels.” Who, then, is “he himself”? You, Jew, say that it is Jesus; but the one who accuses you, as liable to the same charges, will refer “he himself” to Moses.
translator_notes: Quotation marks: double quotes are Celsus’s own words (and Scripture); single quotes mark the hypothetical speeches Origen puts in the mouth of a critic of Moses, which parody Celsus’s sentences word for word. Nested Scripture inside such a speech keeps double quotes, and the innermost speech (‘Let us go...’) is left unmarked to avoid a third level. Celsus’s report of Jesus’ warning about others with like powers paraphrases Matthew 24:24 (compare Matthew 7:22–23); cited as ‘compare’ because Celsus does not quote it. Deuteronomy 13:1–3 is quoted from the LXX (LXX 13:2–4 in Rahlfs; English 13:1–3); ‘and so on’ renders καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. ‘Satan contriving such things’ repeats Celsus’s charge from 2.49 indirectly, so it is not quoted; no single verse is cited for it. ‘Prophet of God and his servant’ (θεράπων) echoes LXX Numbers 12:7. τὸν μὲν θεόν in the Jew’s mouth is rendered ‘a god’ (the speaker does not grant the claim). ‘Compelled by the truth...’ adapts Celsus’s sentence in 2.49.

title: Moses also wrote of his own death
english: After this the Jew of Celsus, in his speech to those of his own people who have believed, says, as if to us (to keep to the part assigned to the Jew from the start): “What, then, drew you to him, unless it was that he foretold that after dying he would rise again?” (compare Matthew 16:21). This too, like what came before, will be turned against Moses in the same way. For we shall say to him: ‘What, then, drew you to him, unless it was that he wrote such things about his own death: “And Moses, the servant of the Lord, died there in the land of Moab, by the word of the Lord; and they buried him in the land of Moab, near the house of Phogor. And no one knows his burial to this day” (Deuteronomy 34:5–6)?’

For just as the Jew makes it a charge that Jesus foretold that after dying he would rise again, so the man who argues the like about Moses will reply to the one who says this that Moses too wrote (for Deuteronomy also is his) that “no one knows his burial to this day” (Deuteronomy 34:6), dignifying and exalting even his burial as unknown to the human race.
translator_notes: The staged Greek is corrupt in the bracketed clause: ‘ἀνέγραψενμδαση;αὐτοῦ’ and ‘ὅτι θυοτ;Οὐδεὶς’ contain stray characters (likely encoding debris for brackets and quotation marks). Read as [καὶ Μωϋσῆς ἀνέγραψεν· αὐτοῦ γάρ ἐστι καὶ τὸ Δευτερονόμιον] ὅτι ‘Οὐδεὶς οἶδε...’; the bracketed words (Koetschau’s square brackets, a suspected insertion) are translated as a parenthesis. ἢ διότι in Celsus’s question rendered ‘unless it was that’. δῆθεν and the parenthesis mean Origen answers ‘as if to us’ while keeping Celsus’s frame of a Jew addressing Jewish believers. Jesus’ foretelling of his resurrection (Matthew 16:21; Mark 8:31) is cited as ‘compare’ since Celsus paraphrases. Deuteronomy 34:5–6 is quoted from the LXX: ‘servant’ renders οἰκέτης; ‘near the house of Phogor’ keeps the LXX form of Beth-peor. Verse numbers agree in LXX and English.

title: Tales of return from Hades
english: After this the Jew says to his countrymen who believe in Jesus: “Come, then, let us even grant you that this was said. How many others produce such marvels to persuade simple hearers, and make a profit out of the deception? So they say of Zamolxis among the Scythians, the slave of Pythagoras (Herodotus, Histories 4.95), and of Pythagoras himself in Italy, and of Rhampsinitus in Egypt: that this last even ‘played dice’ in Hades ‘with Demeter,’ and came back up bearing ‘a gift from her, a golden napkin’ (Herodotus, Histories 2.122). So too of Orpheus among the Odrysians, of Protesilaus in Thessaly, of Heracles at Taenarum, and of Theseus. But this is what must be examined: whether anyone who truly died ever rose again with the very same body. Or do you think that the stories of the others are myths and seem so, while you have contrived a seemly or plausible ending for your drama: his cry on the stake as he breathed his last (Matthew 27:46, 50), and ‘the earthquake’ (Matthew 27:51, 54), and the darkness (Matthew 27:45)? That he did not help himself while he lived (compare Matthew 27:42), yet rose when dead and showed the marks of his punishment and how his hands had been pierced (John 20:20, 25–27): who saw this? A frantic woman, as you say (compare John 20:11–18), and anyone else there may have been from the same sorcery, who either dreamed it in some state of mind and, as he wished, saw a vision shaped by a deluded opinion, which has happened to countless people before now, or, what is more likely, wanted to astound the rest with this marvel-mongering, and by such a lie to give an opening to other charlatans.”

Since, then, it is a Jew who says these things, we make our defence of our Jesus as to a Jew, still turning the argument against Moses as well and saying to him: ‘How many others produce such marvels as Moses did, to persuade simple hearers, and make a profit out of the deception?’ Indeed, it is more open to one who disbelieves Moses to cite Zamolxis and Pythagoras, who produced marvels, than to the Jew, who is not at all a keen student of the histories of the Greeks. And the Egyptian who disbelieves the wonders told of Moses will cite Rhampsinitus with some plausibility, saying that Rhampsinitus is far more believable when he is said to have gone down to Hades, played dice with Demeter, snatched a golden napkin from her, and shown it as a token that he had been in Hades and had come back up from there, than Moses, who wrote of himself that he entered “into the thick darkness where God was” (Exodus 20:21), and that he alone, apart from the rest, drew near to God. For he wrote thus: “And Moses alone shall come near to God, but the others shall not come near” (Exodus 24:2).

So we, the disciples of Jesus, will say to the Jew who says these things: You who bring charges over faith in Jesus, make your defence to us now, and tell the Egyptian and the Greeks: what will you say to the charges you have brought against our Jesus, charges that would have struck Moses first? And even if you strive with all your might to defend Moses, as indeed the facts about him do admit a forceful and clear argument, you will, without noticing it, in your very defence of Moses have commended Jesus, against your will, as more divine than Moses.
translator_notes: Staged Greek shows πιστεύωμενηι ὑμῖν; read πιστεύωμεν ὑμῖν (‘let us even grant you’), the ηι being debris. The source also shows a stray closing bracket after αὐτῷ σώματι; Origen repeats the phrase in 2.57 unbracketed, so it is translated as genuine. Koetschau brackets [καὶ τὰς χεῖρας ὡς ἦσαν πεπερονημέναι] as doubtful; translated (‘and how his hands had been pierced’) and flagged here. Inside Celsus’s speech, single quotes mark Koetschau’s quotation marks for Herodotus’s words (Rhampsinitus, Histories 2.122) and ‘the earthquake’ (τὸν σεισμόν is the exact wording of Matthew 27:54; the event is 27:51). Zamolxis as slave of Pythagoras: Herodotus, Histories 4.95 (Herodotus spells Salmoxis/Zalmoxis). Pythagoras’ descent to Hades in Italy is a story told by Hermippus (Diogenes Laertius 8.41); not cited inline. Orpheus, Protesilaus, Heracles at Taenarum and Theseus are myths, not cited. ‘Could not help himself’ alludes to the taunt in Matthew 27:42; ‘frantic woman’ refers to Mary Magdalene (John 20:11–18; Mark 16:9), which Origen discusses in 2.59–60; both cited as ‘compare’ because Celsus does not quote. σκόλοψ rendered ‘stake’ to keep Celsus’s contemptuous word. ἀγύρταις rendered ‘charlatans’ (begging wonder-workers). Exodus 20:21 and 24:2 are quoted from the LXX; numbering agrees with English. In Origen’s comparison the genitive Μωυσέως is a genitive of comparison with an absolute participle, rendered ‘than Moses, who wrote of himself’. Note Origen’s change from Celsus’s ‘gift’ (δῶρον) to ‘snatched’ (ἁρπάσαντα), kept.

title: A public death rules out pretence
english: The Jew in Celsus says that the heroic tales of those who are said to have gone down to Hades and come back up from there are marvel-mongering, taking it that the heroes vanished for a time, stole themselves away from the sight of all men, and afterwards showed themselves as though they had come back up from Hades. For his words seem to suggest something of this kind about Orpheus among the Odrysians, Protesilaus in Thessaly, Heracles at Taenarum, and Theseus too. Come, then, let us show that the account of Jesus’ being raised from the dead cannot be compared with these.

For each of the heroes spoken of in those places could, had he wished, have stolen himself away from human sight and, when he decided, gone back again to those he had left. But since Jesus was crucified before all the Jews, and his body was taken down in the sight of their people (compare John 19:38), how is it possible to invent a like tale, saying that he, like the heroes of the stories, went down to Hades and came back up from there?

We say, too, that perhaps something like this might also be said in defence of Jesus’ crucifixion, especially because of the stories told about the heroes who are thought to have gone down to Hades by force: that if, for the sake of argument, Jesus had died an obscure death, so that his death was not evident to the whole people of the Jews, and then after that had truly risen from the dead, there would have been room for what was suspected about the heroes to be said about him too. Perhaps, then, besides other reasons why Jesus was crucified, this too may contribute to his having died openly on the cross, so that no one could say that he withdrew from human sight of his own accord, and seemed to have died but had not died, but, when he wished, appeared again and staged a marvel of rising from the dead.

Clear and evident, I think, is the argument drawn from his disciples. They gave themselves to a teaching that put their lives in danger, and they would not have taught it with such vigour if they had made up the claim that Jesus had been raised from the dead; and all the while they not only prepared others to despise death but themselves did so long before.
translator_notes: βίᾳ νομιζομένων (‘thought to have gone down to Hades by force’) is taken with the heroes (Heracles and Theseus forced their way into Hades); the phrase is compressed and could also mean ‘thought, against the evidence, to have gone down’. The source shows a doubled αὐτὸν αὐτὸν in ‘λέγειν αὐτὸν αὐτὸν’; read as one αὐτόν (‘saying that he’). (ἀλλ᾿) is an editor’s supplement, translated (‘but’). μή ποτε twice rendered ‘perhaps’, as Origen offers a tentative reason. Taking down of the body in public: John 19:38 (compare Luke 23:53); allusion, not quotation. Jesus’ descent to Hades is raised here only as the opponent’s comparison and is not cited. The disciples’ readiness to die is not tied to one verse and is left uncited.

title: Elijah and Elisha raised the dead
english: Consider whether it is not very blindly that Celsus’s Jew, as though it were impossible for anyone to rise from the dead with his very body, says: “But this is what must be examined: whether anyone who really died ever rose with his very body.” The Jew would not have said this if he believed what is recorded in the third and fourth books of Kingdoms about children, one of whom Elijah raised and the other Elisha (1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:18–37).

And this, I think, is also why Jesus came to dwell among no other nation than the Jews, who had grown used to marvels: so that, by setting what they already believed beside what was done by him and recorded about him, they might accept that he, around whom greater things took place and by whom more wonderful things were accomplished, was greater than all those men.
translator_notes: The third and fourth books of Kingdoms are the Septuagint titles for 1 and 2 Kings; cited by English names. Elijah raises the widow’s son at 1 Kings 17:17–24; Elisha raises the Shunammite’s son at 2 Kings 4:18–37 (the raising itself at 4:32–37). Celsus’s question is quoted from the Greek ἀλλ᾿ ἐκεῖνο σκεπτέον onward; αὐτῷ σώματι rendered ‘with his very body’.

title: Our Scriptures are not myths
english: After the Greek stories he set out, about men who, as it were, worked wonders and men who supposedly rose from the dead, the Jew says to the Jews who believe in Jesus: “Or do you think that the stories of the others are myths and are taken for myths, while you have devised a fitting or convincing ending for the drama, his cry on the stake as he breathed his last (Matthew 27:50; Luke 23:46)?”

We shall answer the Jew that we have held the stories you set out to be myths. But what stands in the Scriptures we share with you, in which not you alone but we too take pride, we say is in no way myth. That is why we believe those who wrote about the people who rose from the dead there, as men who were not telling marvellous tales; and in the present case we believe the one who both foretold it, and was foretold, and rose.

And in this he who rose from the dead is more wonderful than they: prophets, Elijah and Elisha, raised them (1 Kings 17:22; 2 Kings 4:35), but none of the prophets raised him; the Father in heaven did. That is why his resurrection has also achieved greater things than theirs. For what has come to the world from the children raised through Elijah and Elisha that is as great as what has come through the resurrection of Jesus, which is preached and has been believed by divine power?
translator_notes: Celsus’s ‘cry on the stake as he breathed his last’ alludes to the loud cry at death (Matthew 27:50; Mark 15:37; Luke 23:46); cited inside his question because it is a clear allusion. σκόλοψ rendered ‘stake’ to keep Celsus’s scornful word distinct from σταυρός. μύθους εἶναί τε καὶ δοκεῖν rendered ‘are myths and are taken for myths’. τῷ ἐνταῦθα is taken as Jesus, the one who rose ‘in the present case’, set against the children who rose ‘there’ (ἐκεῖ) in Kings.

title: Did Jesus fail to help himself?
english: He thinks that both the earthquake and the darkness are a marvellous tale (Matthew 27:45, 51). We made our defence about these earlier, as far as we could, citing Phlegon, who recorded that such things occurred at the time of the Saviour’s passion. He also says that “while he was alive Jesus did not help himself, but when dead he rose and showed the marks of his punishment, and how his hands had been pierced” (John 20:20, 27).

We ask him: what does “helped himself” mean? If it refers to virtue, we shall say that he helped himself very much indeed. For he neither said nor did anything improper; but truly “he was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent” (Isaiah 53:7), and the Gospel testifies that “so he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7; Matthew 27:12–14). But if he takes “helped himself” in the sense of things indifferent and bodily, we say that we have shown from the Gospels that he came to these things of his own will.

Next, after stating what comes from the Gospel, that on rising from the dead he showed the marks of his punishment and how his hands had been pierced, he asks: “Who saw this?” And slandering the account of Mary Magdalene, who is recorded to have seen him (John 20:11–18), he said: “A frenzied woman, as you say.” And since she is not the only one recorded to have seen Jesus risen, but others too, Celsus’s Jew slanders these as well, and says: “and anyone else involved in the same sorcery.”
translator_notes: The earlier defence citing Phlegon is at Against Celsus 2.14 and 2.33. The clause ‘while he was alive... pierced’ is indirect speech (ὅτι) in Origen but is repeated almost word for word below, so it is marked as Celsus’s wording. ‘So he did not open his mouth’ is the end of Isaiah 53:7 (LXX οὕτως οὐκ ἀνοίγει τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ); Origen says the Gospel bears witness to it, i.e. Jesus’ silence before his judges (Matthew 26:63; 27:12–14; Mark 15:5). τὰ μέσα is the Stoic term for things morally indifferent, rendered ‘things indifferent’. On ‘as you say’ (ὥς φατε): Celsus may be glancing at Mary Magdalene’s seven demons (Mark 16:9; Luke 8:2); uncertain, so not cited inline. γοητεία rendered ‘sorcery’; the jibe may mean either fellow members of the same band of sorcerers or people under the same spell, so ‘involved in’ is kept open to both.

title: Apparitions show the soul survives
english: Then, as though this could happen, I mean that someone has an apparition of a dead man as if he were alive, he goes on like an Epicurean and says that “someone dreamed in a certain state of mind, or by his own wish had an illusion through mistaken belief, and reported such a thing; which,” he says, “has already happened to countless people.”

Even if this seemed to have been said with great cleverness, it nonetheless establishes a necessary doctrine: that the soul of the dead does subsist, and that whoever has taken up this doctrine has not believed in vain in its immortality, or at least in its survival; as Plato too, in his work on the soul, says that “shadowy apparitions” of people already dead have appeared to some around tombs (Plato, Phaedo 81d). Now the “apparitions” that occur concerning the soul of the dead arise from something that underlies them: the soul that subsists in what is called the luminous body.

But Celsus, not wanting this, would have it that some people dream even while awake and, according to their own wish, have illusions through mistaken belief. To believe that this happens in sleep is not unreasonable; but that it happens while awake, to those who are not wholly out of their minds and delirious, or melancholic, is not credible. Foreseeing this, Celsus said the woman was frenzied, though the written account, from which he draws the material for his charges against the events, does not show this.
translator_notes: Celsus’s explanation is indirect speech in Origen (λέγει with participles); it is marked as Celsus’s words because Origen restates its key terms (δόξῃ πεπλανημένῃ, κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν βούλησιν) as his. ‘Like an Epicurean’ reflects Origen’s charge that Celsus is an Epicurean. The Plato reference is Phaedo 81d (ψυχῶν σκιοειδῆ φαντάσματα around tombs); ‘his work on the soul’ is Origen’s name for the Phaedo. αὐγοειδὲς σῶμα (‘ray-like body’) rendered ‘luminous body’, the term for the soul’s subtle vehicle; Origen marks it as a borrowed term (‘so-called’). Celsus’s πάροιστρος (ch. 59) is picked up here by παροιστρῶσαν, both rendered ‘frenzied’.

title: Thomas and the marks of the nails
english: So, as Celsus thinks, Jesus too after death was sending out an appearance of the wounds he received on the cross, and was not truly wounded in that way. But as the Gospel teaches (Celsus believes some parts of it, the ones he wishes, so that he may accuse, and disbelieves others), Jesus called to himself one of the disciples who disbelieved and thought the wonder impossible. For that disciple had agreed with the woman who said she had seen him, on the view that it is not impossible for the soul of one who has died to be seen; but he did not go on to think it true that he had been raised in a solid body. That is why he said: “Unless I see,” “I will not believe”; and he added: “Unless I put my hand into the mark of the nails and touch his side, I will not believe” (John 20:25).

Thomas said these things because he judged that the body of a soul can appear to physical eyes, the soul being “in all things” like its former form, “in stature and fair eyes and voice,” and often “wearing such clothes about its skin” (Homer, Iliad 23.66–67). And Jesus, calling Thomas to him, said: “Bring your finger here and see my hands; and bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing” (John 20:27).
translator_notes: The Greek says Thomas had agreed with ‘the woman’ (τῇ φασκούσῃ, feminine singular) who said she had seen Jesus; in John 20:25 it is the other disciples who tell Thomas. Translated as the Greek stands; a reading τοῖς φάσκουσι would be worth checking in Koetschau’s apparatus. Thomas’s words are Origen’s abridged paraphrase of John 20:25. σῶμα ἀντίτυπον rendered ‘solid body’ (a body that resists touch). The verse lines are Homer, Iliad 23.66–67 (the ghost of Patroclus), adapted by Origen to the feminine ψυχή (ἐϊκυίης, ἐχούσης). φέρε in John 20:27 rendered ‘bring’ for both hand and finger, as in the Greek.

title: Between solid body and bare soul
english: And it was in keeping with everything prophesied about him, which included this too, and with what he did and what happened to him, that this should prove the greatest wonder of all. For it had been foretold in the prophet, speaking in the person of Jesus: “My flesh will dwell in hope; and you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor let your Holy One see corruption” (Psalm 16:9–10).

And at his resurrection he was, as it were, in a kind of borderland between the solidity of the body he had before the passion and the appearing of a soul bare of such a body. Hence, when “his disciples” were together, “and Thomas with them, Jesus comes, though the doors were shut, and stood in their midst and said, ‘Peace be with you.’ Then he says to Thomas, ‘Bring your finger here’”, and what follows (John 20:26–27).

In the Gospel according to Luke, too, as Simon and Cleopas were talking “with each other about all that had happened” (Luke 24:14), Jesus came up to them and “went along with them. But their eyes were held so that they did not recognize him. And he said to them, ‘What are these words that you are exchanging with each other as you walk?’” (Luke 24:15–17). And when “their eyes were opened and they recognized him,” then Scripture says in these very words: “And he vanished from them” (Luke 24:31).

So even if Celsus wants to put the events concerning Jesus, and those who saw him after the resurrection, on the same footing as other apparitions and others who have seen apparitions, yet to those who examine the facts fairly and wisely the greater wonder will be plain.
translator_notes: Psalm 15:9–10 in the Septuagint is Psalm 16:9–10 in English Bibles; the same lines are quoted at Acts 2:26–27. LXX κατασκηνώσει rendered ‘will dwell’. παχύτης (thickness, density) rendered ‘solidity’. Luke 24:18 names only Cleopas; Origen names his companion Simon, as he does elsewhere; kept as the Greek has it. In the John quotation ‘Then he says to Thomas’ compresses John 20:26–27. ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν rendered ‘he vanished from them’. The closing contrast plays on φαντάσματα / φανεῖται (apparitions / will be plain); not reproducible in English. τὸν ὅσιόν σου capitalised ‘your Holy One’ because Origen reads the psalm as spoken in the person of Jesus.

title: Why the risen Jesus was not seen by all
english: After this Celsus, in a way not to be lightly dismissed, finds fault with what is written and says that “if Jesus really wished to show divine power, he ought to have appeared to those very men who had abused him, and to the one who condemned him, and in short to everyone.”

For indeed it is plain to us too, from the Gospel, that after the resurrection he was not seen in the way he formerly appeared, publicly and to all. Rather, in the Acts it is written that, “appearing over forty days,” he proclaimed to the disciples “the things concerning the kingdom of God” (Acts 1:3). And in the Gospels it is not said that he was always with them; but in one place, after eight days, he appeared in their midst “when the doors were shut” (John 20:26), and in another in some other such way.

Paul too, at the end of the First Letter to the Corinthians, implying that he was not seen publicly as in the time before the passion, writes: “For I delivered to you first of all what I also received, that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,” “and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles. Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared to me also” (1 Corinthians 15:3–8).

I take it that what this passage contains is great and wonderful, beyond the merit not only of the many among believers but even of those who have advanced far; in it the reason might be made plain why, after rising from the dead, he did not appear in the same way as in the former time. But out of many points, as befits such a work as this, written against the treatise attacking the Christians and their faith, see whether, by setting out a few with good reason, we shall be able to reach those who will hear our defence.
translator_notes: Celsus’s objection is indirect speech (ὅτι ἐχρῆν...) and is marked as his words. οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτως rendered ‘in a way not to be lightly dismissed’: Origen grants it some force. The 1 Corinthians quotation skips verse 4 (buried and raised on the third day), as the Greek does; the gap is marked by the two separate quotation segments. ‘The treatise attacking the Christians’ (τὸν κατὰ Χριστιανῶν... λόγον) is Celsus’s book; λόγος rendered ‘treatise’. καθικέσθαι rendered ‘reach’ (to touch or move the hearers).

title: One Jesus seen in many ways
english: Jesus, though one, was many in aspect; and he was not seen alike by all who saw him. That he was many in aspect is clear from “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6), and “I am the bread” (John 6:35), and “I am the door” (John 10:9), and countless other sayings. That even when seen he did not appear the same to all who saw him, but according to what each beholder could receive, will be clear to those who consider why, when he was about to be transfigured on the high mountain, he did not take even all the apostles, but only Peter and James and John (Matthew 17:1–2). For they alone could take in the sight of his glory at that time, and were able also to perceive Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory (Luke 9:30–31), and to hear them talking together, and the voice from heaven out of the cloud (Matthew 17:5).

And I think that even before he went up the mountain, where only the disciples came to him and he taught them about the beatitudes (Matthew 5:1–12), when he was somewhere below the mountain and, “when evening had come” (Matthew 8:16), was healing those brought to him, freeing them from every disease and every sickness (Matthew 4:23), he did not appear the same to the sick who needed his healing as to those who, because they were healthy, were able to go up the mountain with him.

Moreover, since he privately explained to his own disciples the parables that had been spoken in a veiled way to the crowds outside (Mark 4:11, 34), then just as those who heard the explanation of the parables were superior in their hearing to those who heard the parables without explanations, so too were they superior in their sight: certainly the sight of the soul, and, I believe, of the body as well.

That he did not always appear the same is shown by what Judas said, when about to betray him, to the crowds who came out with him, as to men who did not know him: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one” (Matthew 26:48). I think the Saviour himself also indicates something of this in the words: “Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me” (Matthew 26:55; Mark 14:49).

Since, then, our view of Jesus is that he is so great, not only in the divinity within him, hidden from the many, but also in his body, which was transfigured when he wished and for those he wished, we say this: all were able to see Jesus while he had not yet “stripped off the principalities and the powers” (Colossians 2:15) and had not yet died “to sin” (Romans 6:10). But once he had stripped off “the principalities and the powers” and no longer had anything the many could take in by sight, not all who had seen him before were able to see him. Hence, sparing them, he did not appear to all when he had risen from the dead.
translator_notes: ἐπίνοια is Origen’s term for the many titles or aspects under which the one Christ is conceived; rendered ‘aspect’. χωρέω (have room for, be able to receive) rendered ‘could receive’ / ‘could take in’ / ‘were able to’, avoiding the calque ‘had room’. ‘Seen in glory’ (ὀφθέντες ἐν δόξῃ) is Luke 9:31’s wording, hence the Luke citation; the voice from the cloud follows Matthew 17:5 (also Mark 9:7; Luke 9:35). ‘When evening had come’ and the healings echo Matthew 8:16, which in Matthew follows the Sermon on the Mount; Origen’s ‘before he went up’ is kept as the Greek has it. ‘Every disease and every sickness’ is the wording of Matthew 4:23 (also 9:35). ‘Privately to his own disciples he explained’ echoes Mark 4:34; ‘those outside’ Mark 4:11. Judas’s words match Matthew 26:48 (also Mark 14:44). The temple saying mixes Matthew 26:55 and Mark 14:49 (ἤμην follows Mark). Colossians 2:15 and Romans 6:10 supply the quoted phrases ‘stripped off the principalities and the powers’ and ‘died to sin’; Origen applies them to the risen Jesus.

title: Seen only by those with eyes to see
english: And why do I say “to all”? For not even with the apostles and disciples themselves was he always present, or always visible to them, since they could not take in the sight of him without a break. For once he had completed the dispensation, his divinity shone more brightly. Cephas, that is Peter, as it were the “firstfruits” of the apostles, was able to see it; after him the Twelve, Matthias having been appointed in place of Judas (Acts 1:26); and after them “five hundred brothers at one time.” “Then he appeared to James, then to all the” other “apostles” besides the Twelve, perhaps to the Seventy (Luke 10:1); “and last of all” to Paul, as to “one untimely born” (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). Paul knew well in what sense he said, “To me, less than the least of all the saints, this grace was given” (Ephesians 3:8); and perhaps “less than the least” means the same as “untimely born.”

Just as, then, no one could readily find fault with Jesus for not taking all the apostles up the high mountain, but only the three already named, when he was about to be transfigured and to show the brightness of his garments and the glory of Moses and Elijah talking with him (Matthew 17:1–3), so no one could reasonably blame the apostles’ accounts for relating that after the resurrection Jesus was seen not by all, but by those whom he saw had gained eyes able to see his resurrection.

I think these words said about him also help the defence of what is before us: “For to this end Christ died and rose, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living” (Romans 14:9). Notice in these words that Jesus “died” “that he might be Lord of the dead,” “and rose, that he might be Lord” not only “of the dead” but “also of the living.” And the apostle does know as the dead over whom Christ is Lord those he lists in this way in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable” (1 Corinthians 15:52); and as the living, those who will be changed, who are other than the dead who will be raised. About these too the passage reads: “and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52), said right after “the dead will be raised first” (compare 1 Thessalonians 4:16).

In the First Epistle to the Thessalonians as well he sets out the same distinction in other words, and says that those who sleep are one group and the living another: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, about those who are asleep, so that you may not grieve as the rest do who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. For this we tell you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will by no means go before those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thessalonians 4:13–15). The interpretation of these passages that seemed right to us we have set out in the commentaries we dictated on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians.
translator_notes: Opening ‘why do I say “to all”’ takes up Celsus’s demand (2.63) that Jesus should have appeared ‘to all’; marked as a quoted phrase. ‘ἀπαρχή’ (firstfruits) for Peter is set in quotation marks by the edition; it is Origen’s use of a Pauline word (compare 1 Corinthians 15:20, 23, where Christ is the firstfruits), not a quotation about Peter, so no citation is placed on it. The list follows 1 Corinthians 15:5-8; Origen’s glosses (‘the other apostles besides the Twelve’, ‘perhaps the Seventy’) are kept outside the quotation marks as in the edition; the Seventy cited to Luke 10:1. Matthias: Acts 1:26. ‘ἐλαχιστότερος’ is a comparative built on a superlative; rendered ‘less than the least’ to keep Origen’s point that it matches ‘untimely born’. ‘ἐπισταμένῳ πῶς ἔλεγεν’ rendered ‘understood what he meant when he said’. Romans 14:9: Origen reads ‘ἀπέθανε καὶ ἀνέστη’ (died and rose); the received NT text has ‘ἀπέθανεν καὶ ἔζησεν’ (died and lived); rendered as Origen quotes. ‘σαλπίσει’ (impersonal ‘it will trumpet’) rendered ‘the trumpet will sound’. The phrase ‘the dead will be raised first’ combines 1 Corinthians 15:52 with 1 Thessalonians 4:16 (‘the dead in Christ will rise first’); cited with ‘compare’. Transfiguration cited to Matthew 17:1-3 (compare Mark 9:2-4; Luke 9:28-31). The commentary on 1 Thessalonians mentioned at the end is lost. Stray full stops in the edition’s punctuation (e.g. ‘Ἰακώβῳ. ἔπειτα’) read through.

title: God appears by measure and judgement
english: And do not be surprised if not all the crowds who have believed in Jesus see his resurrection, when Paul, writing to the Corinthians as to people who could not take in more, says: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2). Of the same kind is this saying too: “For you were not yet able; but even now you are still not able, for you are still fleshly” (1 Corinthians 3:2–3).

So the word, doing everything by divine judgement, has recorded of Jesus that before the passion he appeared to the many without distinction, and even this not always, but that after the passion he no longer showed himself in the same way, but with a certain judgement that measured out to each what was fitting. It is recorded that “God appeared to Abraham” (Genesis 12:7; compare 17:1; 18:1) or to one of the saints, and this “appeared” did not happen always but at intervals, nor did he appear to all. In just the same way, I ask you to understand that the Son of God also appeared by a judgement like the one by which God appeared to them.
translator_notes: ‘βλέπουσιν’ is present tense: Origen speaks of believers in general, not only eyewitnesses, so ‘see’ is kept in the present. ‘ὁ λόγος’ here most likely means the Christian word, i.e. the scriptural account (as in 2.68-69, where ‘ὁ λόγος’ is the account that records the truth); rendered lowercase ‘the word’. The phrase ‘doing everything by divine judgement’ could suit the divine Word inspiring Scripture; the lowercase rendering leaves that open without forcing it. ‘ἁπαξαπλῶς’ rendered ‘without distinction’ (lit. ‘simply, in general’), set against the later ‘with a certain judgement’. ‘ὤφθη ὁ θεὸς τῷ Ἀβραάμ’: LXX Genesis 12:7 and 17:1 read ‘ὤφθη κύριος τῷ Αβραμ’, and LXX Genesis 18:1 ‘ὤφθη δὲ αὐτῷ ὁ θεός’; Origen’s wording is a general paraphrase of these appearances; cited to Genesis 12:7 (compare 17:1; 18:1). ‘μοι νόει’ (ethical dative) rendered ‘I ask you to understand’. The last clause ‘τῇ παραπλησίᾳ περὶ ἐκείνων εἰς τὸ ὦφθαι αὐτοῖς τὸν θεὸν κρίσει’ is compressed; rendered by sense. Reviewer: Genesis citation shown inline as ‘Genesis 12:7; compare 17:1; 18:1’.

title: Sent to be known and to be hidden
english: We have answered, then, as far as we could in a work of this kind, the claim: “If he really wished to display divine power, he ought to have appeared to the very men who had abused him, and to the one who condemned him, and in short to all.” He ought not, then, to have appeared to the one who condemned him, nor to those who had abused him. For Jesus was sparing both the one who condemned him and those who had abused him, so that they might not be struck with “blindness,” as the men of Sodom were struck when they plotted against the beauty of the angels who were guests in Lot’s house. This is made plain by these words: “The men stretched out their hands and drew Lot into the house to them, and shut the door; and they struck the men who were at the door of the house with blindness, from small to great, and they wore themselves out looking for the door” (Genesis 19:10–11).

So Jesus wished to display his power, which was divine, to each of those able to see it, and in the measure of what each could take in. Surely it was for no other reason that he took care not to be seen than out of regard for the capacities of those who could not take in the sight of him.

And Celsus brings this in to no purpose: “For he certainly no longer feared any man, once he had died and was, as you say, God; nor was he sent in the first place for this, to stay hidden.” For he was sent not only to be known but also to stay hidden. For even those who knew him did not know all that he was; something of him escaped them, and to some he was not known at all. And he opened the gates of “light” to those who had been sons of “darkness” and “night,” but who had given themselves to becoming sons of “the day” and of “light” (1 Thessalonians 5:5). And the Lord came to us as Saviour, as a good physician, to those full of sins rather than to the righteous (Matthew 9:12–13).
translator_notes: The opening claim repeats Celsus’s words from 2.63 (‘ἐχρῆν... ὀφθῆναι’); the Greek introduces them only with ‘πρὸς τὸ’ (against the words), so no speaker label is added beyond ‘the claim’. ‘τῇ ὥρᾳ’ rendered ‘the beauty’ (ὥρα in the sense of youthful bloom), not ‘the hour’. ‘ἀορασία’ (blindness) is the LXX word of Genesis 19:11; the quotation is LXX Genesis 19:10-11 (‘παρελύθησαν ζητοῦντες’, they wore themselves out looking). ‘διὰ τὰς δυνάμεις τῶν μὴ χωρούντων’ rendered ‘out of regard for the capacities’: δυνάμεις here means the limited powers of the viewers, not miracles. Celsus’s sentence is set in double quotation marks; ‘θεὸς ὤν, ὥς φατε’ is Celsus reporting the Christian claim, rendered ‘God’ since it names the Christian belief that Jesus is God. ‘ἵνα λάθῃ’ rendered ‘to stay hidden’ (lit. escape notice) in both Celsus’s and Origen’s clauses, so Origen’s turn of Celsus’s word stays visible. ‘sons of light... day... night... darkness’ is a clear allusion to 1 Thessalonians 5:5. The physician saying alludes to Matthew 9:12-13 (compare Mark 2:17; Luke 5:31-32); not a quotation. ‘ἦλθε σωτὴρ ὁ κύριος ἡμῖν μᾶλλον ὡς ἰατρὸς ἀγαθὸς τοῖς ἁμαρτιῶν μεστοῖς ἢ τοῖς δικαίοις’ rendered with ‘rather than’ governing ‘those full of sins’ vs ‘the righteous’.

'For not all that he was was known even to those by whom he was known' recast in the active, 'For even those who knew him did not know all that he was' (2026-10-24), because the output guard reads 'was was' as a doubled word. Same sense of οὐ γὰρ πᾶν, ὃ ἦν, καὶ οἷς ἐγινώσκετο ἐγινώσκετο.

title: He could vanish when he willed
english: Let us see how Celsus’s Jew puts it: “In any case, to display his divinity he ought at least to have done this much: to vanish from the stake at once.” This too seems to me like the argument of those who set themselves against providence, who sketch for themselves things other than what exists, and say, “It would have been better if the world were as we have sketched it.” Where what they sketch is possible, they are shown to be making the world worse, so far as it lies with them and their sketch; and where they seem to be painting something not worse than what exists, they are shown to want what is impossible by nature. So either way they are ridiculous.

Here too, then, that it was not impossible for him, as one of a more divine nature, to become invisible whenever he wished, is clear in itself. It is plain also from what is written about him, to anyone except those who accept some of the writings in order to attack the word, and think others are fictions. Now it is written in the Gospel according to Luke that after the resurrection Jesus “took the bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it” to Simon and Cleopas; and when they had taken the bread, “their eyes were opened, and they recognised him; and he vanished from their sight” (Luke 24:30–31).
translator_notes: Speaker: ‘ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος’ rendered ‘Celsus’s Jew’; his words in double quotation marks. ‘σκόλοψ’ (stake, pale) is Celsus’s word, distinct from ‘σταυρός’ (cross) used by Origen in 2.69; rendered ‘stake’ throughout. ‘εἰ δ᾿ οὖν τό γε τοσοῦτον ὤφειλεν’ is elliptical (‘if anyway he had to do at least this much’); rendered ‘In any case, to display his divinity he ought at least to have done this much: to vanish from the stake at once’. The quoted sentence of the critics of providence (‘it would have been better...’) is a reported generic objection, set in quotation marks as direct speech in the Greek (‘λεγόντων ὅτι... ὡς διεγράψαμεν’, first person). Doubtful reading: ‘οὐκ ἀδύνατον ἥξειν ὡς ἐν τῇ θειοτέρᾳ φύσει’ does not construe cleanly (‘ἥξειν’, ‘would come’, seems corrupt; an infinitive like ‘ἦν αὐτῷ’ or similar is expected); rendered by the evident sense ‘it was not impossible for him, as one of a more divine nature, to become invisible whenever he wished’. ‘μὴ... προσιεμένοις..., ... οἰομένοις’: the negative governs both participles, describing readers who do not pick and choose (accept some texts to attack, dismiss others as fiction); ‘ὁ λόγος’ = the Christian word/teaching, lowercase as in 2.66. Luke 24:30-31 is quoted closely; ‘ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν’ rendered ‘vanished from their sight’. Origen names the companion of Cleopas ‘Simon’ (not named in Luke 24:18; compare Luke 24:34, ‘he has appeared to Simon’); kept as he gives it. Reviewer: ‘εἰ δ᾿ οὖν’ read as ‘in any case / failing that’; ‘τό γε τοσοῦτον’ is the object of ‘ὤφειλεν’ and is spelled out by ‘ἀφανὴς γενέσθαι’. The ‘μὴ’ clause is rendered with ‘anyone except those who...’ so the negation covers both participles without ambiguity.

title: Why he did not vanish from the cross
english: We wish to show how it would not have been more useful for the whole dispensation that he should vanish bodily from the stake at once. The things recorded as having happened to Jesus do not hold the whole contemplation of the truth in the bare wording and the history. For each of them is shown, to those who read Scripture with more understanding, to be also a symbol of something.

His crucifixion holds the truth made plain in “I have been crucified with Christ” (Galatians 2:20), and in what is meant by “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14). His death was necessary because of the words “For the death he died, he died to sin once for all” (Romans 6:10), and because the righteous man says “being conformed to his death” (Philippians 3:10), and “For if we have died with him, we shall also live with him” (2 Timothy 2:11). In the same way his burial too reaches those who are conformed to his death, who have been crucified with him and have died with him, as Paul has also said: “For we were buried with him through baptism” (Romans 6:4), and we rose with him (compare Colossians 2:12).

As for what is recorded about the burial, the tomb, and the one who buried him, we shall expound it more fittingly and at greater length elsewhere, where these are our chief subject. For now it is enough to mention the clean linen cloth in which the pure body of Jesus had to be wrapped (Matthew 27:59), and the new tomb “which” Joseph “had hewn in the rock” (Matthew 27:60), “where no one had yet lain” (Luke 23:53), or, as John says, “in which no one had yet been placed” (John 19:41). Consider whether the agreement of the three evangelists can move anyone. They took care to record that the tomb was quarried or hewn in rock (Matthew 27:60; Mark 15:46; Luke 23:53), so that whoever examines the meaning of what is written may see something worth reflecting on about these things too, and about the newness of the tomb, which Matthew and John relate, and about no dead body having been there, as Luke and John say.

For he was not like the rest of the dead: even in death he showed signs of life, the water and the blood (John 19:34), and was, if I may call him so, a new kind of corpse. It was right, then, that he should be placed in a new and clean tomb, so that, just as his birth was purer than every birth, because he was born not from intercourse but from a virgin, so his burial too might have purity. This purity is shown through the symbol of his body being laid in a new tomb, one not built of gathered stones with no natural unity, but standing in a single rock, united throughout, quarried and hewn.

The interpretation of these things, and the ascent from what is recorded to have happened to the realities that the events signified, one could expound in a greater and more divine way, setting out such matters more fittingly in a work given to them. As for the literal sense, one might explain it this way too: it was fitting for one who had decided to endure being hung on a stake to keep what followed consistent with that purpose too, so that, having been taken down as a man because he had died as a man, he might also be buried as a man.

Moreover, suppose it had been written in the Gospels that he vanished from the stake at once: Celsus and the unbelievers would have found fault with what was written, and would have brought a charge in this form too, saying: “Why ever did he vanish after the cross, and not contrive this before he suffered?” If, then, having learned from the Gospels that he did not vanish from the stake at once, they think they can find fault with the account for not inventing, as they demanded, that he vanished from the stake at once, but for relating the truth, is it not reasonable that they should also believe in his resurrection? And should they not believe that when he chose, at one time, “the doors being shut,” he “stood in the midst” of the disciples (John 20:19, 26), and at another, having given bread to two of his followers, at once “vanished from their sight” (Luke 24:31), after speaking certain words to them?
translator_notes: Text: ‘ἐν φιλῇ τῇ λέξει’ is a misprint or OCR slip for ‘ἐν ψιλῇ τῇ λέξει’ (in the bare wording); read as ‘ψιλῇ’. ‘εἰ γὰρ (συν)απεθάνομεν’: the edition supplies ‘συν’ in brackets; read with it, matching 2 Timothy 2:11. Galatians: ‘Χριστῷ συνεσταύρωμαι’ ends Greek verse 2:19 in critical editions but stands at 2:20 in English Bibles; cited as Galatians 2:20. Galatians 6:14: Origen reads ‘τοῦ κυρίου μου’ (my Lord) where the NT text has ‘ἡμῶν’ (our); rendered as Origen quotes. ‘δι᾿ οὗ’ rendered ‘through whom’ (it may also be ‘through which’, the cross). ‘the righteous man says’ (τὸν δίκαιον λέγειν) = Paul in Philippians 3:10; ‘συμμορφιζόμενος’ rendered ‘being conformed’. ‘καὶ συνανέστημεν αὐτῷ’ (and we rose with him) stands outside the quotation marks in the edition; it is Origen’s continuation, echoing Romans 6:4-5 and Colossians 2:12 (‘buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him’); cited with ‘compare’. ‘σκόλοψ’ (stake) is Celsus’s word, kept as ‘stake’; ‘σταυρός’ (cross) is kept as ‘cross’. ‘καθαρὰ σινδών’ (Matthew 27:59) and ‘τὸ καθαρὸν σῶμα’ use the same adjective; rendered ‘clean linen cloth’ and ‘pure body’, and ‘καινῷ καὶ καθαρῷ μνημείῳ’ as ‘new and clean tomb’. Tomb quotations: ‘ὃ ἐλατόμησε τῇ πέτρᾳ’ = Matthew 27:60 (NT ‘ἐν τῇ πέτρᾳ’); ‘οὗ οὐκ ἦν οὔπω οὐδεὶς κείμενος’ = Luke 23:53; ‘ἐν ᾧ οὐδέπω οὐδεὶς ἐτέθη’ = John 19:41 (NT ‘ἦν τεθειμένος’). The ‘three evangelists’ who record the rock-cut tomb are Matthew (27:60), Mark (15:46) and Luke (23:53, ‘λαξευτῷ’); Origen does not name them, so the combined citation sits beside that clause. ‘ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, καινὸν... νεκρόν’ rendered ‘if I may call him so, a new kind of corpse’ (‘kind of’ added only to make the English idiom work; the Greek is ‘a new corpse’). ‘ἔδει’ rendered ‘It was right’. ‘λογάδες λίθοι’ = gathered/unhewn stones. ‘κατὰ τὸν κρίναντα... ἦν’ rendered ‘it belonged to him who had decided’; ‘τῇ ὑποθέσει’ rendered ‘that purpose’. The question ‘Why ever did he vanish after the cross...’ is a hypothetical objection Origen puts in Celsus’s mouth, not a quotation from the True Doctrine; set in double quotation marks as direct speech. ‘ἐγκαλεῖν οἴονται τῷ λόγῳ’: rendered ‘the account’ (the Gospel narrative). The closed doors: John 20:19 and 20:26 both read ‘τῶν θυρῶν κεκλεισμένων’ and ‘ἔστη εἰς τὸ μέσον’ (Origen ‘ἐν μέσῳ’). ‘δυσὶ τῶν γνωρίμων’ rendered ‘two of his followers’ (lit. acquaintances, disciples known to him). The final rhetorical question is split into two English questions; no clause is added: ‘καὶ ὡς βουληθεὶς...’ depends on ‘πιστεῦσαι’, so the second question repeats ‘believe’. Reviewer: in ‘ἐγκαλεῖν οἴονται τῷ λόγῳ’ the λόγος is the subject of ‘μὴ πλασαμένῳ ... ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀληθὲς ἱστορήσαντι’, so it is rendered ‘the account’ rather than ‘the word’.

title: Jesus did not hide, and Celsus contradicts himself
english: On what grounds has Celsus’s Jew said that Jesus was in hiding? For he says of him: “Who, sent as a messenger, ever hides himself when he ought to announce what he has been commanded?” Yet the one who said to those seeking to arrest him, “Day after day I was in the temple, teaching openly, and you did not seize me” (Mark 14:49; compare Matthew 26:55; John 18:20), was not hiding.

As for the next point, which Celsus repeats, we have answered it once and will be content with what we said before. For above we have also written a reply to this: “Or did he, while he was disbelieved in the body, preach freely to all, but, when he could have produced strong faith by rising from the dead, show himself secretly to one little woman alone and to his own band of followers?”

But it is not even true that he appeared to one little woman alone. For it is written in the Gospel according to Matthew: “After the sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake; for an angel of the Lord came down from heaven, approached and rolled away the stone” (Matthew 28:1–2). And a little later Matthew says: “And behold, Jesus met them” (clearly, the Marys mentioned before), “saying, ‘Greetings.’ And they came up, took hold of his feet and worshiped him” (Matthew 28:9).

An answer has also been given to “So when he was being punished he was seen by all, but when he had risen, by one,” when we offered our defense on the point that he was not seen by all. And now too we will say that what was human in him was visible to all, but what was more divine in him (I mean not what consists in a relation to something else, but what is so by its own distinguishing character) was not open to all to receive.

Notice also how Celsus at once contradicts himself. Thus, having said just before that he appeared secretly to one little woman and to his own band of followers, he immediately adds: “So when he was being punished he was seen by all, but when he had risen, by one, whereas the opposite ought to have happened.” Let us hear what he thinks ought to have happened. It was the opposite of his being seen by all when punished and by one when risen; for, so far as his own wording goes, he wanted something both impossible and unreasonable: that when punished he should be seen by one, but when risen, by all. Or how will you explain “whereas the opposite ought to have happened”?
translator_notes: Celsus’s words are marked in double quotation marks as Origen frames them: the messenger question; the earlier objection Origen recalls (‘Or did he...’); ‘So when he was being punished... by one’; and the closing ‘whereas the opposite ought to have happened’ (οὗπερ ἐχρῆν τοὐναντίον). πρὸς τὸ οὐ πᾶσιν ἑωρᾶτο (‘on the point that he was not seen by all’) names the topic of Origen’s own earlier defense, so it is left unquoted rather than attributed to Celsus. Celsus plays on ἄγγελος/ἀγγέλλειν; rendered ‘messenger... announce’. The staged text reads ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ ἱερῷ, an obvious dittography; translated once. The temple saying is a conflation: ἤμην... ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ διδάσκων καὶ οὐκ ἐκρατήσατέ με matches Mark 14:49; καθ’ ἡμέραν and the setting match Matthew 26:55 (ἐκαθεζόμην); παρρησίᾳ comes from John 18:20; Luke 22:53 is a further parallel. Origen’s Matthew 28:1-2 lacks δέ after ὀψέ and has Μαρία for Μαριάμ; otherwise it agrees with the NT text. At Matthew 28:9 he has ὁ Ἰησοῦς with the article. ὀψὲ σαββάτων rendered ‘After the sabbath’ (it can also mean ‘late on the sabbath’). γύναιον is a diminutive, kept as ‘little woman’ because Celsus uses it to belittle. θιασῶται, members of a religious band, rendered ‘band of followers’. The parenthesis on ‘relation’ versus ‘differentia’ uses Stoic categories (πρός τί πως ἔχοντα versus κατὰ διαφοράν): Origen distinguishes what is said of Christ in relation to others from what he is by his own distinctive character; rendered by sense, without adding a subject. The ‘earlier’ answers point back to Origen’s replies earlier in Book 2 to the ‘one woman’ and ‘not seen by all’ objections; no chapter numbers added.

title: Who sent Jesus, and why
english: Jesus also taught us who it was that sent him, in the words “No one has known the Father except the Son” (Matthew 11:27; compare Luke 10:22), and in “No one has ever seen God; and he who is indeed the only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known” (John 1:18). It was he who, speaking of God, declared to his true disciples what concerns God; and since we find traces of this in the Scriptures, we have starting points for speaking about God. In one place we hear, “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5); in another, “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

Moreover, the purposes for which the Father sent him are countless. Let anyone who wishes learn them, partly from the prophets who proclaimed him beforehand, partly from the evangelists; and he will learn not a few things from the apostles as well, and above all from Paul. Further, he gives light to the godly and will punish sinners. Celsus did not see this when he wrote: “and to give light to the godly, and to have mercy on those who sin or who have repented.”
translator_notes: The chapter answers Celsus’s challenge about the sender implied in the messenger question of 2.70. Matthew 11:27 is quoted loosely (NT: οὐδὲ τὸν πατέρα τις ἐπιγινώσκει εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός; Luke 10:22: τίς ἐστιν ὁ πατὴρ εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός). John 1:18 is quoted with the reading μονογενὴς θεός and an added emphatic καὶ... γε ὤν (‘he who is indeed’), kept. 1 John 1:5 and John 4:24 agree with the NT apart from word order. ‘God is spirit’ is lowercase because it names God’s nature, not the Holy Spirit. κολάσει is taken as the future of κολάζω (‘will punish’), parallel to φωταγωγεῖ; it could be read as the dative noun (‘by punishment’), which would not change the sense much. The closing words are Celsus’s, quoted as Origen gives them: future participles of purpose (‘to give light... to have mercy’); ἢ μεταγνόντας rendered ‘or who have repented’. Origen’s point is that Celsus mentions light and mercy but leaves out punishment. The fuller context of Celsus’s sentence is not given here; no connective has been supplied, and the staged text may be damaged at this point.

title: The voice from heaven was heard only by some
english: After this he says: “If he wished to escape notice, why was the voice from heaven heard proclaiming him Son of God? But if he did not wish to escape notice, why was he punished, or why did he die?” By this he thinks he is exposing a disagreement in what is written about him. He does not see that Jesus wished neither that everything about him should be known to all, to anyone at all, nor that everything concerning himself should remain hidden.

At any rate, the voice from heaven that proclaimed him to be the Son of God and said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), is not recorded to have been within the hearing of the crowds, as Celsus’s Jew supposed. Moreover, the voice from the cloud on the very high mountain was heard only by those who had gone up with him (Matthew 17:1–5; compare Mark 9:2–7; Luke 9:28–35). For the divine voice is of such a kind that it is heard only by those whom the speaker wishes to hear it. I do not yet add that the voice of God recorded in Scripture is by no means struck air, or a stroke of air, or whatever else it is called in the treatises on voice, and that for this reason it is heard by a hearing higher and more divine than the hearing of the senses. And whenever the speaker wishes his voice not to be audible to all, the one who “has” the higher “ears” (Matthew 13:9) hears God, while the one whose soul’s hearing has been deafened does not perceive God speaking.

So much in answer to “Why was the voice from heaven heard proclaiming him Son of God?” As for “If he did not wish to escape notice, why was he punished, or why did he die?”, what we have said at length above about his passion is enough.
translator_notes: Celsus’s two-part dilemma is in double quotation marks, and Origen repeats both halves at the end. ‘Son of God’ is capitalised because it reports the Christian claim about Christ. Matthew 3:17 is quoted exactly (ηὐδόκησα); Mark 1:11 and Luke 3:22 have ‘you are’. ‘The very high mountain’ renders Origen’s superlative ὑψηλοτάτῳ (Matthew 17:1 and Mark 9:2 have ὄρος ὑψηλόν); the voice from the cloud is Matthew 17:5. ‘Struck air’ (ἀὴρ πεπληγμένος) and ‘stroke of air’ (πληγὴ ἀέρος) are standard philosophical definitions of voice (Stoic and earlier); no source added inline. οὐδέπω δὲ λέγω ὅτι οὐ πάντως is taken as ‘I do not yet add that... is by no means’, a statement Origen holds back for now; οὐ πάντως could also be read ‘not necessarily’. The clause beginning διόπερ is taken as part of what is held back. ‘Has ears’ alludes to the Gospel saying ‘he who has ears, let him hear’ (Matthew 13:9; also Matthew 11:15; Mark 4:9); cited at Matthew 13:9. ‘At length above’ refers to Origen’s earlier discussion of the passion in Book 2.

title: He had already called all to the light
english: After this Celsus’s Jew sets out as a consequence what does not follow. For from “He wished, by the punishments he suffered, to teach us to despise even death,” it does not follow that “after rising from the dead he should openly call all to the light and teach why he had come down.” For he had called all to the light earlier, saying, “Come, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

And why he had come down is recorded in the discourses he delivered at length: in the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–12) and in what is proclaimed after them, in parables, and in his conversations with the scribes and Pharisees. And in the Gospel according to John are set out the things he taught, which show the grandeur of Jesus’ speech, a grandeur not of phrasing but of substance. And it is clear from the Gospels that “his word was with authority” (Luke 4:32; compare Matthew 7:28–29), at which they marveled.
translator_notes: Celsus’s two clauses are put in double quotation marks: the premise he grants (‘He wished... to teach us to despise even death’) and the conclusion he draws (‘after rising... he should openly call all to the light’). The ‘us’ is the Christians’ claim as Celsus’s Jew reports it; kept. καί before θανάτου is rendered ‘even death’. Matthew 11:28 is quoted without πρός με (‘to me’); rendered as Origen has it. ‘What is proclaimed after them’ refers to the rest of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:13-7:27); only the Beatitudes are cited inline. The conversations with the scribes and Pharisees are too general for a single citation. In ‘And in the Gospel according to John...’, τὸ κατὰ Ἰωάννην εὐαγγέλιον stands without a construing verb and is taken as setting the frame; παριστάντα (neuter plural) agrees with ὅσα ἐδίδαξεν, so it is the things taught that show the grandeur (‘which show’). ὅσα is rendered ‘the things he taught’, not ‘all that he taught’, to avoid a claim of completeness the Greek does not make. μεγαλοφωνία (‘grandeur of speech’) with ‘not in words but in realities’ is rendered ‘not of phrasing but of substance’. ‘His word was with authority’ matches Luke 4:32 exactly.

title: Israel disbelieved God even when he was present
english: To all this Celsus’s Jew adds: “These points, then, we have drawn for you from your own writings, and for them we need no other witness; for you contradict yourselves.” But we have shown that, in conflict with our writings, the Gospels, much nonsense has been talked in the Jew’s speeches, whether addressed to Jesus or to us. And I do not think he has proved how we contradict ourselves; he only thinks so.

And since his Jew adds to this, “In short, O most high and heavenly one, what god, when present among men, is disbelieved?”, we must say to him that even according to the law of Moses God is recorded to have been most clearly present with the Hebrews, not only in the signs and wonders in Egypt (Exodus 7:3), and further in the crossing of the Red Sea (Exodus 14:21–29) and the pillar “of fire” and the cloud of light (Exodus 13:21–22), but also when the Ten Commandments were proclaimed to the whole people (Exodus 20:1–17; Deuteronomy 5:4–22); and yet he was disbelieved by those who knew these things. For if they had believed what was seen and heard, they would not have made a calf (Exodus 32:1–6), nor “exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass” (Psalm 106:20), nor said to one another about the calf, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 32:4).

And consider whether it is not in keeping with the same people both to have disbelieved, long ago, such great marvels and so many manifestations of God throughout the whole wilderness, as is written in the law of the Jews, and, at the extraordinary coming of Jesus, not to be won over by the words he spoke with authority (compare Matthew 7:29) and by the marvels he did in the sight of all the people.
translator_notes: Celsus’s words are marked: the Jew’s summing-up (‘These points... you contradict yourselves’) and the mocking question ‘In short, O most high and heavenly one, what god... is disbelieved?’ ‘god’ is lowercase there because Celsus speaks of a god in general; ‘God’ is capitalised where Origen means the God of Israel. ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ὑμῖν ἐκ τῶν ὑμετέρων συγγραμμάτων has no verb; ‘we have drawn for you’ supplies the sense. περιπίπτετε ἑαυτοῖς (‘you fall foul of yourselves’) rendered ‘you contradict yourselves’, and the same in Origen’s reply. εἴτε πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν εἴτε πρὸς ἡμᾶς is rendered ‘whether addressed to Jesus or to us’: Celsus’s Jew first speaks to Jesus himself and then to Jewish believers, so πρός marks the addressee here, not hostility. Psalm 106:20 is LXX Psalm 105:20 (ἠλλάξαντο τὴν δόξαν αὐτῶν ἐν ὁμοιώματι μόσχου ἔσθοντος χόρτον); Origen has ἑαυτῶν and ἐσθίοντος; ‘calf’ follows the LXX μόσχος (the Hebrew has ‘ox’). ‘These are your gods, O Israel...’ is Exodus 32:4 (repeated at 32:8); σε is a supplement in the staged text, kept. The staged text splits κατεσκεύασαν across a space; read as one word. ‘Signs and wonders in Egypt’ is cited at Exodus 7:3, where the phrase is used; the plagues themselves run Exodus 7-12. ‘The cloud of light’ is taken as the pillar of cloud of Exodus 13:21-22. Disbelief ‘throughout the whole wilderness’ recalls passages such as Numbers 14:11 and Psalm 78 (LXX 77); not cited inline because no single text is quoted. ‘With authority’ echoes Matthew 7:29 (ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων), marked ‘compare’.

title: Unbelief at both beginnings
english: And I think this is enough for anyone who wishes to show that the unbelief of the Jews toward Jesus was consistent with what was recorded about the people from the beginning. For to the Jew in Celsus who says, “What god, when present among men, is disbelieved, and that when he appears to those who are hoping for him? Or why ever is he not recognized by those who have long been expecting him?”, I would say this: Are you willing, sirs, to answer our questions? Which mighty works seem greater to you, so far as your own judgment goes: those in Egypt and in the wilderness, or those which we said Jesus did among you? If in your view those are greater than these, is it not plain at once that despising the lesser also fits the character of those who disbelieved the greater? For this is what is supposed about the things we tell of Jesus.

But if the mighty works told of Jesus are said to be equal to those recorded by Moses, what is strange in what has happened to a people that disbelieved at the beginning of both orders of things? For the beginning of the giving of the law came in the time of Moses, and in it the sins of the unbelievers and the sinners among you are recorded; and we acknowledge that the beginning of a second giving of law and of a second covenant came about with Jesus. And by your unbelief toward Jesus you bear witness that you are sons of those who in the wilderness disbelieved the divine manifestations (compare Matthew 23:31). And what our Savior said will be said to you also, who disbelieved him: “So you are witnesses, and you approve the deeds of your fathers” (Luke 11:48). And in you the prophecy is fulfilled that says, “Your life will be hanging before your eyes, and you will not believe your life” (Deuteronomy 28:66). For you did not believe the Life that had come to dwell among the human race.
translator_notes: Celsus’s question (‘What god... long been expecting him?’) is in double quotation marks. Origen’s imagined reply to the Jew runs from ‘Are you willing, sirs’ to the end; it is left unquoted, introduced by ‘I would say this:’, so that double quotation marks stay reserved for Celsus’s words and Scripture. ὅτι before βούλεσθε is taken as introducing direct speech (it could be a corrupt τί, ‘What will you answer...?’). ὦ οὗτοι, a direct, slightly brusque address, rendered ‘sirs’. τοῦτο γὰρ ὑπολαμβάνεται (‘this is supposed’) is impersonal: the Jews suppose Jesus’ works to be the lesser; kept impersonal. τί ξένον ἀπήντησε is a rhetorical question expecting ‘nothing’; rendered ‘what is strange in what has happened’. κατ᾿ ἀμφοτέρας τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν πραγμάτων rendered ‘at the beginning of both orders of things’ (the Mosaic lawgiving and the new covenant). ἡμῖν with ὁμολογεῖται taken as ‘by us’ (‘we acknowledge’); κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν, parallel to ἐπὶ Μωϋσέως, rendered ‘with Jesus’. ‘Sons of those who...’ echoes Matthew 23:31 (μαρτυρεῖτε ἑαυτοῖς ὅτι υἱοί ἐστε τῶν φονευσάντων τοὺς προφήτας), marked ‘compare’. Luke 11:48 is quoted exactly. Deuteronomy 28:66 LXX has the singular (ἡ ζωή σου... ἀπέναντι τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν σου... καὶ οὐ πιστεύσεις τῇ ζωῇ σου); Origen gives plurals, ἐνώπιον and οὐ μὴ πιστεύσητε; rendered as he quotes it. The verse was read in the early Church as a prophecy of Christ hanging on the cross, and Origen’s last sentence plays on it; ‘Life’ is capitalised there because it names Christ, while the quoted verse keeps lowercase ‘life’ so that the play stays visible.

title: The woes of Jesus and the woes of the prophets
english: Celsus, bringing the Jew on as a speaking character, could find nothing to put into his mouth in his discourse that could not be thrown back at him from the writings of the Law and the Prophets. For he finds fault with Jesus, saying this about him: “He threatens and reviles rashly whenever he says, ‘Woe to you’ (compare Matthew 23:13–29; Luke 6:24–26) and ‘I tell you beforehand.’ For in these words he openly admits that he cannot persuade, which would not happen to a god, nor even to a sensible man.”

But see whether these charges do not plainly turn back on the Jew. For in the writings of the Law and the Prophets God threatens and reviles when he pronounces woes no less than those in the gospel. Such are these words in Isaiah: “Woe to those who join house to house and bring field near to field” (Isaiah 5:8); and “Woe to those who rise early in the morning and pursue strong drink” (Isaiah 5:11); and “Woe to those who drag their sins along as with a long rope” (Isaiah 5:18); and “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20); and “Woe to the strong among you, who drink wine” (Isaiah 5:22). And you could find countless others. And how are the words “Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins, evil seed, lawless sons” (Isaiah 1:4), and what follows, not like the threats he speaks of? These words are followed by threats so great that they are no less than those he says Jesus spoke. Or is it not a threat, and a great one, that says: “Your land is desolate, your cities burned with fire; strangers devour your country in your presence, and it is laid waste, overthrown by foreign peoples” (Isaiah 1:7)? And how are there not insults against the people in Ezekiel as well, where the Lord says to the prophet, “You dwell in the midst of scorpions” (Ezekiel 2:6)?

Did you, then, Celsus, know what you were doing when you made the Jew say of Jesus that “he threatens and reviles rashly whenever he says, ‘Woe to you’ and ‘I tell you beforehand’”? Do you not see that the very things your Jew says in accusing Jesus could be said to him about God? For, by the Jew’s way of thinking, the God of the prophets is plainly found open to like charges, as one unable to persuade.

Further, to those who think that Celsus’s Jew is right to bring these charges against Jesus, I would say this on the point: a great many curses are written in Leviticus and Deuteronomy (see Leviticus 26:14–39; Deuteronomy 27:15–26; Deuteronomy 28:15–68). However the Jew defends them when he stands up for the Scripture, in that way, or even better, we will defend what are taken to be the insults and threats spoken by Jesus. And we shall be better able than the Jew to defend the Law of Moses itself, since we have been taught by Jesus to hear the writings of the Law with more understanding than he does. Yet the Jew too, if he sees the intent of the prophetic words, will be able to show that God does not threaten and revile rashly when he says “Woe” and “I tell you beforehand,” and how God would say such things for the conversion of human beings, things that Celsus thinks not even a sensible man would do. And Christians, who know one God, the same in the prophets and in the Lord, will show the good reason behind what are thought to be threats and what Celsus calls insults.

Let me also say a few words on this point to Celsus, who claims both to be a philosopher and to know our teachings. My good man, if Hermes in Homer says to Odysseus, “Why, unhappy man, do you go once more alone across the hilltops?” (Homer, Odyssey 10.281), you accept the defence that Homer’s Hermes speaks to Odysseus like this to turn him; for flattery and pleasing words belong to the Sirens, beside whom lies “a heap of bones” (Homer, Odyssey 12.45), and who say, “Come here, much-praised Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans” (Homer, Odyssey 12.184). But if my prophets, and Jesus himself, say “Woe” and what you take for insults to turn their hearers, is nothing then wisely arranged for the hearers by such words, and does he not apply such speech to them as a healing remedy of Paeon?

Unless, perhaps, you would have God, or one who shares in the divine nature, when he speaks with human beings, look only to what belongs to his own nature and is worthy of himself, and no longer consider what is fitting to declare to the people who are being guided and led by his word, and to speak with each according to that person’s own character. And how is it not laughable that this inability to persuade should be said of Jesus, when it applies equally not only to the Jew, who has many such things in his prophecies, but also to the Greeks? Among them each of those who won great fame for wisdom was unable to persuade those who plotted against him, or the judges, or the accusers, to cease from wickedness and to travel by way of philosophy toward virtue.
translator_notes: Celsus’s words (Koetschau’s quoted fragment) taken as running from ‘He threatens’ through ‘nor even to a sensible man’. The anarthrous θεός in the Jew’s mouth is rendered ‘a god’ (generic); Origen then turns the charge onto ὁ θεός of the prophets, rendered ‘God’. ‘Woe to you’ is a clear allusion to the gospel woes (Matthew 23; Luke 6:24–26; also Luke 11:42–52); ‘I tell you beforehand’ (προλέγω ὑμῖν) has no exact gospel match (compare Matthew 24:25, Mark 13:23 προείρηκα; Galatians 5:21 προλέγω), so it is left uncited. Isaiah quotations follow the LXX (5:22 LXX οἱ ἰσχυροὶ ὑμῶν οἱ τὸν οἶνον πίνοντες; Origen’s ἰσχύοντες). Ezekiel 2:6 follows LXX wording. Curses in Leviticus and Deuteronomy are cited to the main curse passages (Leviticus 26:14–39; Deuteronomy 27:15–26; 28:15–68); this is a general reference, not a quotation. Staged text reads ἀπιλεῖ (read ἀπειλεῖ), ποιαῦτα (read τοιαῦτα), and a full stop after γραφῇ that breaks the sentence ‘about which as the Jew would defend ... so we shall defend’; translated as one sentence. Homer: Odyssey 10.281 (Origen’s τίπτ᾿ αὖ for the vulgate πῇ δὴ αὖτ᾿), 12.45, 12.184. Παιώνιον φάρμακον: Paeon is the physician of the gods in Homer. ‘one who shares in the divine nature’ may echo 2 Peter 1:4 (θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως) but the wording differs; uncited. ‘One God, the same in the prophets and in the Lord’ may recall Hebrews 1:1–2; uncited. τοῦ λόγου αὐτοῦ (‘his word’) kept lowercase: it may mean his speech or the divine Word; ambiguous. The Greek examples of sages unable to persuade judges and accusers point at Socrates without naming him. Reviewer: λοιδορέω/λοιδορία now rendered consistently as ‘revile’/’insults’ in both Celsus’s charge and Origen’s reply, so the reader sees the charge turned back in the same words. Second reviewer: κούφως rendered ‘rashly’ (thoughtlessly, with levity) wherever Celsus’s charge and Origen’s answer use it.

title: The resurrection and the demand to see
english: After this his Jew says, evidently in keeping with what Jews hold: “We hope, of course, to rise again in the body and to have eternal life, and that the one who is to be sent to us will be the pattern and pioneer of this, showing that it is not impossible for God to raise someone up together with the body.” Now we do not know whether the Jew would say that the Christ he expects shows in himself a pattern of the resurrection; but let it be so: let it be granted that he both thinks and says this. And we will answer the one who said that he had spoken to us out of our own writings: My good man, did you read the passages by which you suppose you can accuse us, but not go through those on the resurrection of Jesus, and on his being “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:18; compare Revelation 1:5)? Or, because you do not want these things to have been said, have they then not been said?

But since the Jew in Celsus still speaks of the resurrection of bodies and accepts it, I do not think this is the right moment to discuss the matter with one who both believes and says that there is a resurrection of bodies, whether he has worked out such a belief clearly in his own mind and can champion the doctrine well, or whether he cannot, but assents to the doctrine in a rather mythical way. Let that, then, be our answer to Celsus’s Jew.

And since after this he says, “Where is he, then, so that we may see and believe?” (compare Mark 15:32) we will say to him: Where, then, is he now who speaks in the prophets and who has worked wonders, so that we may see and believe that God has a portion?
