Or are you allowed to offer a defence for God’s not always appearing to the race of the Hebrews, while we are not granted the same defence concerning Jesus, who once rose again and persuaded his disciples of his own resurrection, and persuaded them so thoroughly that by what they suffer they show everyone that, with their eyes on eternal life and on the resurrection shown to them in word and in deed, they make light of all the hardships of this life?
translator_notes: ὁ Ἰουδαῖος αὐτῷ λέγει: αὐτῷ read as ‘his’ (Celsus’s) Jew, matching Origen’s usual ὁ παρ᾿ αὐτῷ Ἰουδαῖος; it could also mean ‘says to him’. ‘evidently in keeping with what Jews hold’ is Origen’s aside, not Celsus’s words; the quoted fragment runs from ‘We hope’ to ‘with the body’. ‘the firstborn from the dead’ matches Colossians 1:18 exactly (πρωτότοκος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν); Revelation 1:5 lacks ἐκ. The Jew’s claim to speak ‘out of our own writings’ refers back to his earlier statement in this book (around 2.74). μερίς ἐστι τοῦ θεοῦ rendered ‘that God has a portion’ (existential reading, no subject in the Greek); it likely recalls Israel as the Lord’s portion (Deuteronomy 32:9 LXX μερὶς κυρίου), but the allusion is not certain and is left uncited. ἅπαξ rendered ‘once’ (not ‘once for all’). Reviewer: ἵνα ἴδωμεν καὶ πιστεύσωμεν in the Jew’s demand is word for word the taunt at the cross in Mark 15:32 (John 6:30 adds σοι), so it is marked ‘compare’. πεμπόμενον is a present participle with future sense in context (‘will be the pattern’), hence ‘the one who is to be sent’. Second reviewer: μερίς sentence left for owner check against Koetschau’s apparatus.

title: Jewish unbelief and the calling of the Gentiles
english: After this the Jew says: “Or did he come down for this, that we might disbelieve?” To him it will be said: He did not come for this, to produce unbelief in the Jews; but knowing beforehand that it would come about, he foretold it, and he made use of the Jews’ unbelief for the calling of the Gentiles. For “through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles” (Romans 11:11). Of these Gentiles the Christ who speaks in the prophets says: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Psalm 18:43–44); and “I was found by those who did not seek me; I became manifest to those who did not ask for me” (Isaiah 65:1; compare Romans 10:20). And it is clear that the Jews also suffered punishment in this life, after they had done to Jesus what they did.

But if the Jews bring charges against us, let them answer this: “Wonderful indeed is God’s providence and kindness toward you, who are being punished and have been deprived of Jerusalem, of what is called the sanctuary, and of the most solemn worship!” For whatever they say in defence of God’s providence, we shall establish it more firmly and better, saying that God’s providence has been wonderful, since it made use of that people’s sin so that those from the Gentiles, “strangers to the covenants” (Ephesians 2:12) and aliens to the promises, might be called through Jesus into the kingdom of God.

The prophets also foretold this: that because of the sins of the Hebrew people God would choose not one nation but picked people from every quarter, and that, choosing “the foolish things of the world” (1 Corinthians 1:27), he would make the senseless nation (compare Deuteronomy 32:21) become versed in the divine words, with the kingdom of God taken from them and given to these (Matthew 21:43). For the present it is enough, out of many, to set down the prophecy about the calling of the Gentiles from the Song in Deuteronomy, which runs thus and is spoken in the person of the Lord: “For they made me jealous with what are no gods; they provoked me to anger with their idols; and I will make them jealous with what is no nation; with a senseless nation I will provoke them to anger” (Deuteronomy 32:21).
translator_notes: LXX renumbering: Psalm 17:44–45 LXX = Psalm 18:43–44 English (Hebrew 18:44–45); compare 2 Samuel 22:44–45. Isaiah 65:1 is also quoted at Romans 10:20; Origen’s order (εὑρέθην before ἐμφανής) follows Romans 10:20, not the LXX order. The Jew says κατῆλθεν (‘come down’); Origen answers with ἦλθεν (‘come’); kept distinct. Difficult sentence: λεγέτωσαν δ᾿ Ἰουδαῖοι, ἐὰν ἡμῖν ἐγκαλοῦντες φάσκωσιν. The quoted taunt is addressed to the Jews (ὑμῖν ... στερηθεῖσι τῆς Ἱερουσαλήμ), and Origen then answers ‘whatever they say in defence of God’s providence’, so the sense must be: if Jews accuse us, let them answer this taunt against themselves. Rendered by sense; the staged wording may be corrupt (a reading such as ἡμῶν ἐγκαλούντων would ease it) and should be checked against Koetschau’s apparatus. ‘strangers to the covenants’ quotes Ephesians 2:12 (ξένοι τῶν διαθηκῶν); ‘aliens to the promises’ paraphrases the same verse. ποιήσει τὸ ἀσύνετον ἔθνος γενέσθαι ἐν τοῖς θείοις λόγοις: γίνεσθαι ἐν taken as ‘be engaged in, become versed in’. ‘the kingdom of God taken from them and given to these’ is a clear allusion to Matthew 21:43. λογάδας = picked men, chosen ones. Deuteronomy 32:21 here has the plural ἐπ᾿ οὐ θεοῖς, rendered ‘what are no gods’.

title: No mere man could win the world
english: Then, as the conclusion to all of this, the Jew says about Jesus: “He, then, was a man, and such a man as the truth itself makes plain and the argument shows.” But I do not know whether a man who dared to sow throughout the whole world the worship of God and the teaching that come from him could, without God, do what he wishes and prove stronger than all who oppose the spread of his teaching: kings and governors, the Roman Senate, rulers everywhere, and the common people. And how could a human nature that had nothing higher in itself convert so great a multitude? It would be no wonder if these were only the sensible; but they include the most irrational too, people given over to their passions and, because of their unreason, all the harder to bring over to a more self-controlled life. But because Christ was the power of God and the wisdom of the Father (1 Corinthians 1:24), for this reason he has done these things and still does them, even though neither Jews nor Greeks wish it, who do not believe his word.

We, then, will not cease believing in God according to the precepts of Jesus Christ, and seeking to turn those who are blind about the worship of God, even if those who are truly blind revile us as blind, and those who beguile the people who agree with them, whether Jews or Greeks, accuse us of beguiling people. A fine kind of beguiling indeed, which makes people self-controlled instead of licentious, or at least advancing toward self-control; just instead of unjust, or advancing toward justice; wise instead of foolish, or on the road to wisdom; and brave and steadfast instead of cowardly, mean-spirited and unmanly, showing this above all in the struggles for piety toward God who created all things!

So Jesus Christ came, proclaimed beforehand not by one prophet but by all. And this too was a mark of Celsus’s ignorance: to make the Jewish character say that a single prophet had foretold the Christ. And since the Jew in Celsus has been brought on saying these things as though in keeping with his own law, and ended his speech somewhere about here, after saying other things not worth remembering, I too will end here the second book of what I have dictated in answer to his treatise. And, if God grants it and the power of Christ dwells in our soul, we shall try in the third to deal with what Celsus wrote next.
translator_notes: Celsus’s quoted words are only ‘He, then, was a man ... the argument shows’. ὁ λόγος δείκνυσιν beside αὐτὸ τὸ ἀληθές may play on the title of Celsus’s book (Ἀληθὴς Λόγος, ‘True Doctrine’); rendered ‘the argument’. ‘the power of God and the wisdom of the Father’ adapts 1 Corinthians 1:24 (θεοῦ δύναμιν καὶ θεοῦ σοφίαν), with ‘Father’ for the second θεοῦ. ‘proclaimed beforehand not by one prophet but by all’ may echo Acts 3:18, 24 (all the prophets), but no clear verbal match; uncited. The charge that Celsus’s Jew spoke of one prophet refers back to the Jew’s earlier words. βουκολέω (lit. ‘tend cattle’, hence ‘beguile, cheat’) rendered ‘beguile’ throughout to keep Origen’s play on βουκόλησις. The four virtues listed are the classical cardinal virtues (self-control, justice, wisdom, courage). τὸ δεύτερον = the second book of the reply; ὑπαγορευθέντων = dictated. Reviewer: the participles ἀλογωτάτων, τοῖς πάθεσιν ἐγκειμένων and χαλεπώτερον μετατιθεμένων are read as describing one group, not three.
